en: The Scripture of Great Compassion, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Dharma Code of the Great Assembly of Adornments from which All Bodhisattvas Are Born. Chapter One: The Dharma Code.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha—a place where the Buddhas of antiquity had dwelt and where the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power had established his presence;

it was a site of practice and a Dharma throne for which the assembly of bodhisattvas offered boundless praise. There, devas, nāgas, spirits, gandharvas, and others all took refuge and prostrated themselves in worship, as they proclaimed their roots of virtue and the majestic radiance of the Tathāgata throughout that buddha-field.
Bodhisattvas who aspire to and delight in the Dharma-gate, as well as devas and other beings, enter into immeasurable and limitless merit.

The Tathāgata, having practiced what he taught and attained equal and perfect enlightenment, turns the wondrous wheel of Dharma as the supreme leader, skillfully proclaiming and transforming others, and has attained mastery over all phenomena.
The Perfection of Deliverance: Clearly understanding the inclinations and dispositions of sentient beings, one observes their faculties and leads them to the other shore.

Being fully awakened to all things, one eliminates all hindrances; wherever one dwells, one performs the work of a Buddha without any worldly occupation, remaining steadfastly established in practice such that none can withstand it.

There was a great assembly of six million bhikṣus and all the people, who had extinguished the dust of desire and were free from all obscurations and hindrances; they were sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, practicing the profound and wondrous Dharma.

That from which they arise does not stem from perversion; they are supple and harmonious, fully endowed with dignified deportment and ritual propriety, and they draw near to the path of the Tathāgata, who is the benefactor of the great multitude.

The assembly of bodhisattvas was beyond measure or calculation; they practiced without obstruction, had attained definitive realization of universal wisdom, and possessed all-encompassing, swift, and penetrating insight.

Furthermore, these great bodhisattvas, with great kindness and great compassion, raised up clouds of Dharma and manifested flashes of lightning, raining down ambrosia to fully satisfy the long-standing hunger and thirst of sentient beings.
With a mind equal toward all, his resolve is like the earth; all false imaginings, attachments, and fetters have been cast away, as he joyfully bestows vast grace.

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are like the celestial palace of the sun, the abode of holy wisdom; its brilliant light shines everywhere, extinguishing the great darkness and illuminating the world, pointing out the path and proclaiming the roots of virtue.
Like a lotus flower in full bloom, he dries up the moisture of affection and love, sets his will deep as a pool, and establishes himself in right action.
Possessing great supernormal powers, he traverses the void, like the lunar palace illuminating the darkness of night as it moves through its course.

With an impartial mind toward all sentient beings, they cause them to attain their respective dispositions, such that none fail to rejoice; through skillful means and expedients, they provide benefit without harm, remaining unchanged in their commitment to the Way and its principles as they universally manifest their conduct.

Their resolve is as firm and immovable as Mount Sumeru; they constantly cultivate pure conduct and make offerings to the Triple Gem, remaining unshakable by any sensory realm and transcending all phenomena of the mundane world.

Though they may disparage or slander others, they manifest intimacy toward all buddha-fields; their spiritual radiance shines afar and their resolve is like the great ocean, for their vessel is vast and filled to the brim with the water of the Dharma.
Cultivating the bodhisattva practices, he is venerated by all sentient beings, like a lion or a sovereign, most honored among them.

He upholds the Four Noble Truths, harbors great compassion, and his mind yearns for loving-kindness and pity. Observing with serene stillness, his insights are universally manifest; regarding the profound and wondrous Dharma, he is without fear.

He vanquishes all non-Buddhists; throughout incalculable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he remains ultimately without obstruction. If a bodhisattva practices without weariness, all virtues will be fully perfected.

Their names were: the Bodhisattva Universal Vision of the Infinite; the Bodhisattva All-Seeing Array of All Lands Appearing Everywhere; the Bodhisattva Accomplished in the Tathāgata Lineage Without Regression; the Bodhisattva Who Manifests Dignified Conduct to Transform Multitudes and Demonstrates Absence of Anger; the Bodhisattva Banner of Immeasurable Eloquence with Transformed Sounds; the Bodhisattva King of the Accumulated Pure Golden Light and Majesty; the Bodhisattva Who Discerns Radiance and Resolves Sentences through Eloquence; and the Bodhisattva Born of Immeasurable Merit and Accumulated Parental Deeds—countless bodhisattvas of such a kind.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One proclaimed a Dharma door named "The Birth of All Bodhisattvas.

When sixteen years had passed since the Buddha attained Perfect Enlightenment, he saw that those of pure conduct were flourishing everywhere; beholding all the bodhisattvas gathered together, he desired to expound the Tathāgata’s treasury of dhāraṇī-dharmas, and the multitude of bodhisattvas arrived like clouds.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"I shall further increase the various practices of the bodhisattvas so that they may protect and establish the path of practice.

There was once a sutra that expounded the Gate of the Unsurpassed—namely, the infinite transformations performed by the Tathāgata—for the assembly of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, intended to cause them to enter the realm of the Tathāgata."
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of the Buddha’s sphere of activity, manifested the Tathāgata-samādhi-samāpatti.

As soon as the Buddha had entered this meditative absorption of the Buddha-sphere manifestation, a high seat spontaneously appeared in the space above, through the sublime power of the World-Benefactor.

Just as the great trichiliocosm Buddha-field is vast, lofty, and far-reaching—extending upward to the realm of desire and the formless realm—all is the correct practice of the Buddhas, brought forth through the transformative power of the Tathāgata’s merits.

The assembly of bodhisattvas, whose natures and conducts are pure, illumines the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions and gladdens the mental dispositions of immeasurable beings; there is not a single palace of the devas, nāgas, or spirits that does not receive their radiance.

He invited the bodhisattvas from the ten directions to praise his immeasurable renown and virtues; they all sat within countless multi-storied pavilions adorned with lattices. Some had walls made of purple gold, eaves and windows of *śrīgarbha* jewels, doors and casements of agate, balustrades of *candragarbha* jewels, door-panels of *vimalaprabhāsa* jewels, multi-storied galleries of *samantaprabhāsa* jewels, and enclosures made of every kind of precious gem.

They hung strings of pearls and erected various banners and streamers; they lit lamps and suspended silk canopies. They used the finest sandalwood for plastering the walls, and they burned extraordinary, wondrous sandalwood, pleasing and manifold fragrances, as well as famous incenses from across the great ocean that bring transcendence.
Various jewels produced by dragons and diverse kinds of flowers were scattered upon it, while rows of trees made of many precious gems stood in orderly succession.

The various incense burners of precious materials were lofty and exquisite; their radiant adornments pervaded the Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions, pure, wonderful, and gladdening the hearts of men, all appearing universally within the high seat.

Those lion thrones were beyond counting; hundreds of thousands of millions of them appeared spontaneously, high, resplendent, vast, and lofty, which all admired and delighted in, none failing to rejoice.

Within all the regional divisions of these four great domains, forty thousand palaces naturally arose, exceedingly tall and vast. Furthermore, their railings were forty-nine zhang high and twenty li wide; *yāma-prabhāsa* pearls, *vimala* jewels, and *brahma-śrī* jewels were suspended from the banners and canopies, while the latticed pavilions were adorned with purple gold and emitted natural sounds.
From the ground upward to the high seats, which were both lofty and sublime, they were spontaneously transformed and manifested without any creator.

In this way, the transformations arising within these four continents, as well as those in the trichiliocosm, were likewise; all four continents were equal and without distinction, with infinite palaces all arising spontaneously.
At that time, the World-Honored One, peaceful and serene, arose from samādhi; immediately, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and a great radiance shone everywhere without exception.

The Buddha was surrounded by bodhisattvas, disciples, and a vast retinue; above them, the devas sang praises of his merit and rained down various flowers. Celestial garments were scattered to cover the void, and manifold famous incenses were burned. Musical instruments gathered in the sky resounded spontaneously, and all the buddha-fields of the ten directions trembled naturally.

Having illuminated immeasurable Buddha-lands, the Buddha’s great supernormal powers manifested infinite transformations; his realm was boundless, his majestic spiritual power limitless, his holy light infinite, and his moving influence unfathomable. Then, on Vulture Peak, he suddenly vanished from sight.
Accompanied by the great assembly—gods, nāgas, spirits, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas—they attended upon the World-Honored One, desiring to hear the Dharma.

Furthermore, the Four Heavenly Kings, together with the various devas, seeing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was about to go forth to preach the Dharma, joined their palms above them and rained down celestial flowers as an offering to the Great Sage,
praising him in verse: "The majestic radiance of the sun and moon, And the natural brilliance of the luminous pearl—
The Buddha’s light completely eclipses them all, Extinguishing the three evil realms."
The light pervaded the Buddha-fields, transcending Mount Sumeru and the Iron Ring Mountains;
all took refuge in the Most Victorious One, each harboring boundless joy.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, together with the various devas, having each praised the World-Honored One with these verses, were filled with immeasurable delight and veneration.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the Trāyastriṃśa gods, seeing the Great Sage intending to proceed to the great hall, went to the place of the high seat and presented offerings. They rained down celestial incense, scattering it over the Buddha, and with palms joined, they praised him in verse, saying:
“With spiritual power, you have reached the ultimate; You manifest peerless transformations.
Appearing throughout billions of buddha-fields, The Most Victorious One has risen like the sun.”
"Having subdued all realms of Māra, universally adorned with pure virtues, his supernormal powers are sovereign; I prostrate to the Peerless One.
After the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven had praised the Buddha with these verses, they attended upon the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Heavenly King Gambhīraśubha, seeing the Buddha wishing to proceed to his palace’s high seat, rained down celestial robes and, with palms joined, praised the Buddha:
“Abiding securely in immeasurable wisdom, Universally knowing the nature of all sentient beings, Unattached like empty space,
You have distanced yourself from the affairs of the three worlds.”
With single-minded focus they enter into all modes of conduct and fully understand the natures of all sentient beings;
therefore, they are worthy of veneration and are looked up to and honored throughout the three periods of time.
When King Yama had finished praising the Buddha with these verses, he attended upon the World-Honored One.

The King of Tuṣita Heaven, together with the various devas, seeing the World-Honored One about to proceed to the great high seat in the palace, rained down precious jewels as an offering to the Buddha and, with palms joined, praised him, saying:
"You proclaim and expound the meaning of the sūtras; You observe them as being like illusions or a mirage.
Since they possess no written words, How could there be images of thought or mind?"
"Out of compassion for sentient beings, the Buddha praised the honored Dharma;
by taking refuge in the knowledge that phenomena are of their own nature, one excels in understanding the absence of self.
When the King of the Tuṣita Heaven had finished praising the Buddha with these verses, he attended upon the World-Honored One.

The Deva King Nirmāṇarati, together with his celestial retinue, saw the World-Honored One approaching the great high throne in the palace. Raining down precious necklaces as an offering upon the Buddha, he joined his palms and praised him, saying:
“Manifesting the Dharma-body, Which is like empty space throughout the ten directions;
The Most Victorious One appears in physical form, Out of compassion, bringing forth transformation.”
"The Dharma you proclaim has no form; your supreme conduct is universally impartial.
You pay homage to the Dharma of natural wisdom, clearly discerning the meaning of all things.
Thus did the gods of the Heaven of No-Strife (*Tuṣita*) praise the Buddha in verse, attending upon the World-Honored One.

The Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas and the various heavenly beings, seeing the World-Honored One about to proceed to the high seat in the palace lecture hall, rained down celestial jewels as an offering to the Buddha, and with palms joined, they praised him, saying:
“With precepts free from all defilements, You stand established in purity;
Exhorting and transforming those who are most honored, Your concentrated mind is immovable.”
With wisdom beyond compare, like the ocean free from anger and resentment,
having transcended both beginning and end, I bow my head to the one who has attained mastery.
Upon the soles of the divine feet, the mark of the wheel stands naturally.
Manifesting the cultivation of loving-kindness and compassion, taking this as the foremost from the very beginning;
having liberated oneself from the three paths, one bows to the Buddha’s virtuous conduct.
It is because of this sorrowful compassion that one increases [one's practice] with equanimity.
Taking tranquility as its flower, liberation constitutes its fruit;
like the king of bees, he exhorts and transforms his retinue.
Abiding peacefully like a lotus, I bow my head to him in prostration.
Well-established in the prohibitive precepts, Abiding on the ground of peace and truth;
By the power of his diligence, He excels beyond reach by others.
I bow my head to the one of true nature, Most venerable and immovable.
Compassionate pity is his purity; the site of enlightenment has become radiant.
Wisdom is free from defilement, and majestic brilliance dispels the darkness.
Countless hundreds of sentient beings all together take refuge and bow their heads in homage.
Thus he attains ultimate awakening; with head bowed, I pay homage to the Great Sage.
The traces of his gate of liberation resound through the void;
his wisdom gallops across the far reaches, and his radiance illuminates the ten directions.
The flowers of sentient beings number in the hundreds of thousands; you cause them to be opened and understood, awakening them so they may leave behind defilement.
I bow my head to the One Who Is Unattached. Examining him, there is no peer; how could anyone surpass him?
Seeking him throughout the ten directions, the Teacher cannot be found.
His meritorious achievements are exceedingly numerous; he is fully endowed with every virtue.
Now I offer my praise, yet his resolve remains insatiable.
The asuras, the nāgas, and the sovereign lords all turn to him in homage;
countless devas and humans alike join in praising his virtue.
"The fame he extols is vast and inconceivable;
I raise my voice in praise and pay homage to the World-Honored One, whose meritorious deeds are spread everywhere.
Having praised the Buddha with these verses, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas attended upon the World-Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One, manifesting transformations through the immeasurable realm of a Buddha, moved by the shared admiration of hundreds of thousands of devas and humans, proceeded to the precious high seat.
At that time, as soon as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, ascended the high seat, the palaces of the four quarters all came to know and see him;
likewise, throughout the entire trichiliocosm, in all places within the four quarters, it was the same—all came to know and see him.
At that time, the Great Sage sat upon a lion throne, a high seat protected by three thousand jewels; the assembly of bodhisattvas and the great disciples likewise sat down in succession.

Thereupon, the Great Sage entered a samādhi called the "Unobstructed Dharma-Gate Recreation," and through this meditative absorption, from every single pore of his holy body, he emitted rays of light as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Their majestic brilliance illuminated all the Buddha-worlds of the eastern direction, reaching everywhere without exception;
it was likewise so for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, illuminating all realms completely and without omission.

The lands of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions were illuminated; accordingly, in all those lands, the diligent suffering and tortures of every hell were entirely stilled, animals were liberated, and hungry ghosts attained peace.
At that time, the various afflictions of all sentient beings were eliminated; they were no longer deluded by lust, anger, ignorance, or folly, and were free from the hardships of defilement and toil.
They looked upon one another with hearts of loving-kindness, regarding each other as fathers, mothers, elder brothers, younger brothers, sons, or even as their own bodies, without any distinction.
The Tathāgata’s radiance illuminated all the bodhisattvas, and by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the assembly of bodhisattvas spoke these verses amidst the brilliant light:
“With immeasurable power of diligence, Vast and universal, they dwell nowhere;
Furthermore, through the power of their ardent exertion, They transcend billions of kalpas.”
The power of the Ten Strengths flows abroad, reaching everywhere throughout the ten directions;
the majestic radiance of Śākyamuni shines extensively upon all things.
Those who seek the meaning of the Dharma therefore travel to hundreds of thousands of lands.
Having paid homage to the Buddha and listened to the sublime Dharma, they have arrived in this world of endurance.
Those among the bodhisattvas of the ten directions who dwell in the Tuṣita Heaven—
may they all observe this light as the Buddha unfolds it to bring peace to sentient beings.
The hosts of Māra, the dust-like followers of heterodox paths, are subdued by the power of his diligence;
like the lotus emerging from the sun, he shines upon the ten directions like Mount Sumeru.
His body radiates boundlessly, its brilliance pervading all things.
I go there to hear the Honored One’s Dharma, as he turns the most supreme wheel of the Dharma.
Today, peerless and incomparable, he proclaims this matchless sutra;
out of compassion for sentient beings, the One of Ten Powers thus turns the Honored Wheel of the Dharma.
"Today this great assembly has gathered; such a vast and universal gathering is difficult to encounter.
Those with firm faith who wish to see the Buddha should now proceed to the Sahā world.
At that time, the light universally announced this to all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions.

Having spoken these verses, he shook the buddha-lands, brought peace to sentient beings, and illuminated the entire dharma-realm. He purified all realms of worldly affliction, extinguished the darkness of the world, and eclipsed the palaces of Māra. Together with the bodhisattvas and their countless retinues, he returned to the Sahā world; then, suddenly, he vanished from atop the Buddha’s head.

At that time, in the eastern direction, there was the world-system named Immeasurable Merit Jewel Fortune Universal Farewell; its Buddha was named Tathāgata Stainless Pure Light Ocean Flower Uninterrupted Light Speech King.

In that buddha-field, there was a bodhisattva named Śīrṣakośapuṣpa-dharmavaśavartin—invited by that light—who, surrounded by a retinue and assembly of bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges rivers, suddenly vanished from that land and, in the space of a mere moment, arrived here in this Sahā world-system.

He approached the precious high seat and stood before the World-Honored One; prostrating at his feet, he circumambulated the Buddha ten thousand times. He rained down *nakṣatra-prabhāsa* pearls, various jewels, and necklaces as offerings scattered over the Buddha, and praised him with these verses:
"The hair of the Ten-Powered One’s meritorious achievements Reaches throughout the ten directions.
I praise this peerless one, Whose virtuous legacy has crossed to the other shore."
We have come to this land for the sake of hearing the Dharma;
all hear the renown of his title, the Lion of the Śākyas.
The World-Honored One is impartial, his stainless light shining everywhere.
Just as all phenomena have no fundamental basis, so too there is no anger or resentment.
Seeing sentient beings in peril and fear, he immediately causes them to attain liberation;
as the King of all Dharmas, he is like a master illusionist well-trained in his art.
At that time, the countless assembly of bodhisattvas, having praised the Buddha, each used their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to magically create a seat and sat upon it.

From the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Anantaguṇaratnavyūhavāk in the world of Vāk in the southern direction, there was a bodhisattva named Ratnastaṃbha, accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of ten great rivers. Suddenly disappearing from that land, in the space of a mere moment they arrived at this Sahā world. They approached the precious high seat and stood before the Buddha; covering the Buddha with a canopy of white pearls, they prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him ten thousand times, and praised him in verse, saying:
“The World-Honored One is all-encompassing, Raining compassion upon all sentient beings.”
He opens wide the flames of radiant light, Through emptiness, free from self.
By means of the eightfold even and upright path, He dries up the abyss of worldly desires;
In the silent seclusion of the kings of trees, He nurtures the grove of pure and white virtue.
Then, by the light of wisdom, he transforms and extinguishes the mother of darkness;
he awakens sentient beings who have long been in a dream, who are drowning in the current of beginning and end.
To reveal the true path, he dries up the pool of craving and affection.
"May they attain the pure eye, and may they be delivered as before, to the supreme state.
When the countless bodhisattvas had finished praising the Buddha with these verses, each used their supernormal powers to magically transform and create a seat, and all took their places upon them.

At that time, from the world-system called *Ābhāsvara* in the western direction, the land of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One *Samantaprabha*, there was a bodhisattva named *Ghoṣavibhūti-rāja*. Accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, he suddenly vanished from that land and, in the space of a mere moment, arrived here in this Sahā world. He approached the precious high seat and stood before the Buddha, raining down crystal and pearls as an offering to the World-Honored One.
Prostrating at his feet and circumambulating the Buddha ten thousand times, he offered this hymn of praise: "The conduct of your holy body Is like the realm of empty space;
Your vows are entirely pure, And the number of kalpas is immeasurable."
His body is pure and stainless, forever free from all outflows;
he pervades the ten directions throughout inconceivable Buddha-lands.
His preaching is like a timely rain, with the thunderous resonance of sublime Brahma-sounds.
He brings joy to all classes of beings, responding to what their hearts desire.
His mind has no fixed course of action, nor is there anything it does not do;
the various sounds he articulates emerge in response to the minds of sentient beings.

When the countless bodhisattvas had finished praising the Buddha with verses, each of them used their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to magically transform and create a seat, and they all sat upon them.

At that time, from the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Immeasurable Virtue Jewel Light in the northern realm of Various Jeweled Brocade, there was a bodhisattva named Sāgarabuddhi. Accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of ten great rivers, he suddenly vanished from that land and, in the space of a mere moment, arrived at this Sahā world. He approached the precious high seat, stood before the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha ten thousand times, and praised him with these verses:
“Your body is the color of purple-polished gold; You have awakened through giving and tranquility.”
He shines excellently throughout the ten directions, swiftly manifesting his body everywhere.
His essence has no peer; if all people observe him, they will extinguish the dust of all desires and rejoice in long-lasting peace and security.
The most excellent disciples, gazing upon the Light of the World,
all direct their will toward him with joyful veneration, like the King of Mount Sumeru’s summit.
Through the power of their various supernormal faculties (*ṛddhi*), they manifest manifold transformations.
"One cannot see the most supreme, majestic marks upon the crown of his head.
At that time, after countless bodhisattvas had praised the Buddha with these verses, each used their supernormal powers to transform their seats and sat upon them.

At that time, from the world-system called Aśoka in the southeast—the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Sarvaduḥkhapraśamanasamantatamas, there was a bodhisattva named Samantaprabhāsa. Accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, he suddenly vanished from that land and, in a mere moment, arrived here in this Sahā world. He approached the precious high seat, stood before the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha ten thousand times, and offered a jeweled canopy as an offering to the Buddha.
Then, he praised him with these verses: "Within a single pore, He contains infinite buddha-fields;
Sentient beings suffer no distress, And the lands are not cramped."
The supreme practice of salvation for those who lack eyes;
the Buddhas are most wondrous, being the radiant light of superior consciousness.
Within a single buddha-field, they manifest countless buddha-lands.
Whatever manifestations appear therein, the buddha-fields neither increase nor decrease.
According to appropriate skillful means, his great renown enters at the proper time;
he universally enters all transformations, moved by his supernormal powers.
When those countless bodhisattvas had finished praising the Buddha with verses, each manifested a seat through their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and sat upon it.

At that time, from the world-system called *Sudarśana* in the southwest—the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Mahākāruṇika-saṃdarśaka-loka-sattva—there was a bodhisattva named Mahākāruṇyābhigaveṣin. Accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, he suddenly vanished from that land and, in a mere moment, arrived at this Sahā world. He approached the precious high seat, stood before the Buddha, rained down exquisite garments as an offering to cover the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and praised him with these verses:
"Your precepts are most pure; The Honored One among Men is like a precious jewel."
Guard yourself throughout the long night, as a yak protects its tail.
Upon seeing those who violate the precepts, respond with compassion;
do not lament your own condition, nor disparage others.
Abiding like Mount Sumeru, your mind is fixed and cannot be moved;
Your wisdom is like the rivers and seas, and your honor transcends all spirits.
Having already crossed over all states of existence and the prisons of conditioned bondage, [you are truly liberated].
"Transforming billions of sentient beings, you heal their diseases of worldly toil.
When the countless bodhisattvas had finished praising the Buddha with these verses, each used their supernormal powers to magically transform and create a seat, upon which they all sat down.

At that time, from the world-system called Free from Darkness and Gloom in the northwest, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata King of Radiant Purity, there was a bodhisattva named Net of Radiance. Accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of ten great rivers, he suddenly vanished from that land and, in the space of a mere moment, arrived at this Sahā world. He approached the precious high seat and stood before the Buddha, covering the Buddha with precious necklaces and ornaments. Prostrating at his feet and circumambulating him a hundred thousand times, he praised him in verse:
"The body awakens to birth and death, Like a magician’s conjuration;
That which is manifested and moved Is like an illusion—non-existent."
Suppose a master creates an illusion; all sentient beings are just like this.
Their realm cannot be moved, yet sentient beings have no inherent nature.
It is like a person lying in sleep and dreaming, perceiving various forms.
Upon awakening, nothing is seen; all perceptions of form are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The Sage teaches that phenomena are like dreams; conditioned things arise from thought.
Seeing that there is regression, one neither regresses nor turns back.
When those countless bodhisattvas had finished praising the Buddha with verses, each used their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to magically transform and create a seat, and they all sat upon them.

At that time, from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Śūnyanagaravimalacitta in the northeastern world-system called Vimalaviśuddha, there was a bodhisattva named Anantabodhivimala. Accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, he suddenly vanished from that land and, in the space of a moment, arrived here in this Sahā world. He approached the precious high seat and stood before the Buddha, covering the Buddha above with a canopy of interlaced lattices resonant with the sound of constant drums. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and praised him with these verses:
“Clearly knowing the profound and wondrous Dharma, Equally understanding the pointing toward spontaneity (*svayambhū*);”
Contemplating the characteristics of all emptinesses, And all phenomena that exist;
Universally knowing the entire world, And the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings—
Their minds are like space, With pure wisdom that is bottomless.
The conduct of the multitudes of beings, and all the restlessness throughout the three periods of time—
he practices them all with a single mind at a single moment, fully knowing everything that exists.
Without the notion of a "sentient being," his mind is truly free from discursive thought.
"Having already eliminated all deluded thoughts, their skillful means are universally equal.
At that time, after countless bodhisattvas had praised the Buddha with these verses, each manifested a seat through their supernatural powers and sat upon it.

At that time, from the world-system called Illumination in the nadir direction, within the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Deep Blue Lotus Head, there was a bodhisattva named Eloquence Adornment. Accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, he suddenly vanished from that land and, in a mere moment, arrived here in this Sahā world. He approached the precious high seat and stood before the Buddha, covering the Buddha with a canopy of interlaced bright pearls.

Bowing his head at the Buddha’s feet, he circumambulated him a hundred thousand times and praised him in verse: “As many atoms as there are Within billions of buddha-fields, So many sons of the Victorious One Have come to the Most Excellent One.”
Each desires to pose their own inquiry regarding countless billions of kalpas;
yet with but a single word, he transforms the minds of all.
His noble wisdom is beyond analogy, his skillful wisdom is peerless.
The dhāraṇīs and concentrations are immeasurable; his merits have no limit or bottom.
His great achievements cannot be circumscribed; though proclaimed throughout countless kalpas and extolled from every pore, they can never be fully exhausted.
When the countless bodhisattvas had finished praising the Buddha in verse, each used their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to magically transform and create a seat, and they all sat upon them.

At that time, from the world called Adorned (*Vyūha*) in the zenith—the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Renowned Name (*Yaśas*)—there was a bodhisattva named King of the Transformation of All Dharmas (*Sarvadharmavikurvaṇarāja*). Accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, he suddenly vanished from that land and, in the space of a moment, arrived at this Sahā world. He approached the precious high seat and stood before the Buddha; a canopy of various ornaments and interlaced nets of gold and purple jewels covered the Buddha above. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and praised him in verse:
"All karmic activities are securely established, Now manifesting without limit or bottom."
Having attained mastery over the mind, the Teacher’s conduct is likewise so.
This is known only by the Buddhas; it is not within the reach of ordinary beings.
Just as space is without limit, such is the fundamental nature of all living things.
His conduct is without peer; today he has manifested the bottomless [truth].
Having attained Buddhahood and turned the wheel of Dharma, the Guide’s parinirvāṇa is like [this]:
just as when something is sown, the Dharma does not fail to yield its fruit.
"The Most Victorious Ones of the ten directions are beyond all measure and limit.

At that time, after countless bodhisattvas had praised the Buddha with these verses, they each manifested their seats through supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) in the air above the Buddha and sat upon them.

Chapter Two: The Chapter on the Lamentation of the Assembly from the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*. At that moment, in an instant, the bodhisattvas of the ten directions all assembled and appeared before him. This multitude of bodhisattvas was beyond measure, beyond calculation, and could not be contained even by hundreds of thousands of millions; urged by the light, they gathered in the Sahā world-system and approached the precious high seat to stand before the World-Honored One.

Then the Buddha, having arisen from his meditative absorption, emitted a brilliant radiance, and from it a natural sound issued forth; this natural sound proclaimed throughout the trichiliocosm, causing all to hear his teaching.

At that time, those in the Buddha-field who were faithful and those who were faithless—whether they were bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs worthy of offerings, young men or young women, humans or non-humans, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, or mahoragas—upon hearing the Buddha’s voice, their bodies and minds became serene; they increased their reverence and grew still with awe. Sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, marvelous jeweled palaces spontaneously appeared, and they all proceeded toward them together.
In the space of a mere moment, they arrived at the precious high seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Sage three times, and each took their place upon a couch.

Furthermore, by the command of this Light-Sound [Brahmā], the Brahmā Śikhin, the Brahmā Sahampati, the Brahmā Hṛṣṭa, the Great Brahmā, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, the Apramāṇābha Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Śuddhaśarīra Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudatta Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and the Ekabhadra Heaven—all gathered at the precious high seat in the blink of an eye. They prostrated at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha seven times, and instead of remaining on the ground, each sat upon their respective seats.
At that time, the World-Honored One beheld the great assembly gathered together.
A divine radiance named "Manifesting the Power of All Bodhisattvas" issued forth from between his eyebrows; after circling the bodhisattvas seven times, it vanished into the crowns of their heads.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Śīrṣakośapuṣpa-dharmavaśavartin who, encountering this radiance, immediately attained the samādhi of "All Adornments.
As soon as he had entered this samādhi, his precious high seat spontaneously became a Buddha.

There was a lion throne eighty billion *ya* and hundreds of thousands of *zhang* in height, with feet made of exquisite jewels, railings of various treasures, and spread with wonderful garments; it was strewn with all kinds of flowers and adorned with delightful precious gems.

All the bodhisattvas, beholding this transformation of conditions that severs all longing, cause the entire assembly to behold their own radiance; they gladden all sentient beings by manifesting their mental intentions, so that whatever they seek or aspire to is immediately fulfilled without any hesitation.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrīkusumadharmavaśavartin, through the samādhi of "Praising the Kalpas and Bestowing upon All Evil Realms," entered right concentration and separately manifested a great lion throne for the Tathāgata, which was orderly and serene.
Rising from samādhi, he reverently and respectfully joined his ten fingers in *añjali* and praised the Buddha with this verse:
“The radiance of the sun Shines only upon the mundane world;
But the majestic power and virtue of the Lord of Devas Delightfully attend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.”
That Brahmā, the Honored King of Gods, yearned for the Brahma Heaven;
yet by the Buddha’s holy majesty and transformative power, the realms were shaken in such a manner.
Observing that all phenomena are autonomous and naturally like empty space, [he attained realization].
If they are like an illusion or a mirage, and also like the moon reflected in water;
whatever is done or created is entirely without a master.
Understanding them as deceptive, one perceives sentient beings as pure.
The mind yearns for form, yet where does this form reside?
The mind is of its own nature; that which it follows is entirely unreal.
Though all things are pure, even this is like a magical illusion.
Regarding that which is natural, where could there be any falsehood?
Being able to discern original purity, one governs the mind with freshness and clarity;
when its sphere arises with ease, it is free from the dust of desire.
When one contemplates all thoughts and recollections, and the mind has already been liberated from them,
then one sees these various kinds as the workings of illusion.
Just as nothing exists in space, yet it arises from the earth.
Manifesting the lands of the world, with various bright pearls and jewels;
having formerly served as a Dharma King, you have established this lion throne.
You should now occupy this seat and transform hundreds of millions of sentient beings.
The standing silk banners and canopies, the great standards and various ornaments—
these come from nowhere, nor do they go anywhere.
If one can understand that all phenomena come from nowhere, [one realizes their true nature].
He is then able to manifest various supreme transformations for the sake of sentient beings.
With the sublime Brahma-voice of the Great Sage, what he expounds is excellent and delightful;
acting as a great lamp for the world, his majestic spiritual power and virtue are limitless.
Out of compassion for me, you should ascend the high seat and expound the sutras, severing birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Those pure beings, having gathered here from the ten directions,
each sit in their proper order, desiring to hear the meaning of the Dharma of compassion.
Regarding the original causes that have been set forth, they pray for an explanation of this wisdom.
"The Sage sits upon the lion throne, calmly proclaiming the Dharma.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, seeing that the Bodhisattva Flower-Treasury of All Dharmas Sovereign possessed a pure disposition, immediately took his place upon the great, pure lion throne of the Dharma Master and forthwith expounded the practices of all bodhisattvas and the goals they should establish.

Furthermore, there is a sutra titled "The Unobstructed Gate," which purifies the bodhisattva path, [manifests] the power of the Buddhas' Dharma, accomplishes the precious body, serves as the dwelling of noble wisdom, and attains mastery over all phenomena.
Entering into the dhāraṇīs, they analyze and explain them, discerning the gateways of great supernormal powers and wisdom;
entering the subtle, non-regressive wheel from which none can turn back, they guide all those who ride the vehicle of meditative concentration;

entering the Single Vehicle and the indestructible Dharma-realm, they proclaim the nature and fundamental origins of sentient beings and their destinies, acting as leaders to elucidate and bring forth all phenomena.
They destroy all Māras and enter the Dharma of compliance;
they eliminate all afflictions and the sixty-two views, transforming and guiding others to enter the Dharma of gentle compliance;
and they cause all sensual desires, false views, and violations of discipline to enter unimpeded wisdom.

They exhort the multitude toward the roots of virtue, universally reaching all without exception; they proclaim provisional wisdom so that all may enter the equality of the Buddhas' sagely state, entirely free from obscuration and without any fixed gateway.

The various dharmas he proclaims are distinguished according to their meaning; he enters into all dharmas—neither with thought nor without thought, neither responding nor not responding—and awakens to the profound and subtle twelvefold dependent origination.
The merit of his noble wisdom extends even to the Heaven of Māra; he adorns the Buddha’s body, speech, and mind with all splendor.

His aspirations and inclinations are illuminated by wisdom that cannot be obscured; he enters the Noble Truths to transform and guide the śrāvakas, and he understands the heart’s destination and the discipline of the pratyekabuddhas.

Universally attaining the laws of all Bodhisattvas regarding the spheres of all wisdom, they achieve mastery over all phenomena they enter and proclaim the meritorious fame and titles of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha preached such a Dharma scripture of boundless likeness.
As he spoke these words, he taught and exhorted the virtues of the bodhisattvas:
"Your sincere vows have all been fully realized."

He manifested the transformations of the Tathāgata to move the hearts of all, untied the web of doubts and entanglements of the assembled multitude, subdued the realms of all Māras, and illuminated the meaning of the Tathāgata’s instructions, fully preparing the fundamental practices of a Buddha so that they might be perfected.
Therefore, as the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne and proclaimed the Unobstructed Gate,

at that time the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu, receiving the Buddha’s sacred intent, entered the meditative absorption of the Buddha-Adornment Samādhi, causing the entire assembly to attain Buddha-adornment and establishing majestic spiritual power.

Then, the Bodhisattva Renowned Power, receiving the Buddha’s holy command, entered the samādhi of the Red Lotus to establish the assembly; he caused all the flowers to become Dharma-flowers, and scattered these flowers over the World-Honored One and all the Bodhisattvas in samādhi.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgarabuddhi, receiving the Buddha’s sacred command, entered the meditative absorption of the Samādhi of Universal Fragrance, causing a wondrous-flavored sandalwood to be produced and manifested from all his pores.

4. Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, receiving the Buddha’s holy command, entered the meditative absorption of the Samādhi of Radiant Concentration, causing all lights to establish the assembly so that none failed to receive peace and comfort.

5. The Bodhisattva Mahākaruṇācintin, receiving the Buddha’s holy command, established the assembly through the meditative absorption of the *animiṣa-samādhi*, gazing upon the Tathāgata with eyes that did not dare to blink.

6. The Bodhisattva Vigatarajovimatisamudghāta, receiving the Buddha’s holy command, established the assembly through the meditative absorption of the Dharma-joy Samādhi; they yearned for the True Dharma, delighted in the Dharma, were intent upon the Dharma, and took pleasure in the joy of the Dharma.

7. Bodhisattva Bianyan, receiving the Buddha’s holy command, entered the samādhi of the "Trace of Vows and Concentration" to establish the assembly, causing all to eliminate the afflictions of the five hindrances.

8. The Bodhisattva Varṇarājasuta, receiving the Buddha’s holy command, established the assembly through the meditative absorption of the Samādhi of Non-forgetfulness, setting his mind upon the Buddha-way and yearning for the conduct of the Tathāgata.

9. The Bodhisattva Courageous Mind, receiving the Buddha’s holy command, established the assembly, causing all demons and external enemies to submit and none to fail to be transformed by his teaching.
10. The Bodhisattva Subduing All Demons, receiving the Buddha’s holy command, entered the meditative absorption of the Samādhi of Destroying the Demon’s Field.

Immediately upon attaining samādhi, all the Māras within the trichiliocosm—numbering in the hundreds of billions—along with their demonic armies, moved with extreme swiftness; each suddenly vanished from their palaces and appeared before the Buddha at the precious high seat. They prostrated themselves at his feet, circumambulated the World-Honored One incalculable and countless times, and offered extraordinary and wondrous objects as offerings to the Great Sage. With reverent awe and palms joined in single-minded devotion, they exhorted the Teacher of Gods to proclaim the sūtras: "We pray that you will, in due time, open the way for transformation and deliver instruction.
Today, we have come to offer our support, established by the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattvas who have subdued the Māras."
"O Heaven among Heavens!
I shall relinquish all demonic activities that disturb sentient beings; it is for the sake of the Dharma that I have come here.
Therefore, Great Sage, please examine the intent and conduct of my person."
At that time, the World-Honored One, perceiving the thoughts in Māra’s mind, praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, O worthy ones!
You have been able to relinquish your demonic activities and exhort the Tathāgata to preach the sūtra and the Dharma.”
For this reason, by virtue of this, your bodies shall receive this retribution, and you shall all transcend and cross over all demonic activities. Why is this?
It is like a house that has been dark for hundreds of thousands of years; as soon as a single lamp enters within, the darkness is instantly dispelled.

In this way, though these people have given rise to the dark desires of worldly toil for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, through the transformative power of the mind of a single root of goodness, they extinguish all afflictions so that none remain.
It is like the palaces of various people for a single day, the halls for a single month, and a great precious gem; each individually emits the brilliance of light to dispel all darkness.

In this way, all these people, with single-minded roots of goodness, observe their practice and maintain mindfulness in accordance with it; they eliminate all the darkness of ignorance, the sixty-two views, and the many hardships of the ninety-six paths.

For this reason, today you virtuous ones have come to behold the Tathāgata and further offer your encouragement and support; by virtue of this root of merit, you shall gradually eliminate the darkness of all ignorance and folly, and shall attain the gate of the infinite Dharma of guidance.
The Scripture of Great Compassion, Volume One.
The Scripture of Great Compassion, Volume Two.

Chapter Three: The Chapter on the Unobstructed Dharma-Gates.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmateja, being present in that assembly, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"

The realm of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; he manifests and establishes the majestic radiance of a Great Sage, causing all bodhisattvas to be forever free from doubt as they each practice their respective paths.
You should now proclaim the Dharma Chapter on the Great Assembly of the Unobstructed Gate. Why is this?
This great assembly has now gathered here, and all are bodhisattvas; first, they have donned the inconceivable armor of great virtue.
Second, they delight in great supernormal powers and noble wisdom;
third, they all possess meritorious achievements that pervade the ten directions;
fourth, their cultivated purity is a mind free from defilement and impurity.
Fifth, they illuminate extensively through clear liberation;
sixth, they are all praised and their meritorious achievements proclaimed by all Buddhas;
seventh, they attain sovereign mastery over all dharmas.
8. The various perfections (pāramitās) transcend the shores of both beginning and end;
9. All arise from skillful means (upāya-kauśalya);
10. And they completely dissolve the karmic activities of Māra and the dust of desire.
Eleventh, they subdue all external heterodox paths;
twelfth, they are able to analyze and expound upon the meanings and principles of chapters and verses through skillful means;
thirteenth, their wisdom is unimpeded, and through the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they transcend to the other shore.
14. His mind is autonomous, his courageous stride is unimpeded, and he has attained the noble dhāraṇīs;
15. He establishes the unobstructed and possesses uninterrupted eloquence;
16. He thoroughly understands the origins and inclinations of the faculties of sentient beings—whether they are complete or deficient, fully endowed or lacking.
Seventeenth, he observes all sentient beings and expounds the Dharma according to their respective capacities for understanding;
eighteenth, the sūtras and paths he proclaims eliminate all karmic offenses and calamities without exception;
nineteenth, his voice is at all times supple, harmonious, and elegant, like the cry of a sorrowful phoenix, the roar of a dragon from the sea, and the sound of Brahmā.
Twenty: Out of compassion for sentient beings, he manifests parinirvāṇa, and likewise, out of compassion, he enables the multitude to attain salvation;
Twenty-one: His mind constantly harbors the practice of infinite loving-kindness (*maitrī*);
Twenty-two: His will and nature maintain the thought of unobstructed pity (*karuṇā*).
Twenty-three: His dwelling is firm and immovable, and his words and deeds correspond;
twenty-four: He cultivates and establishes the banner of the Dharma to manifest throughout the ten directions;
twenty-five: His resolve is as strong as a diamond, indestructible like the Iron Ring Mountains.
Twenty-sixth, they fulfill all their aspirations without failing their original vows;
twenty-seventh, they penetrate deeply into the subtle and wondrous, discerning the profound mysteries of the twelve links of dependent origination;
twenty-eighth, they eliminate the two extremes and sever all views—including the view of eternalism and the sixty-two types of doubt—as well as the habitual attachments resulting from them.
29. Furthermore, like a Dharma King of the Mahāyāna multitude, he entices, leads, and compels others to enter the Path;
30. As a great guide for the masses, he brings them to the state free from calamity;
31. Throughout incalculable kalpas, he has delighted in the treasure of the Dharma and accumulated wisdom.

32. Acting as a great king of physicians to treat the illnesses of all people; 33. Eradicating the diseases of formless afflictions and stagnant accumulations of sentient beings (the thirty-third dharma-sūtra is missing from the original);
34. These bodhisattvas are children nurtured by the Great Lion King; 35.
Regarding all conditioned phenomena, whether hearing various sounds or listening to the explanation of the Tathāgata’s secret meanings, they do not feel fear.
36. Adorning their bodies with the primary and secondary marks;
37. Fully performing sacrifices with great compassion;
38. Their minds being courageous and free from cowardice.
Thirty-nine: Subduing the four māras and the realm of craving and desire;
forty: skillfully bestowing bridges to awaken those who are asleep;

forty-one: through such faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and meditative reflection, as well as liberation, concentration, and right attainment, he has successfully cultivated what ought to be practiced.
Forty-two: Always with earnest diligence, he desires to deliver sentient beings;
forty-three: He has attained *dhāraṇī*, grasping and restraining all things;
forty-four: Whether there is gain or loss, praise or defamation, fame or infamy, suffering or pleasure—regarding these eight worldly concerns, he remains unattached.
45. His mind attains entry into joy and gladness, delighting in and loving the scriptures;
46. He proclaims and disseminates the treasure of the Dharma; 47.
He is filled with wisdom and fully masters the emptiness of the Path.
Forty-eight: His conduct is as pure and radiant as a lotus flower;
forty-nine: He eliminates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*);
fifty: His light is so pure that it eclipses the brilliance of the sun, the moon, Śakra, and Brahmā.
Fifty-one: They have all attained the Samādhi of the Ocean;
fifty-two: they govern the treasure of all dharmas through the Way;
fifty-three: regarding the Three Jewels, they have attained mastery such that none can sever or obstruct them.
Fifty-fourth, clearly discerning and explaining all realms;
fifty-fifth, upholding the essentials of the sūtras of all Buddhas;
fifty-sixth, accumulating and gathering immeasurable merit and laudatory praise.
Fifty-seven: establishing the karmic activity of infinite merit;
fifty-eight: attaining proximity to and the full possession of the Buddha’s wisdom;
fifty-nine: thoroughly comprehending the beginning and end of incalculable future kalpas.
"In the sixty-first Dharma-text, there is a slight omission.
The Bodhisattva Dharmatejorāja addressed the Buddha, saying,
"So it is, World-Honored One!"
The merit of this assembly of great bodhisattvas is such as this; it was my thought, O Great Sage, that I should personally reflect:

"May the World-Honored One proclaim for these bodhisattvas the Dharma Chapter of the Great Assembly on the Unobstructed Gate, from which the multitude of bodhisattvas arises, reaching the unprecedented state of the God among Gods."
The appearance of the Buddhas brings great benefit; they are able to gladden and satisfy the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, enabling them to achieve full perfection.

For those future Bodhisattvas who possess the roots of virtue and wisdom, and for those Bodhisattvas who have first resolved to attain awakening and wish to fulfill their pure conduct, [the Buddhas] cause them to enter the One Vehicle so that they may never regress.

The assembly of Bodhisattvas, being fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma and having reached the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) as those in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*), ensure that their karmic fruits and retributions are not lost.
If there are sentient beings whose cognition is clear and whose resolve is determined, they bring forth the causal conditions to transform them and lead them into the Way.

For those who are not yet determined, they cause them to look up toward and enter into infinite compassion (*anukampā*). As for those sentient beings who remain forever in false views, they explain the proper place [of refuge] to them, thereby causing the net of their delusions to be severed.

Because those who delight in the Three Vehicles are the cause for the appearance of a Buddha and his self-adornment, all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, humans and non-humans, worldly beings, and asuras are likewise able to receive his salvation.

Why is this so? It is truly wonderful that a Buddha has appeared in the world; such a phenomenon is unprecedented, difficult to encounter, and rare. This essential core of the scriptures has now manifested in the world for all to behold and know.
"I only pray, Great Sage!

At the very moment these true beings resolve their minds, may they establish and transform this high seat of the Dharma, something that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas could not attain even in hundreds of thousands of kalpas."
For this reason, I thought to myself:
"How difficult to reach, how difficult to reach! This is truly unprecedented.

These people are able to manifest such physical forms and transformations of supernatural power; who, upon seeing this, would ever again give rise to the practice of a śrāvaka or the mind of a pratyekabuddha?"
Why is this? Because anyone who has first resolved to attain the mind of a bodhisattva surpasses the multitudes of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Now, I wish to provide an analogy.
World-Honored One, it is like this:

suppose a foolish child, from birth, has been mired in ignorance; he discards a great jewel of moonlight and instead takes up a crystal bead, seeing things inverted and yet considering himself correct.
The conduct of the multitude is likewise thus: they abandon the Mahāyāna and instead seek the vehicles of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha.

Yet, if there should be someone whose nature is truly authentic who gives rise to the aspiration for unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment—whether they have already given rise to that mind or are only now doing so—they too shall, before long, fully accomplish such essential dharmas.

When the Bodhisattva Dharmatejarāja spoke these words, three hundred thousand koṭis of devas and humans within that assembly all resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.

Chapter Four: The Chapter on the Adornment of the Dharma. At that time, the World-Honored One beheld all the bodhisattvas who had gathered for this great assembly—bodhisattvas who had all come together for the sake of the Dharma, each upholding the wondrous treasury of the Tathāgata, proclaiming all the practices of bodhisattvas, abiding in the profound essentials of the chapter on the gateway of the unobstructed Dharma, and cultivating and governing the scriptural canons. Furthermore, there was a light named "Fearless Eloquence" which, at that moment, was emitted from the mark of the Great Man between his eyebrows. Having circled the bodhisattvas seven times, it then circled the body of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī-Kumārabhūta one hundred thousand times before entering the crown of Mañjuśrī-Kumārabhūta’s head.

Having just been graced by this light and sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, [the bodhisattva] circumambulated the various bodhisattvas hundreds of thousands of times. That light illuminated his lion throne entirely, and his physical presence and deportment became even more radiant; his brilliance was so towering and magnificent that it increased twofold, surpassing all other bodhisattvas.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva Sarvashvararāja beheld the Tathāgata’s boundless majestic transformations, he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, and joined his palms toward the space above the World-Honored One. There, he manifested a magnificent jeweled canopy of the Tathāgata—established by the Buddha—with a banner made of lapis lazuli reaching as high as the Yama Heaven. It was adorned with extraordinary and rare treasures, celestial-blue lapis lazuli, and exquisite precious caskets; it was further embellished with hanging strings of pearls, silken streamers, and banners, and surrounded on all sides by a lattice of purple gold. This canopy covered the entire great assembly of bodhisattvas, its breadth and height being as vast as the trichiliocosm.
Having established such jeweled canopies in this manner and offered them to the Tathāgata, they rained down celestial flowers, and majestic musical instruments resounded spontaneously.
Thereupon, he praised the World-Honored One with these verses:
“Your radiance is all-pervading, leaving nothing unseen; The range of your vision reveals the profound meaning.”
Mastery over all dharmas and sovereign freedom, Inconceivable, leading toward all virtues.
The Great Sage, the True Being, radiates light; His pure mouth proclaims eloquence.
The light of the Dharma circles me a hundred thousand times, Then vanishes into the crown of my head, no longer visible.
Just as the original intention was conceived and remembered, so too is the illumination of eloquence maintained;
that which is known now surpasses the former by hundreds of thousands, all through receiving the grace of the Hero among Men, the Teacher of the Path.
His body is majestic and his mind is pure; leaping with joy, he obtains his wishes at the proper time.
Thus one knows that the wisdom of the Perfectly Awakened One is immeasurable, and that his great eloquence has entered my person.
The Buddha is truly difficult to approach; his majesty is boundless. Those who are weak and inferior do not delight in it, yet now, by receiving the Buddha’s holy intent, we have seen it all.
We shall again pose our questions out of compassion for sentient beings.
The sphere of practice entered by the assembly of Bodhisattvas, their equal engagement with the world and their guidance of the multitudes,
the radiance they produce and the places they transform— these should once again be inquired of and presented to the Avinivartanīya (the Non-regressing One).
Innumerable hosts of Māras have all gathered here, yet you alone traverse the supreme vehicle of the Path;
for the sake of those who likewise seek the subtle and wondrous Dharma, I ask the Most Victorious One.
One should firmly uphold this field of Māra, and always receive this Buddha-wisdom with earnest attention;
now is the very time for the World-Honored One to speak, opening the treasury of Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
My humble body possesses clear wisdom that reaches all things; the Honored One among men has immeasurable insight.
He is able to comprehend the most supreme and infinite knowledge; I shall now inquire concerning his boundless skillful means.
The World-Honored One’s noble wisdom is sovereign;
having practiced and studied throughout the long night, he has well followed the Honored One of Skill as the Dharma King, and now solely proclaims the conduct of the Teacher of the Path.
After the Bodhisattva Sarvārthasiddhi had praised the Buddha with these verses, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“The realm of the Tathāgata is inconceivable, and the practices of the bodhisattvas are beyond measure. I and this assembly have never grown weary of listening to and examining the sūtras and dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
Beholding sentient beings, the Most Victorious World-Honored One practices great compassion; therefore, I ask about this meaning.
What, O World-Honored One, is meant by a bodhisattva’s adornment and self-ornamentation, and how does one accord with the meaning through the conduct of a bodhisattva?

What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s inconceivable attainment of the light of the Dharma, which is free from the afflictions of darkness and obstruction, and which achieves purity through the great Dharma-gates?
What is meant by a bodhisattva being honored among sentient beings, practicing great compassion and loving-kindness as the foremost, accomplishing their conduct without abandoning sentient beings?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the various activities practiced by Buddhas and bodhisattvas, honoring the true Dharma, and harboring no thoughts of affliction?
Excellent, World-Honored One!

We pray that you will analytically explain the Dharma-gate of the practices, abodes, and various attainments of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—how a Bodhisattva subdues the hosts of Māras, eliminates the net of doubt, enters the realm of the Tathāgata, and roams the domain of Bodhisattvas;

how they understand the aspirations of all sentient beings, purify their mental activities, encompass Buddha-lands, maintain the field of Māra, and follow the teachings of the Tathāgata, thereby swiftly attaining mastery over all dharmas without obstruction or hindrance.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra:
"Excellent, excellent,
O Noble Being!"

It is well that you have been able to question the Tathāgata, desiring to thoroughly resolve the matters concerning all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; you, O son of noble family, are capable of attaining a clear understanding of the practices of immeasurable Tathāgatas.
Son of noble family!
Listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for you.
Just as the various practices of bodhisattvas and the other meritorious achievements of bodhisattvas are fully perfected, they swiftly attain mastery over all dharmas.
The Bodhisattva Sarvashura and the great assembly received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"There are four matters with which a bodhisattva adorns themselves."
What are the four?
First is the adornment of precepts, never violating the prohibitions;
second is the adornment of meditative concentration, reaching a state of never being distracted.
The third is the adornment of wisdom, such that the mind is free from obscuration and hindrance;
the fourth is the adornment of dhāraṇī, such that what is heard is never forgotten.
These are the four adornments of a bodhisattva.
"In that regard, what is meant by 'adornment through precepts'?
Son of good family!
One who knows uses a single matter to adorn themselves with precepts."
What is this one thing?

It is to always have compassion for sentient beings with a mind free from malice, to feel pity and sympathy for all the common people and every living creature, and to revere and love them so that none fail to find joy in it.
"Furthermore, there are two matters by which one adorns oneself with ethical discipline. What are these two?
First is to block off the evil realms; second is to open the gates to the auspicious realms."
"Furthermore, there are three matters by which one is adorned with precepts.
What are these three?

First, the conduct of the body is pure and free from defilement; second, the speech of the mouth is pure and its words are not coarse or harsh; third, the mind is pure and never corrupted or distracted."
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which one adorns oneself with precepts. What are these four?

First, that whatever one aspires to will surely bear fruit without deviation; second, that whatever vows one pledges will be successfully accomplished; third, that whatever one admires and delights in will certainly be achieved without fail; fourth, that whatever one plans and envisions will be transcended and realized."
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are five matters by which one is adorned with the precepts.
What are these five?

First, to practice diligently together with those who observe the prohibitions and precepts; second, to study and learn wisdom without ever becoming indolent or negligent; third, to apply oneself with zeal toward liberation without harboring arrogance or self-indulgence; fourth, to cultivate the factors conducive to penetration without ever ceasing or relaxing; fifth, to increase one's diligent effort in accordance with unsurpassed, ultimate nirvāṇa. These are the five.
"Furthermore, there are six matters by which one adorns oneself with precepts. What are these six?
First, to be without transgression and to harbor no resentment."
Second, to be without deficiency or omission, nor to abandon or discard anything;
third, to be without defilement and without loss or decline;
fourth, to be free from blemish by cultivating a single pure practice.
Fifth, to listen extensively and receive teachings without following after desires or defilements;
sixth, if there is something to be heard, not to rely on or look up to others for it—
these are the six.
"Furthermore, there are seven matters by which one is adorned with precepts.

What are the seven? First, purity of the category of precepts; second, purity of giving; third, purity of patience; fourth, purity of diligence; fifth, purity of meditative concentration; sixth, purity of wisdom; and seventh, purity of skillful means without negligence."
These are the seven.
Furthermore, there are eight matters by which one is adorned with precepts.
What are these eight?

First is the perfection of one's dwelling; second, the ultimate nature of that ground; third, the full completeness of what is governed; fourth, the thoroughness of natural precepts; fifth, reaching accomplishment without being burned or harmed; sixth, attaining non-attachment when a Buddha appears in the world; seventh, universal penetration without obstruction; eighth, obtaining the fulfillment of questions from a virtuous teacher. These are the eight.
“Furthermore, there are nine matters by which one adorns oneself with the precepts.

What are these nine? First, to have no fear regarding noble wisdom; second, to be without timidity when observing or seeing anything; third, to clearly understand the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); fourth, to discern skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*); fifth, to practice the coolness [of liberation] and be free from the fever of affliction; sixth, to guard the prohibitions and precepts as a bee gathers nectar from flowers; seventh, to cultivate the mind so that it is free from sensual desire; eighth, to keep the mind harmonious and not harbor coarseness or wildness; ninth, to attain the state of balanced tranquility and equanimity.”
These are the nine.
Furthermore, there are ten matters by which one is adorned with precepts.
What are these ten?
First, adorning the body by being fully endowed with all the marks;
second, adorning the mouth so that one's words and deeds correspond;
third, adorning the mind so that it is free from blemish.
The fourth is the adornment of the buddha-field, which fulfills all vows;
the fifth is the adornment of transforming sentient beings, through which one's will and nature become pure;
the sixth is the adornment of birth, wherein one commits no transgressions among any evils.
Seventh, the Bodhisattva practices the adornment of training in the conduct of the Tathāgata;
eighth, the adornment of noble wisdom, without harboring self-conceit;
ninth, the adornment of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), encouraging and assisting in all virtues.
The tenth is: the power of fearlessness, adorned by the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), taking the establishment of precepts as the foundation, never abandoning the prohibitions;
this, O Bodhisattva Saṃkusumitarāja!
"Adorned with ten matters.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"What is called the Bodhisattva’s adornment of meditative concentration?"
There is certainly one thing.
What is this one thing?
It is to always maintain a mind of loving-kindness and compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, there are two matters that adorn the concentrated mind.
What are these two?
First is the cultivation of dignified deportment and ritual propriety; second is a nature and conduct that are straightforward and free from flattery or artifice."
“Furthermore, there are three matters that adorn the concentrated mind.
What are these three?
First, the absence of flattery; second, a nature that is pure and harmonious; third, the absence of hypocrisy.”
"Furthermore, there are four matters that adorn the concentration of the mind.
What are the four?

First, being benevolent and harmonious toward others rather than perverse and rebellious; second, not harboring malice or seeking out the faults of others; third, not violating prohibitions that lead to various calamities and hardships; and fourth, not following the foolish and ignorant into the darkness of delusion."
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are five matters that adorn the concentration of the mind, namely, the removal of the five hindrances.
What are these five?
The first is sensual desire; the second is ill will; the third is sloth and torpor; the fourth is restlessness and remorse; and the fifth is doubt.
"Furthermore, there are six matters that adorn the concentrated mind, namely the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*).

What are the six? First, constant mindfulness of the Buddha; second, constant mindfulness of the Dharma; third, constant mindfulness of the Noble Saṃgha; fourth, constant mindfulness of the prohibitive precepts; fifth, constant mindfulness of giving; and sixth, constant mindfulness of the devas."
“Furthermore, there are seven matters that adorn the concentration of the mind, namely: not abandoning the mind of enlightenment while cultivating the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*).

What are the seven? First is the factor of awakening of mindfulness; second is the factor of awakening of the dharma; third is the factor of awakening of joy; fourth is the factor of awakening of diligence; fifth is the factor of awakening of faith; sixth is the factor of awakening of concentration; and seventh is the factor of awakening of equanimity.”
"Furthermore, there are eight matters that adorn meditative concentration, namely the Eightfold Noble Path.

What are these eight? First is right view; second is right livelihood; third is right speech; fourth is right action; fifth is right mindfulness; sixth is right effort; seventh is right intention; and eighth is right concentration."

"Furthermore, there are nine matters that adorn the concentrated mind: namely, that a bodhisattva does not abandon the mind of enlightenment, always establishes great compassion, dwells nowhere, and does not forsake any sentient being."
What are the nine? First:

having eliminated craving and desire, and having stilled all evil and unwholesome karma, one dwells in tranquility and serene joy; with this mindfulness accompanying it, one cultivates the first dhyāna.

Second: that person, having stilled discursive thought and its activity, becomes inwardly composed and focused; being without thought and without activity, they dwell in tranquility and serene joy, cultivating the second dhyāna.

The third is: to perpetually contemplate the practice of joy and detachment from desire while remaining ever serene; his body is at ease, just as described and observed by the noble ones, and his mental activity is peaceful as he cultivates the third dhyāna.

The fourth is: to eliminate both suffering and pleasure, having thoroughly exhausted past states; observing this state where there is neither sorrow nor joy, he cultivates the fourth dhyāna, free from both suffering and pleasure.

The fifth is: to transcend all perceptions of form entirely, reaching the ultimate limit of the nature of things which is like the earth; no longer dwelling on various perceptions, he dwells in the wisdom of immeasurable space and practices therein.
Sixth: Transcending all perceptions of space, one dwells in infinite consciousness and practices with the wisdom of that consciousness;
seventh: completely surpassing all wisdoms of consciousness, one does not reckon a self-body and practices without employing the wisdom of consciousness;
eighth: transcending everything, one practices in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception without employing the wisdom of consciousness.

Ninth: They emerge from all states of perception and non-perception, yet they enter into all that is deluded by conceptual thought; they maintain focused contemplation as their formal meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), yet through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) they do not realize the ultimate limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), remaining instead in their original vows to transform and enlighten sentient beings.
“Furthermore, there are ten matters that adorn the concentrated mind.

What are the ten? First, the mind is without arising and harbors no ill will; second, one is fully endowed with the practice of tranquility; third, one does not abandon one’s vows; fourth, one dwells in quiet seclusion; fifth, one does not lose the roots of virtue; sixth, the mind is serene and detached; seventh, body and mind rest from scheming and calculating; eighth, one attains peace regarding all dharmas; ninth, the mind attains mastery; tenth, one attains the nature of the noble ones.”
"These are the ten matters that constitute the adornment of meditative concentration.
The Buddha addressed the son of good family:
"What is called the bodhisattva’s adornment of wisdom?"
There is one matter that constitutes the adornment of wisdom. What is this one?
It is to be free from impulsiveness regarding all phenomena.
“Furthermore, there are two things that constitute the adornment of wisdom:
first, the relinquishing of doubt; second, the departure from all objects of craving.
Furthermore, there are three things that constitute the adornment of wisdom:”
First, the severing of ignorance and folly;
second, the burning away of nescience and the destruction of the aggregates and realms;
third, the eternal extinction of all that is dark, obscure, and dim.
"Furthermore, there are four matters that constitute the adornment of wisdom:

first, understanding how to sever all sufferings; second, comprehending how to cut off all habitual tendencies; third, clarity regarding the realization of the goal; and fourth, not abiding in the path."
"Furthermore, there are five matters that constitute the adornment of wisdom:
first, the purity of precepts and prohibitions without seeking any gain;
second, the purity of meditative concentration leading to the perfection of wisdom."
Third, purifying the category of liberation and dwelling among sentient beings;
