fourth, purifying the category of knowledge and vision so as to be free from all obstructions throughout the three periods of time;
fifth, purifying the category of phenomena to thereby perfect one's practice.
"Furthermore, there are six matters that adorn wisdom:

namely, the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) purifies the three spheres—purifying one's own sphere because the body is like a mirage, purifying the sphere of others because people are like dreams, and purifying the sphere of the path because there is no expectation of reward;

the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) purifies the three spheres—purifying the sphere of the body because it is like a shadow, purifying the sphere of speech because it is like an echo, and purifying the sphere of the mind because it is like an illusion."

The Perfection of Forbearance (Kṣānti-pāramitā) also purifies the three fields: it abandons coarse speech so that one’s words are pure; it eliminates resentment and always delights in praise; and even if one’s body were to be cut into pieces, one observes the Dharma-body as pure and undefiled. The Perfection of Vigor (Vīrya-pāramitā) also purifies the three fields:

it is pure and tireless, delighting in wandering through birth and death while viewing them as a dream; because its firm and pure resolve is like a diamond, there is neither what is appropriate nor what is inappropriate, for the pure practitioner transcends conceptual attachments.

The Perfection of Meditation (Dhyāna-pāramitā) purifies the three fields: the purity of ignorance is withdrawn into wisdom; the purity of abandonment enters into all dharmas without attachment; and the purity of diligent mind gives rise to supernormal powers (abhijñā).

The Perfection of Wisdom is also pure in three spheres: it is pure in its four reflections because it transforms sentient beings; it is pure in its dhāraṇīs because it gathers the True Dharma; and it is pure in its vows because it adorns the Buddha-lands.
Furthermore, there are seven matters of the adornment of wisdom that protect and sustain the mind:
first, regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, neither arising nor ceasing;
second, regarding the four right efforts, maintaining tranquility of body and mind.
Third, as for their supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*), they clearly understand all faculties (*indriya*);
fourth, as for their five faculties, they subdue and cast off all demonic influences and worldly afflictions;
fifth, as for their five powers (*bala*), they clearly understand the natural state of all phenomena.
Sixth, as for his awakening-mind, there is nothing it does not penetrate, thereby attaining what has never before occurred;
seventh, as for his path, there is no going and no coming, because there is no coming and going.
“Furthermore, there are eight matters that constitute the adornment of wisdom, namely, not losing noble insight while practicing skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*):

first, the tranquility of observing with wisdom and being serene; second, observing and seeing all phenomena as serene; third, the category of wisdom clarifying the category of phenomena; fourth, the category of realms wherein their nature is fundamentally equal to the objective sphere; fifth, understanding that the sense bases (*āyatana*) are fundamentally without desire; sixth, clarifying the twelve links of dependent origination through the realization of non-self (*anātman*); seventh, attaining sincerity and faith so as to be forever free from anger; eighth, the true observation of all phenomena as being indestructible.”
Furthermore, there are nine matters that constitute the adornment of wisdom:
first, knowing past events because they are fundamentally pure;
second, knowing future events because they are yet-to-be and pure.
Third, knowing the present, because it is ultimately pure;
fourth, knowing with complete clarity, because the principle of retribution is never lost;
fifth, knowing that which is not yet determined, because one guides through causes and conditions.
Sixth, to dwell in clarity regarding what is erroneous for the sake of transformation and edification;
seventh, to know the equality of the Buddhas for the sake of realizing the Dharma-body;
eighth, to be equal toward all phenomena because phenomena are devoid of desire.
The ninth is: the equality of all noble ones, because they cultivate the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, there are ten matters that constitute the adornment of wisdom:
the first is that all things are like dreams, because they are the marks of delusion.
The second is: realizing it is like a dream, because it is the characteristic of conceptualization;
the third is: realizing it is like a mirage, because it is the characteristic of discrimination;
the fourth is: realizing it as it truly is, because it is the characteristic of dependent origination.
Fifth, understanding them as being like reflections, because they arise from the conjunction of form and function;
sixth, understanding them as being like echoes, because they result from the meeting of various conditions;
seventh, understanding the dharma-realm, because it is devoid of any characteristic of destruction.
Eighth, they thoroughly understand that there is no fundamental basis, because they do not dwell in signs;
ninth, they thoroughly understand the ultimate limit (*koṭi*), because there is no sign of movement;
tenth, they are enlightened regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), for that which is unconditioned is characterized by spontaneity.
"It is so, son of good family!
These are the ten practices of a bodhisattva adorned with wisdom.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s adornment of dhāraṇī?
It is adorned by a single thing:
that his mind is always penetrating and never forgets."
"Furthermore, there are two matters of the adornment of dhāraṇī:
first, cherishing and embracing the principles of the Way; second, universally encompassing all things without contradiction.
Furthermore, there are three matters of the adornment of dhāraṇī:"
First, to thoroughly understand all meanings; second, to distinguish and adorn with beautiful words; third, to clearly instruct regarding the destination according to appropriate skillful means.
"Furthermore, there are four matters that constitute the adornment of dhāraṇī:
first, speech that is free from attachment; second, speech that is not harsh or rigid; third, speech that is gentle and harmonious; and fourth, speech that is free from sarcasm and reproach."
"Furthermore, there are five matters of the adornment of dhāraṇī: first, all sounds heard are resolved solely into their essential meaning;

second, all bodily consciousnesses are understood as being resolved solely into wisdom; third, all sūtras and scriptures are resolved solely into the principles of the path; fourth, the voices of all people are realized as being resolved solely into the Dharma; and fifth, while remaining within worldly customs, one is resolved into the practice of transcending the world."
"Furthermore, there are six matters of adornment through dhāraṇī:
first, the correspondence between speech and action;
second, compliance with ultimate sincerity, such that one's words are pure."
Third, not harboring arrogance, acting without attachment;
fourth, being free from flattery and deceit, speaking without error;
fifth, cultivating great compassion and preaching the Dharma as is appropriate.
The sixth is: the conventional wisdom that employs skillful means to preach and explain in accordance with the specific dispositions of beings.

Furthermore, there are seven matters: first, the eloquence of wisdom that responds immediately as soon as it is aroused; second, eloquence that accords with the capacities of others; third, eloquence that is swift and nimble; fourth, unimpeded eloquence; fifth, unobstructed eloquence; sixth, flawless eloquence; and seventh, eloquence that accords with the meaning.
"Furthermore, there are eight matters of the adornment of dhāraṇī:

first, clearly understanding the speech of all devas; second, comprehending the sounds of all nāgas; third, discerning the voices and cries of yakṣas and rākṣasas; fourth, distinguishing the language of gandharvas; fifth, understanding the hymns of asuras; sixth, mastering the vocabulary of garuḍas; seventh, articulating the speech of kiṃnaras; and eighth, recognizing that which is proclaimed from the mouths of mahoragas and all other sentient beings."
"Furthermore, there are nine matters of the adornment of dhāraṇī: first, not relying on the unconditioned;

second, being without cowardice regarding all practices one cultivates; third, preaching the Dharma with valor; fourth, possessing noble wisdom that is free from hypocrisy; fifth, clearly understanding and fully mastering what is preached; sixth, preaching the Dharma in accordance with those who are arrogant; seventh, preaching with sincerity and straightforwardness to transform those who have attained impartiality; eighth, manifesting the conflagration at the end of an eon for those who cling to existing places; and ninth, proclaiming the various teachings according to the vehicle studied by those who have attained their respective realms."
"Furthermore, there are ten matters of the adornment of dhāraṇī:
first, following one's own resolve, not to proclaim coarse or harsh words to sentient beings;
second, having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, to cultivate the clarity of wisdom and no longer aspire to worldly knowledge."
Third, words are inexhaustible, being merely provisional expressions;
fourth, because there is nowhere to abide, one speaks of non-abiding;
fifth, one speaks of the immeasurable praises of all Buddhas.
Sixth, to cast off and eliminate the evil realms, worldly afflictions, and coarse speech;
seventh, to speak of nirvana as being beyond measure or limit;
eighth, to endure sentient beings with the root of non-obstruction.
Ninth, following the teachings of the Buddha;
tenth, enduring analytical discernment and transcendent eloquence.
Such, noble son!
“The Bodhisattva’s ten matters of the adornment of dhāraṇī.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning so that people might understand it more deeply, spoke these verses:
“The great sages have four adornments; by means of these, they accord with the truth.”
The Supreme Vehicle of the Honored One—
precepts, meditative concentration, and supreme wisdom— are thus encompassed by dhāraṇī, clearly understood and discerned.
He is revered and respected by all sentient beings; his body, speech, and mind are always pure.
He has completely severed all doubt; in every phrase and track, he who upholds the precepts is adorned thereby.
Born into the world of the devas, their meritorious deeds spread far and wide; whatever their aspirations may be, they are immediately fulfilled.
They constantly cultivate right practice, regarding conduct as supreme; by upholding the pure precepts, they adorn themselves therewith.
That person attains proximity [to the goal] and swiftly reaches a concentrated mind;
their wisdom and liberation, as well as their noble insight, are like this.
Drawing near to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), those who take refuge in this practice possess pure precepts and observances—this constitutes their adornment.
The precepts are observed without flaw or omission; one does not toy with the Dharma of the precepts.
By nature, one is free from violence and abruptness, and one’s reputation and renown overflow. There is nothing that one does not proclaim and uphold;
for those whose precepts are pure, this constitutes true adornment.
Patience is pure, and so too is diligence; the single mind is pure, and wisdom is without distinction;
skillful means are pure, and there is likewise no negligence.
Firmly established and unshakable by force, having attained the stage of clear discernment,
acting without resentment, not lax in nature, always conscientious in intent,
and pure in precepts— this is true adornment.
Never regressing, their minds give rise to no afflictions or fevers;
maintaining their resolve in practice, they never experience regret or change. For those whose precepts are pure, this constitutes true adornment.
Their minds are tranquil, beyond reproach; those who violate the prohibitions are constantly bound and confined, while those whose precepts are pure—this is true adornment.
When one’s mind cultivates the prohibitions, its merit is boundless;
when one’s disposition is benevolent and harmonious, this intention is peaceful and well-regulated. Thus, for one’s own person, the marks and signs of excellence are adorned;
for one whose precepts are pure, this constitutes true adornment.
When one’s bodily conduct is thus, one adorns the mouth;
that which is protected and adorned is not by the dust of desire, but by adorning the mind— this purity of precepts is true adornment.
Such a person acts thus: adorning the Buddha-lands and transforming sentient beings, causing them to enter the Great Way.
This wise one adorns their place of birth; for this reason, they do not commit any evils.
What is called adornment is to constantly uphold the Buddha-way and cultivate the most supreme.
At the Buddha’s site of enlightenment, one adorns the various powers and takes the four fearlessnesses as adornment.
With noble wisdom free from pride, he universally bestows compassion upon all sentient beings.
He is without flattery or deceit, harbors no trivial thoughts, and does not follow after greed, anger, or delusion.
His will and nature are fierce and resolute, and he is free from the five hindrances.
Cultivate the six recollections and remain free from negligence.
For the sake of the seven factors of enlightenment, honor the Way in this manner; gradually and step by step, contemplate all states of meditative concentration.
Associating with those worthy of approach, one cultivates profound stillness; skillfully conforming to the times, one does not lose the multitude of virtues.
Abiding in the joy of quiet contemplation, though what is observed enters into disorder, one attains mastery over the Path and becomes of the lineage of the sages and saints.
Never hesitating, they do not fail to master the scriptures; they are free from doubt and never indulge in lingering indecision.
Having eliminated ignorance, they are devoid of delusion; they always abide in ultimate sincerity and clearly perceive noble wisdom.
One whose precepts are pure has nothing to be attained; with supreme wisdom, their concentration of mind is pure.
By following these two matters, their liberation is pure; one who harbors no pride possesses the purity of noble insight.
Beholding the three periods of time, one delivers all beings through wisdom; understanding and being free from desire, the Dharma is pure.
This purity is such that one harbors no conceit.
That which possesses wisdom is what constitutes adornment.
To serve as such adornment, if one can purify the three spheres—
the self, sentient beings, and the cultivation of the path— viewing them as like a dream, an illusion, or a magical transformation;
Yet they remain without attachment.
Adorned with the wisdom of ethical discipline, they further purify and cultivate the three types of conduct.
The same applies to mental conceptions: they are like images and magical illusions, and like echoes;
this is wisdom, which constitutes true adornment.
Thus they are able to be pure regarding the three types of matters; none can subdue them, nor can they be shaken.
Universally observing all things, they constantly contemplate the Dharma-body;
adorned with wisdom and diligence, they are likewise pure regarding the three types of matters.
Never weary or indolent, their resolve and nature are firm and strong; they never harbor expectations, nor do they fail to respond.
Thus, through wisdom, they adorn the single mind, and by means of these three matters, they cultivate pure practice.
That which he observes is free from darkness or obscurity.
Adorned with skillful means and wisdom, he is likewise pure regarding the three categories of phenomena.
Skillfully receiving the dhāraṇīs, they realize the meaning of equality; they demonstrate the Dharma to sentient beings and also purify the Buddha-lands.
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, their resolve is non-retrogressive;
regarding the four right efforts, they do not engage in dualistic practices.
With body and mind serene and tranquil, this constitutes the divine foot; understanding all things, one knows the fundamental source of the faculties of sentient beings.
Regarding Māra and worldly desires, they are forever non-existent; possessing mastery over all dharmas, one follows and decisively realizes them.
Coming from nowhere, nor reaching a path of arrival—this is majestic deportment, adorned with wisdom.
Bringing about eternal stillness, it constitutes tranquil meditative concentration;
that which is observed therein is a practice without limit or bottom.
He understands the decline of the aggregates (*skandha*) and cultivates the categories of Dharma; he clearly perceives all realms (*dhātu*) as being like empty space.
He discerns that the sense-bases (*āyatana*) are empty and non-existent; phenomena have no self (*ātman*), arising only from conditions.
Thoroughly understanding the ultimate truth, his wisdom is free from resentment and free from fear;
he contemplates the conditions of dependent origination.
Regarding the wisdom of the three periods of time, he is without obstruction; he clearly understands the three aggregates and their respective destinations.
To clearly understand that the Three Jewels are of one single characteristic is the wisdom by which one is adorned.
To clearly understand that they are illusory transformations is to realize them as entirely deceptive appearances; yet, because one follows these deceptive appearances, they are like a dream.
All things are like the plantain tree, being entirely the marks of delusion; all dharmas have no assembly, being like reflected images.
Arising from the conjunction of conditions, they are like the moon in water, and also like an echo, which emerges in response to its cause.
That which is the dharma-realm has wisdom that is eternally indestructible;
it is clearly understood as being without origin, and its gnosis has no place of abiding.
Whether phenomena move or do not move, the ultimate limit (pūrvakoṭi) is eternally thus.
Conditioned and unconditioned—these two do not exist as a duality.
Profound and essential wisdom, with purity as its path, is the adornment of the Dharma of all Buddhas.
That person has never experienced confusion of mind; having encountered and received the dhāraṇī sūtras, they constantly explain them.
Their principles and meanings are subtle and profound, and they always walk the path of the wisdom of nirvāṇa.
His speech is neither abrupt nor violent, nor is it coarse or harsh; that which he proclaims with his mouth is never improper.
Regarding all the sounds he utters, the assembly should examine their meaning; that which they rely upon—the noble wisdom—is always perfectly clear.
Understanding the meanings and principles of the sūtras, there is nothing they have not heard or mastered; they return to the Dharma and do not conceive of a self.
All dharmas take transcending the world as their essence; by means of this dhāraṇī, they adorn themselves.
That which is proclaimed from the mouth always speaks of ultimate sincerity;
that which is spoken by the mouth constantly tends toward equanimity.
As for whatever one does, one always expounds the scriptures; being timely and not in vain, there is no action performed for its own sake.
This person brings this forth and expounds it with eloquence; they swiftly attain right wisdom, which is always free from obstruction.
Dwelling nowhere, they accord with reality without fail, beautifully adorning themselves like a fine flower garland.
Ghosts and spirits, gandharvas, as well as asuras, kinnaras, and mahoragas—
these too clearly understand what sentient beings say.
These do not come here, nor do they abide within the assembly;
yet one perceives them by approaching them.
This courageous one, in order to proclaim the Dharma, realizes it through wisdom.
Those who are conceited, seeing that their minds are harboring disorder, and observing what has been said, comply with it at the proper time;
those who are arrogant and haughty, upon hearing what is spoken,
harbor no malice despite their pride.
Severing all doubts and causing the web of entanglements to vanish, one then attains direct vision of the Buddha-dharma’s true reality; no longer relying on others, such is wisdom.
Regarding all syllables, they are always understood as being extinguished; that which is discerned and understood has no substantial obstruction in its meaning.
They extol the immeasurable merits of the Buddhas; having attained dhāraṇī, they are adorned thereby.
The objects of knowledge are infinite; through skillful means and expedient methods, he transforms beings according to the time.
He understands all things clearly—the fundamental nature of sentient beings and that which is known by all Buddhas—and has attained analytical eloquence.
Those who adorn themselves with the dhāraṇīs, by means of these, their names shall be heard everywhere.
Even if I were to remain for an eon singing praises of their conduct, I could not reach the end of these meritorious achievements.
Chapter Five: The Eight Radiances. The World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Śūraṅgama:
"A bodhisattva possesses eight radiances; by means of these radiances, they leave behind all inconceivable darkness and cultivate pure conduct."
What are the eight? First is the light of mindfulness;

second is the light of resolve; third is the light of wandering; fourth is the light of the Dharma; fifth is the light of wisdom; sixth is the light of sincerity; seventh is the light of supernormal powers; eighth is the light of practice;
these are the eight great lights of a bodhisattva.
"In that regard, what is meant by 'the light of mindfulness'?
There are eight things that constitute the light of mindfulness.
What are these eight?

He never forgets the roots of the manifold virtues cultivated in the past; he daily accumulates merit for virtues not yet established; he never forgets the teachings as they were heard, attaining knowledge of their meaning and principles and discerning their direction; he does not follow the six elements but achieves the gateway of mindfulness; he severs all that is unrighteous and fulfills wholesome virtues; beholding those with strong resolve, he observes what has been established by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; he protects and upholds the city of Dharma, fixing his will upon the source; and he attains the various radiances of the virtues of all dharmas. For these reasons, these are the eight radiances of a bodhisattva.
"It is said that there are eight further matters regarding the illumination of one's resolve.

What are these eight? To resolve upon understanding the principles of meaning without harboring ostentation; to resolve upon noble wisdom without harboring attachment to consciousness; to resolve upon the Dharma without harboring worldly desires; to resolve upon diligence without harboring contention; to resolve upon the Buddha-way without harboring the paths of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; to resolve upon the sublime without harboring the Lesser Vehicle; to resolve upon the Buddha without harboring the works of Māra; and to resolve upon great kindness and great compassion, never harboring malice toward sentient beings."
These are the eight matters of the radiance of one's resolve.
Furthermore, there are eight matters regarding the radiance of one's practice. What are these eight?

In all places where he travels, he constantly proclaims the Dharma; in his travels, he knows the aspirations and thoughts of sentient beings; in the places where he travels, he possesses analytical wisdom; in the places where he travels, he always understands the profound and subtle twelvefold dependent origination; in the places where he travels, he has eloquent expositions that reach everywhere without obstruction; in the places where he travels, he clearly comprehends the purity and the prior or subsequent increases and decreases [of phenomena]; in the places where he travels, he is universally equipped with all the teachings of the Buddhas—these are the eight.
"The light of the Dharma further possesses eight aspects. What are these eight? Its radiance illuminates the world and provides explanations for entering the roots of goodness;

it further expounds for sentient beings the Dharma that transcends the world to clarify noble wisdom; it instructs them to eliminate all dharmas of transgression; the light of the untainted Dharma skillfully proclaims the Way and its teachings; it does not abide in ignorance or the various outflows, yet perceives the destinations of the sins and blessings within birth and death; having observed this, the light of dust and desire does not fall into extinction, but rather attains realization; this light of the Dharma skillfully examines the source of adventitious defilements; the light of the unconditioned Dharma is pure in the fundamental nature of the mind, naturally fresh and clean, with all dharmas eternally quiescent."
These are the eight matters.
Furthermore, there are eight matters regarding the light of wisdom. What are these eight?

The first is the light of the eightfold noble path; the second is the light of wisdom regarding the tracks of the various paths; the third is the light of illumination for those who come and go (the once-returner); the fourth is the radiance of non-returning; the fifth is the manifestation of the splendor of non-attachment; the sixth is the majestic radiance of the pratyekabuddha; the seventh is the luminous wisdom of the bodhisattva; the eighth is the radiance of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. These are the eight.
"The radiance of utmost sincerity further consists of eight matters. What are these eight? When one falls into cessation through the practice of utmost sincerity, it illuminates that state;

when one’s practice is truthful and constitutes the first stage of the path (*srota-āpanna*), the light of wisdom illuminates that; when one’s practice is truthful and attains the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*), it likewise illuminates that; when one’s practice is truthful and attains the third fruit (*anāgāmin*), it likewise illuminates that; when one’s practice is truthful and attains the fourth fruit (*arhat*), it likewise illuminates that; when one’s practice is truthful and attains the fruit of a *pratyekabuddha*, it likewise illuminates that; when one’s practice is truthful and attains the patience (*kṣānti*) of a bodhisattva, it likewise illuminates that; and when one’s practice is truthful and achieves Buddhahood and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), it likewise illuminates that."
These are the eight.
Furthermore, there are eight matters concerning the light of supernormal powers. What are these eight?

What are called "lights" are those that illuminate everything without exception: the light of the divine eye perceives all forms and images; the light of the divine ear universally hears all sounds by forever stilling all echoes; the light of mindfulness perceives the deeds of incalculable past kalpas; the light of fundamental purity observes the mental activities of all sentient beings as being like empty space; the light of unimpededness allows one to travel by supernormal power to infinite Buddha-lands; the light of wisdom achieves the state of an untainted sage; the light of accumulated merit transforms and edifies sentient beings, causing them to cultivate wholesome karma; and the light of the work of wisdom cuts through all the knots of doubt and delusion of sentient beings. These are the eight matters.
"Furthermore, there are eight matters for the practice of radiance.

They are: first, to cultivate noble wisdom; second, to resolve upon the clarity of wisdom; third, to practice the light of right view; fourth, to honor the light of contemplation; fifth, to illuminate the nature of sentient beings with brilliance; sixth, to cultivate a mind of liberation; seventh, to possess a mind free from anger; and eighth, to cultivate that radiance so as to bring it to ultimate perfection."
"These are the eight.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"By virtue of pure deeds in the past, The mind never for a moment forgets them."
The mind practices that which is practiced by none; it is well-encouraged and never indolent or abandoned.
What has been heard is never forgotten, and one swiftly attains understanding of the meaning of the Dharma.
In the tranquil realm of sublime stillness, the will is firm and one abandons what is not the Dharma.
Thoroughly understanding the gateway of mindfulness, Discerning the karma one has created,
The courageous one beholds it and establishes supreme mastery.
Guarding the city of the Dharma, He regards the Dharma of all sentient beings as equal to one.
The wise one leaves behind all darkness and brings benefit to all living beings.
Having attained radiant illumination, they resolve doubts and eliminate hesitation;
with firm resolve and mastery of wisdom, they swiftly achieve the path of Buddhahood.
Their resolve is set upon righteousness and principle; they do not indulge in luxury or outward adornment.
The wise practitioner does not cling to conceptualizations nor rely upon mere words.
Those whose resolve is fixed on the Dharma skillfully subdue desire and abandon delusion.
With the will set upon pure skillful means, one dwells peacefully in the Way without contention.
Keeping the mind ever fixed on the Way, one does not think of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
constantly cherishing subtle and wondrous deeds, one does not think of the Hīnayāna.
Contemplating the Buddha-way, they do not follow the teachings of the Māras;
always harboring great compassion, they do not afflict sentient beings.
Whatever they proclaim, wherever they travel, they remain free from doubt.
Transforming sentient beings according to the times, wherever the various classes of living beings may go;
his eloquence distinguishes all that he traverses, for his wisdom is without obstruction.
He is clear regarding the dharma of causes and conditions, yet there is no phenomenon of dependent origination.
Thoroughly understanding the wisdom of skillful means, they abide securely upon the summit of their stride;
they are able to universally enter all the dharmas raised up by the Buddhas.
With the light of worldly dharmas, they fully know the karmic actions of all people.
Possessing the transcendent, holy wisdom, he is a hero who acts as the light of insight.
His birth is free from fault or transgression; with great wisdom, he cultivates primordial purity.
He skillfully follows the Path and constantly proclaims the karma of non-offense.
Regarding outflows and the absence of outflows, the light of the Dharma shines brilliantly;
severing all outflows, it brings benefit and profit to sentient beings.
Whether in the conditioned or the unconditioned, the Dharma constantly dwells within wisdom.
Stainless and free from darkness, they enter the practice of cessation;
amidst the afflictions and all disputes, their wisdom is unobstructed.
Clearly discerning the various defilements and desires, their minds are fundamentally pure.
Their wisdom attains extinction; they understand that non-arising is quiescent.
Such types are infinite; this is the luminous activity of the Mahāyāna.
Through the eightfold equal wisdom, they travel and reach the tracks of the Path.
They also clearly understand coming and going, and discern what has not yet been attained.
The unattached ones, the pratyekabuddhas, and the Bodhisattvas, the protectors who roar like lions in the world—all possess the wisdom that can reach this;
they travel through the liberation of the sages and saints.
Utmost sincerity is immeasurable clarity; through courageous and skillful practice, one attains the realization of the fruit. To be free from resentment is the foremost;
for one whose conduct is most sincere, entry into tranquility is the foremost fruit.
The second, third, and fourth [stages], reaching the fruit of a pratyekabuddha;
even if one were to apply further diligence and reach the equanimity of dharma-patience,
just as the Most Victorious One attained the Way, with utmost sincerity he illuminates them all.
Furthermore, with their divine eye, they see the Buddhas of the ten directions;
having perfected the divine ear, they hear the sounds of the ten directions.
They recollect and remember hundreds of millions of kalpas, the light of wisdom from their past lives.
Following along, they know the minds of others; their pure wisdom illuminates all.
They travel through billions of buddha-fields, their supernormal powers shining throughout the ten directions.
Leaping lightly like the void, they attain the wisdom of the unconditioned.
The light of his merit is bottomless; with supernormal powers he benefits sentient beings.
His realm of wisdom is without obstruction, resolving the doubts of the masses.
He practices according to what is right, his will firm in the light of the Dharma-wisdom.
Reaching the fulfillment of infinite clarity, one then becomes the light of supernormal powers.
Cultivating noble wisdom, with a vast mind and bottomless eloquence,
one views right view with equanimity, ultimately free from all fetters and resentment.
"Purifying these eight [realms], this radiance and majesty are infinite;
though he has not yet attained the Way of the Buddha, he constantly performs the work of a Buddha.
— *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Scroll II.
The Scripture of Great Compassion, Scroll Three, translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi, Chapter Six:
On Great Compassion. Chapter Six: On Great Compassion.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Śūraṅgama:
"A bodhisattva has sixteen matters through which they constantly apply great compassion to sentient beings.
What are these sixteen?"

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva eliminates attachment to views and the body; for sentient beings who dwell amidst various false views, he severs their delusions, doubts, and karmic actions, and expounds the Dharma for them—this is the Bodhisattva’s arousal of great compassion for sentient beings.

“Sentient beings dwell in falsehood and perversion—perceiving the impermanent as permanent, suffering as pleasure, the selfless as self, and the impure as pure. To eliminate these perverted practices, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for them and preaches the sūtras.”

“Sentient beings dwell in the conceit of a self—perceiving that which is entirely formless as having form—and for the sake of removing this notion of self, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion toward them and proclaims the Way of the Sūtras.”

"These sentient beings dwell amidst the five hindrances that shroud them from within; they fall into the wounds of desire which bring much harm, and are covered by the conditions of drowsiness, ignorance, hypocrisy, and doubt, failing to comprehend the profound Dharma.
I shall remove these various veils for them; thus, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion toward them and preaches the scriptural teachings."

“Sentient beings dwell within the obstructions of the six sense-faculties—seeing forms with the eye, they conceive thoughts of them as embellishments; hearing sounds, smelling odors, tasting flavors, feeling touches with the body, and cognizing mental phenomena with the mind, they harbor thoughts of them as pleasant sensations and embellishments. For their sake, the Bodhisattva eliminates these six sense-faculties and, out of great compassion, expounds the Way of the Sūtras.”

“Sentient beings dwell in arrogance, self-importance, and pride, seeking honor; they harbor malice and hypocrisy, thinking, ‘Is this my own free will? Is this my own ambition? They despise others while regarding themselves as noble and honorable, claiming their own conduct is upright and superior. They further exalt their mastery of the scriptures and the Way, and being haughty in their physical appearance, they falsely imagine themselves possessed of true wisdom and indulge themselves in self-indulgence. Having attained nothing at all, they claim to have achieved perfection; they envy the virtuous though they are not virtuous, and envy the sages though they are not sages.

Dwelling in false views, they imagine themselves abiding in the Right Path. For these beings, I shall preach to eliminate arrogance, conceit, and self-importance; thus, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for them and preaches the Way.”
“Sentient beings dwell in delusion and on deviant paths, having strayed from the noble way;
I shall eliminate their errors and reveal the noble path. Thus, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for them and preaches the Way of the Sūtras.
“Sentient beings dwell in attachment to deceptive endearments; they crave wives, children, sons, daughters, homes, and property, striving day and night without ceasing.
To eliminate this and cause them to be liberated from such endearments, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for them and preaches the Way of the Sūtras.”
“Sentient beings dwell amidst mutual strife and litigation, harboring resentment and discord, and are full of malice and anger as they engage in many disputes and legal wranglings;
for the sake of eliminating such conflict and hatred, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion toward them and preaches the Way of the Sūtras.”
“Sentient beings dwell under the influence of evil associates, are separated from virtuous friends, and engage in the commission of evil karma;
to eliminate these various evil acquaintances and lead them toward virtuous friends, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for them and preaches the Way of the sutras.”
"The devas dwell in stinginess, greed, and gluttony; they do not know weariness and are devoid of noble wisdom.
To eliminate this stinginess, greed, and gluttony, and to cause noble wisdom to flourish, the Bodhisattva arouses great compassion toward them and preaches the Way of the Sūtras for them."
“Sentient beings abide in unwholesome karma, maintaining views of eternalism or nihilism;
the Bodhisattva, giving rise to great compassion for them, teaches the path of the Dharma so that they may enter into the profound karma of dependent origination.”
“Sentient beings dwell in the darkness of ignorance and delusion, clinging to the notions of self, person, and life-span;
I shall eliminate all their false views and cause them to attain the pure eye of the noble ones—thus does the Bodhisattva give rise to great compassion for them and preach the Way of the sutras.”
“Sentient beings dwell amidst the pleasures of birth and death, having encountered the five aggregates, which are like thieves of the five limbs;
for their sake, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion and preaches the Way of the Sūtras to remove all attachments within the three realms.”
“Sentient beings dwell bound by the fetters of demonic views; they dwell in the conceptualization that ‘this is mine’ and in deliberations over what should or should not be done.

The Bodhisattva, giving rise to great compassion for them, preaches the path of the Dharma to cause them to be liberated from the binding fetters of the demonic net and their reliance upon and attachment to such things.”

“Sentient beings dwell with the gate of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) blocked and the door to the evil destinies (apāya) opened; therefore, one should open the gate of nirvāṇa for them, and the Bodhisattva, giving rise to great compassion (mahākaruṇā), preaches the Way of the Sūtras to them.”
The Buddha said to Śūraṅgama Bodhisattva:
"These are the sixteen matters by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to great compassion and extends it to sentient beings."
Chapter Seven: On Conversion The Sutra of Great Compassion, Chapter Seven: On Conversion At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Śūraṅgama:
"Furthermore, there are thirty-two matters through which the wholesome karma one cultivates eliminates the karma of evil that is contrary to the teachings."
What are the thirty-two?

"When sentient beings abide in the sleep of self-conceit and perceive only their own bodies, the Bodhisattva uses wisdom to transform and guide them, causing them to enter the meaning of the Way; this is the first task of a Bodhisattva."
"If there are those who take pleasure in the small and inferior vehicles and harbor notions of 'self' and 'person,' I shall transform them so that they enter the subtle, infinite Mahāyāna.

If sentient beings dwell in non-Dharma, hold wrong views, or cling to a self-identity, I shall transform them, encouraging and guiding them by means of the principles of the True Dharma in which I myself delight."
“Beholding sentient beings whose precepts are not pure,
yet whose physical actions are fresh and clean and whose fundamental nature is harmonious, he transforms and enlightens those beings by means of such karma.
Seeing sentient beings fallen into false views and the sixty-two doubts, he guides and establishes the masses through right view and the karma of the noble ones.”

"Seeing that sentient beings exist in ignorance and possess perverted thoughts, one transforms them by revealing the light of the Way; through contemplation and compliance, they likewise establish themselves in the meaning of purity and harmony."
"Seeing that sentient beings are far removed from the practice of the Dharma,
he personally cultivates the Dharma and also transforms others to abide in the True Dharma, while further expounding the meaning of the sutras according to the occasion."
"Seeing sentient beings shrouded by stinginess, they themselves are free from craving in body and mind;
they are able to bestow all that they possess as gifts, and they are also able to transform others so that they too may give away all their possessions."
“Seeing sentient beings committing various evils and dwelling in a lack of heedfulness,
he himself upholds the pure precepts and also transforms others, establishing them in pure karma.
Seeing sentient beings engaged in much litigation and dispute, with anger flourishing profusely;”
Personally cultivating patience and practicing the power of a compassionate mind, they likewise transform others to uphold loving-kindness and pity.
Seeing sentient beings dwelling in indolence and falling into many neglects,
they themselves do not grow weary but diligently practice vigor, and likewise transform others to exert effort from dawn until night.

"Seeing that the minds of sentient beings are agitated and their wills are dissolute, he himself restrains his thoughts and practices single-minded dhyāna, ensuring his mind does not wander and remains composed; he likewise transforms others, establishing them in dignified decorum."
"Seeing sentient beings dwelling in perverse cleverness, arrogance, and self-importance;
yet cultivating wisdom within themselves to distance themselves from ignorance and darkness—one then uses great wisdom to transform them, causing them to eliminate their obscurity."
“Sentient beings abide in untimely conduct and thus their bodies naturally perish;
through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they cultivate impartial conduct and likewise transform others, employing expedient strategies according to the times and upholding impartial karma.”
“Sentient beings dwell amidst the dust of desire; their thoughts are perilous and largely impure in practice.
They should permanently eliminate the source of affection and craving within both the appropriate and inappropriate bodies, and likewise transform others to remove all defilements.”
"Seeing that sentient beings dwell in a body of greed and thereby incur the calamities of punishment, imprisonment, and bondage;
he removes from his own person the difficulties of the various fetters born of self-greed, and likewise transforms others so they may abandon the body of greed and all its inversions."
"Seeing that sentient beings are undisciplined and lack tranquility, do not accord with the teachings of the Vinaya, and have not yet attained liberation;

whereas he himself is tranquil, disciplined, and concentrated, having attained liberation in accordance with the teachings of the Vinaya, he likewise transforms others so that they become disciplined, concentrated, and accord with the Vinaya."
"Seeing those among sentient beings who do not practice filial piety and lack reciprocity, thereby destroying the roots of all virtues;

one should personally uphold the Way of Filiality and cultivate kindness and righteousness to protect the source of goodness, exhorting and establishing others to practice filial service, and constantly mindful of reciprocity so as not to lose the roots of virtue."
“Sentient beings dwell amidst obstructions and veils, following evil teachings;
they must transcend these veils and obstructions themselves, and likewise transform others so that all may leave behind such obstructions.
Sentient beings dwell amidst teachings that are not free from evil, neither returning to the former sages nor following the multitudes of blessings;”

Personally upholding the noble precepts and following the teachings of the wise, he also transforms others to comply with ancient virtues and receive instruction from those who have attained prior realization.
"While sentient beings dwell amidst many meaningless and hypocritical practices, rushing about in haste;

I personally accord with righteous principles and devote myself to the roots of all virtues, and likewise transform others to encourage diligent cultivation, establishing the sources of all that is good."
"May all people, who currently abide in conduct of poverty and are devoid of the wealth of the noble ones,

cultivate the inexhaustible sevenfold wealth within themselves— faith, precepts, shame, dread of blame, learning, generosity, and wisdom— and likewise encourage others to establish themselves in these seven noble riches."
“Sentient beings dwell amidst constant afflictions, borne upon the four venomous serpents;
yet they cultivate a body free from illness, peaceful and desireless, and likewise transform all people so that they may eliminate all maladies and forever be free from hardship.”
“Sentient beings dwell in manifold darkness, far removed from the radiance of wisdom;
[the Bodhisattva] cultivates the brilliance of the body to transform and establish all people in the infinite great light.
Sentient beings dwell within the obstructions of the triple world, revolving endlessly through the five destinies of birth and death;”
Having personally severed attachment to the three realms, he transforms all people by removing the fetters of the three realms according to the occasion.
While all people abide in the karma of the left path and depart from the right path,
he himself cultivates the right path and establishes all people so that they dwell upon the right path.
“Sentient beings dwell attached to their bodies and lives, failing to perceive their perils;

yet they do not cherish their bodies or spare their lives, seeing the source of these calamities, and thus they transform others so that they too do not rely upon body or life, but discern and understand all manner of hardships.”
“Sentient beings dwell apart from the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha;
yet, personally cultivating virtue, they do not sever the Three Jewels, and they transform and establish others so that they follow the teachings of the Three Jewels.
They see sentient beings abandoning the True Dharma;”
He protects the sūtras himself and transforms others to protect the great canon, proclaiming the Buddha’s teachings and establishing them in the True Dharma.
Seeing sentient beings dwelling far from the World-Honored One, he teaches them the six recollections;
he personally follows these six recollections and also transforms others to uphold them.
"Seeing sentient beings following the karma of afflictions, sins, and merits;
he himself remains free from the dust of transgressions and also transforms the multitude, causing them to abandon calamity and defilement.
Seeing sentient beings following all unwholesome dharmas and universally abandoning all wholesome dharmas..."
He personally cultivates wholesome dharmas and abandons unwholesome ones, and he also transforms the multitude so that they abide in the true, correct, and compliant Dharma.
"It is thus, son of good family!"
The bodhisattva’s practice of impartial karma should be established; if one can accord with this, one honors the true and supreme great task.
Chapter Eight: The Wisdom of the Path. In the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Chapter Eight: The Wisdom of the Path, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Śūraṅgama-rāja, saying:
“Furthermore, son of good family!
The deeds of a bodhisattva are beyond measure.

Why is this? If one considers the gateways of greed and contention among sentient beings, the bodhisattva’s cultivation of deeds, accumulation of merit, and gathering of various practices culminate in the first gateway of the Dharma.
Furthermore, son of good family!

Suppose all sentient beings filling as many Buddha-worlds as there are sands in the Ganges were each established as śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; the merit of all these sentient beings established in such wholesome karma would not equal even a hundredth, a thousandth, a ten-thousandth, a hundred-millionth, or a hundred-billionth part of the merit of a bodhisattva who has resolved their mind [on enlightenment]—it is beyond comparison.

Why is this so? It is because they have severed the habitual dust and desires of their own fundamental nature; whereas Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas abide in the conjunction of conditions, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas eliminate all conjunctions of conditions upon which the afflictions of sentient beings depend.
Noble son!

Whatever karma all sentient beings may create, and whatever roots of merit the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas establish—compared to the karma of a bodhisattva, these are inferior, they are not supreme, and they have no peer.

Why is this so? It is because ordinary, foolish people habitually follow inverted and contrary karma; Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas likewise follow their respective conditions in their practice; and as for the karma of Bodhisattvas, they possess immeasurable merit that may appear inverted.
"For this reason, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva surpasses all sentient beings and transcends the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvashvararāja, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; a virtuous mind arose within him, and he offered praise and encouragement, saying:
"What the World-Honored One has expounded is most unprecedented—difficult to reach, truly difficult to reach!"
The Tathāgata has proclaimed the adornments of bodhisattvas, the radiance of bodhisattvas, the great compassion of bodhisattvas, and the transformative deeds of bodhisattvas.

We pray that the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, will extend his grace and protection widely, and explain once more: for what reason do the Buddhas give rise to great compassion toward sentient beings?
To what can Great Compassion be compared?
By what means may its nature be likened?
What are its auspicious responses, and in what does it abide?
"How do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, perform their deeds?
Excellent, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata knows all and can see everywhere; regarding all deeds performed, he perceives them with complete success. Pray, explain this in detail for our sake."
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra:
“Listen attentively and reflect well; the Tathāgata shall now proclaim the great compassion of the Tathāgata and the karmic deeds performed by the Tathāgata.”
O son of good family, know this!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not give rise to great compassion, nor do they practice it. Why is this so?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly exercise great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and do not abandon sentient beings; this has been accomplished through the accumulation of countless merits.
For this very reason, they do not regress nor do they forsake sentient beings; this is what is called the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata.
That compassion is immeasurable, beyond calculation, difficult to withstand, and finds no place of containment; from beginning to end, it can never be fully described or contained. Why is this so?
When the Tathāgata attained the Way, he constantly harbored great compassion for all sentient beings; as his Buddha-way is, so too is his great compassion.
What is meant by the Tathāgata’s attainment of the Buddha-way?
Without root and without dwelling, one attains the Great Way.
What is meant by "dwelling in the root"?
It is to calculate the root of the body and establish oneself in the source of insincere thought.
For this reason, the Tathāgata, in accordance with the times, realizes the Path, which is called "rootless" and is likewise without any abiding place.
By means of this, the Tathāgata attains supreme perfect enlightenment, and thereby fully understands that all sentient beings are without abiding and without root.
Understanding their situation, one should proclaim such principles to them so that they may comprehend them; for this reason, the Tathāgata always harbors great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Way is tranquil and, moreover, serene.
What is meant by 'tranquil'? "
What is meant by "serenity"?
It is to be tranquil within and serene without. Why is this so?
That eye is empty; one observes that there is no self and nothing to be grasped.

The eye, ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind are likewise empty; they too have no self and nothing to be grasped. This is called the emptiness of the eye; to discern and eliminate this so as not to be distracted by forms is called tranquility (*śānta*).
The ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind are likewise empty; to discern and eliminate this so as not to be driven by the perceptions of various phenomena is called serenity (*praśrabdha*).
Sentient beings are unable to comprehend this profound stillness; because they do not clearly recognize it, the Tathāgata harbors great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Way is fundamentally pure and also radiant.
That which is called 'purity' refers to the mind being fundamentally pure."
What is meant by saying that its essence is pure and also luminous?
That which is called "pure" is so because it is without attachment and without transgression, being equal to empty space.
Because emptiness is fundamentally pure, it is identical with emptiness; because it is equal to empty space, it is called the "emptiness-equality aggregate.
Because it is ultimately and fundamentally pure and also supremely radiant, it is therefore named "fundamentally pure radiance."
Ignorant ordinary beings do not realize its true nature; instead, they perceive it as defiled by adventitious dust. I shall liberate them and reveal its original purity and radiance.
For this reason, the Tathāgata harbors great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Way has neither diligence nor lack of diligence.
What is meant by neither diligence nor lack of diligence?
To encompass all dharmas is what is called "non-exertion.
For one who has already been able to receive and practice all dharmas, the Tathāgata likewise possesses neither exertion nor non-exertion; thus, he crosses over all torrents.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata does not perceive this shore or that shore within the flowing stream of existence; for this reason, he is said to be "detached from both this and that.
Because the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, has fully understood all phenomena, he has attained Perfect Enlightenment; it is for this reason that he is called the Tathāgata.

This state is neither diligence nor non-diligence, yet foolish and ignorant worldlings do not understand it; I shall proclaim it in detail so that they may comprehend its meaning—for this reason, the Tathāgata harbors great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Way is without conceptualization and without causes or conditions.
What is meant by being without conceptualization and without causes or conditions?
That eye is non-apprehendable within consciousness.
That which is without ideation does not perceive forms, and thus lacks causes and conditions;
the same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—they too are non-apprehendable and devoid of ideation.
When one does not perceive any phenomena, there are no causes or conditions; this state of being without conceptualization and without objective conditions is the practice of the noble ones (*ārya*).
What is meant by "noble practice"?
To have no activity within the three realms is the practice of the noble ones; this very non-activity is the practice of the noble ones.

Foolish and ignorant worldlings cannot understand this noble and holy practice; I shall enlighten them so that they may discern it. For this reason, the Tathāgata harbors great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Way has no going, no coming, and no present; it is equal throughout the three periods of time and severs the three fields.
What are the three fields?

His mind does not regress as it dwells upon the past, nor does it race toward the wisdom of the future, nor does it retreat from mindfulness of present affairs; it abides nowhere within the mind, intellect, or consciousness.
Not dwelling on the past, not anticipating the future, and not playing with the present—by being equal toward these three, one purifies the three spheres.
Foolish worldlings cannot understand this noble practice; I shall awaken them so that they may discern it. For this reason, the Tathāgata harbors great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Way is without body and likewise without number; it has no consciousness of form, nor ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, or consciousness.
That which is cognized is unconditioned and without number."
That which is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not arise, does not perish, and has no location; this is what is meant by being free from the three marks.
Therefore, just as the unconditioned is as it is in its unconditioned nature, the understanding of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is likewise the same.
Why is this? All that exists is of the nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) and is entirely non-existent; that which is non-existent is non-dual.
For this reason, there is neither body nor conditioned activity (*asaṃskṛta*).
Foolish and ignorant worldlings are unable to comprehend this; I shall enlighten them so that they may discern it. For this reason, the Tathāgata harbors great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Way leaves no trace of destruction.
What is meant by 'trace'? "
What is meant by "indestructible"?
That which has no origin is the trace; that which has no abiding place is called "indestructible.
The realm (*dhātu*) is the trace; being without self, it is indestructible.
The ultimate limit (*koṭi*) is the trace; it is without movement and without destruction.
Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the trace; it is without acquisition and without destruction.
Signlessness (*animitta*) is the trace; it is without conceptualization and without destruction.
The wishless is the track, which is neither localized nor subject to destruction;
Nirvāṇa is the track, which is indestructible and immutable.

This track of non-destruction cannot be understood by foolish, ignorant worldlings; I shall therefore awaken them so that they may discern it. For this reason, the Tathāgata harbors great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Way does not achieve perfect enlightenment through the body, nor does it do so through the mind. Why is this? Because..."
The body is foolish and deluded, like grass, trees, walls, tiles, stones, or shadows;
the mind is like an illusion.
To realize the body and mind in this way is called the Way.
One may use provisional words and phrases to speak of flourishing, yet that Way is without words or phrases, and is likewise without body or mind.
Therein, there is neither dharma nor non-dharma, neither the Way nor non-Way, and neither sincerity nor deception.
Why is this so? The Way is beyond words.
Since there is no "Way" within any phenomena, what place could it occupy?
Regarding speech, there is nothing that is spoken; it is like space, which has no location, no place of abiding, and no words.
The Way is also like this: it has no place of abiding and no verbal expressions.
Thus, when one earnestly seeks the Way among all dharmas, there are no words or phrases, for the Dharma itself is also wordless.
If one can thoroughly understand that all dharmas are wordless, this is the source from which all dharmas arise.

Foolish and ignorant worldlings have not yet attained understanding; I shall enlighten them so that they may discern this. For this reason, the Tathāgata harbors great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Way is without grasping and without dependence.
What is meant by being without grasping and without dependence?
One cuts off visual consciousness and does not perceive forms, nor is there anything to be attained;
one does not rely on the ear, nose, body, tongue, or mind, and for one who has cut off the absence of consciousness, there is neither perception nor anything to be attained.

That all dharmas are without acquisition is called being without reliance. By means of this non-appropriation and non-reliance, the Tathāgata has entered the Way and attained supreme perfect enlightenment.
The eye does not rely upon the reception of forms, nor does consciousness regress from it;

the ear regarding sounds, the nose regarding odors, the tongue regarding flavors, the body regarding tangibles, and the mind regarding mental objects likewise have no place of reliance, nor does consciousness regress from them.
Having already ceased to dwell in consciousness, one is then able to discern the mental abodes of all these sentient beings.
What is meant by the mental abodes of sentient beings?
There are four matters regarding the mental abodes of sentient beings.
What are the four?
First is the locus of form and mind; second is sensation; third is perception; and fourth is the locus of volitional formations and consciousness.
He abides nowhere within any location; the Tathāgata clearly understands this at the limit of non-abiding.
Foolish and ignorant ordinary beings cannot comprehend it; I shall awaken them so that they may discern this. For this reason, the Tathāgata harbors great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Way is emptiness.
That which is called 'emptiness' means that the Way is itself empty."
That which is empty is such that all phenomena are empty.

The Tathāgata realized therein the emptiness of no-origination; having understood all phenomena, he attained perfect enlightenment, and because even emptiness is itself empty, he achieved perfect enlightenment.
By means of this single wisdom, one distinguishes the phenomena of emptiness; yet those are non-dual.
As for that non-duality, emptiness and the wisdom of the Path are without duality.
Since they are without duality, all phenomena are without duality.
When duality no longer exists, there is no name and no perception; there is no foundation and no activity; there is nothing to be disseminated, nor anything that can be spoken of.
That which is relied upon and received is the point of resort, but it is not the true meaning of reality.
"What dharma exists that can attain form?
Vimalakīrti replied, "It is called 'emptiness,' which is like empty space.
That which is called 'empty space' is called 'the emptiness of emptiness' because empty space is beyond words; even this absence of words is itself empty."
The locus and function of all phenomena are such as this; reaching the state of namelessness, one does not speak of having names.
Thus, there is neither pride nor speech, and even the locus has no place to abide. Since pride and discourse have ceased and the locus is non-existent, names likewise are thus.
Regarding the Dharma that is taught, one further considers that such Dharma has neither verbal instruction nor non-instruction;
all phenomena are likewise thus.
Birth is also like this, being neither correct nor erroneous.
The Tathāgata is unborn and fully understands that there is no fundamental origin.
That which the Tathāgata knows and that from which he is liberated—being neither unbound nor bound—is called equality.

Foolish and ignorant worldlings are unable to understand this; I shall enlighten them so that they may discern it. For this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Way is equal to space.
That which is space is without equality and without deviation; [the Way is likewise so]."
The Way is also like this: it is without equality and without deviation.
When one calculates among all things that are equal, there is no one who attains the Way; therein, there is neither equality nor deviation.

The Tathāgata, by means of this peerless and non-perverted understanding that all dharmas are fundamentally without origin, has attained supreme perfect enlightenment; furthermore, regarding all dharmas, he neither accepts the correct nor accepts the erroneous, in accordance with the categories of dharmas and the categories of wisdom, just as he upholds the holy intent of the Buddha.
What are the noble dharmas of the Buddha?
That which is received is said to exist; this, however, leads one back to that which is not received.
This state of non-existence has no master, and by means of this spontaneity, one attains fulfillment.
Detached from spontaneity, there is no further wandering; there is neither progress nor retreat—this is called "advancing.
Where there is something to be eliminated, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to sever such conduct.
Foolish and ignorant worldlings are unable to understand this; I shall enlighten them so that they may discern it. For this reason, the Tathāgata harbors great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Way is like the true trace.
What is meant by the 'true trace'? "
Just as the Way is thus, so too is form thus—without origin and without regression;
just as the Way is thus, so too are sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise without origin and without regression;
just as the Way is thus, so too are the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind likewise thus and without regression.

Furthermore, it is like the path: the element of the eye, the element of form, and the element of eye-consciousness, as well as the various elements of the ear, nose, body, tongue, mind, and mental phenomena, likewise have no fundamental basis and are non-retrogressive.

All dharmas are severed from the outflows and bring about the realization of the seeds of the three periods of time and the various sense bases; therein the Tathāgata awakens to the True Reality and attains Perfect Enlightenment, and that which he has fully understood does not arise from inversion.
Furthermore, as with the past, so it is with the middle and the future; that which has no origin does not undergo retrogression, and that which is of the fundamental seed is unarisen.
Other seeds are likewise unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The central essence is serene and detached; this is what is called the trace of the true reality (*tattva*).

Furthermore, as one thing is thus, so are all things; as all things are thus, so is one thing. That which is thus in one thing is likewise so in many, yet it cannot be apprehended—this is the true reality.
Foolish and ignorant ordinary beings cannot understand this; I shall enlighten them so that they may discern it. For this reason, the Tathāgata harbors great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
As for the Way, to enter the chamber is to enter the chamberless.
What is meant by 'chamber'? "
What is meant by "having no dwelling"?
To cultivate all virtues and wholesome dharmas is called having a dwelling; to have no attainment regarding any dharma is called having no dwelling.
Therefore, it is called "no chamber" because the mind has no dwelling place and no location; hence it is called "no chamber.
Because it reaches the gate of liberation through the samādhi of non-conceptualization, it is called "no chamber";
because it observes, conceives, weighs, calculates, transcends, and measures conceptual thoughts, it is called "having a chamber."
That which is the karma of non-consciousness is called "no chamber"; observing the conditioned is called "having a chamber," while observing the unconditioned is "no chamber.
To examine the unconditioned is "no chamber," and to attain entry into no chamber is the Way.
Ignorant and foolish worldlings cannot understand this; I shall enlighten them so that they may discern it. For this reason, the Tathāgata harbors great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Way is without outflows and without anything received.
What is meant by 'without outflows'? "
What is meant by "without grasping"?
To be free from the four outflows (āsrava) is called being without outflow:
first, the outflow of desire; second, the outflow of existence; third, the outflow of ignorance; and fourth, the outflow of views.
To be free from these four outflows means to be without grasping, which is to be free from the four types of grasping:
first, grasping at sensual desire; second, grasping at existence; third, grasping at views; and fourth, grasping at rules and observances.
Apart from these four feelings, both these and those four feelings all return to ignorance; they are entangled by affection and attachment, relying upon the internal and arising from within.
The Tathāgata, the Truly Enlightened One, eliminates the root produced by internal feeling, attains purity within, and leads all sentient beings toward purity.

That which is inwardly pure is free from conceptualization; being free from conceptualization, one eliminates inversion. One contemplates only pliancy and does not abide in ignorance; by not abiding in ignorance, one no longer abides in the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). Being able to not abide in the twelve links of existence, there is nothing that arises. That which does not arise is quiescent; that which is quiescent is without meaning; that which is without meaning is the ultimate meaning. That which is the ultimate meaning is exhaustive; that which is exhaustive is the meaning of non-personhood (*anātman*); the meaning of non-personhood is the meaning of non-attainment. This meaning of non-attainment is the path of the Tathāgata; thus are the twelve links of dependent origination fully understood.

The twelfth is called the meaning of the Dharma (*dhamma-attha*). This meaning of the Dharma is precisely what is termed "beholding dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). To behold dependent origination is to see the Dharma; to see the Dharma is to see the Tathāgata.
One who observes in this manner finds that there is no fundamental basis.
When the nature of things is thoroughly examined from beginning to end, can there be any perception or conceptualization?
How could one speak of "existence"?
To not give rise to conditions regarding any perceptions is what is meant by being without conditions regarding perception;
one who observes in this way is understood by the Tathāgata of Perfect Enlightenment.
In this way, such a semblance-dharma universally practices equality; that which is equal therein is likewise free from partiality or deviance.
Such equality is without any outflows (*āsrava*) and is without anything received.
Foolish and ignorant worldlings are unable to understand this; I shall enlighten them so that they may discern it. For this reason, the Tathāgata harbors great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Way is pure, stainless, and untainted.
What is meant by being pure, stainless, and untainted?
Emptiness is pure; signlessness is free from defilement; wishlessness is unstained. Non-arising is pure;
non-defilement is free from defilement; non-origination is unstained.
The intrinsic nature is pure; liberation is unstained.
Absence of negligence is purity, and the absence of frivolity is freedom from defilement; tranquility and self-mastery are non-attachment.
The absence of a fundamental basis is purity; the Dharma-realm shines forth brilliantly.
The limit of reality is unstained; empty space is pure.
The void is without defilement; the indistinct is untainted.
To eliminate internal impurities and to be without negligence regarding external things is called "stainless.
To have neither internal nor external activity is called "stainless," and not to cultivate the sense bases (*āyatana*) is called "untainted."

Wisdom exhausts faults and attains purity; it realizes purity such that nothing arises in the future and is stainless. By discerning the present and abiding in the *dharmadhātu*, one is unstained. This is called being pure, stainless, and untainted, and thus equanimously governing the single Dharma.
Reaching the trace of ultimate stillness—wherein that which is still is serene and tranquil—and this serenity and tranquility are called benevolence and harmony.
It is thus, noble son!
Just as space is, so too is the Way.
As the Way is suchness, so too are all phenomena;
as all phenomena are suchness, so too are sentient beings;
and as sentient beings are suchness, so too are the lands.
As the lands are, so too is nirvāṇa;
as nirvāṇa is, so one perceives all dharmas.
That they are ultimately quiescent has already been explained: to be without factions among all factions is what is called pure, stainless, and undefiled.

The Tathāgata, regarding those various forms and images, realizes that all phenomena are devoid of form and image, and thereby attains perfect enlightenment. Observing the realm of all sentient beings as being neither pure nor defiled, he recognizes these numerical categories as "sentient beings asleep" and conceives great compassion for them.
"The Tathāgata, through his skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), has summoned the Brahmās; he does not turn the wheel of Dharma without being requested.

At that opportune moment, a multitude of sixty-eight thousand Brahmās suddenly vanished from their celestial palaces and appeared before the World-Honored One in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī. Prostrating at his feet, they entreated the World-Honored One to turn the wheel of Dharma, saying:
'We pray only that the Great Sage will proclaim the Way of the Sūtras; if you preach the Dharma, many shall be saved.'"
At that time, Brahmā uttered this verse in praise:
"Even if all phenomena are tranquil and serene, pure and pristine,
stainless and untainted."
Since it cannot be grasped, being without sound and without action, one fully comprehends it through the wisdom of the Way as the most supreme.
Throughout incalculable eons, he has established compassion, diligently practicing what is immeasurable and cultivating with refined persistence for a long duration.
Desiring to transform and enlighten sentient beings who are deluded, who have long been under the sway of sleep,
and who are shrouded by great ignorance—
since many among these beings have accumulated merit through their past cultivation, they now approach the Most Victorious One.
You must surely distinguish the sublime Dharma as exceptional; we pray that the Tathāgata will, at this time, turn the wheel of Dharma.
Having already subdued the realm where Māra dwells, may you immediately open wide the gate of ambrosia.
For the sake of the multitude, you have extensively expounded the words and traces of the sages and saints; we only pray that the Guide will reveal the path.
If the Perfectly Awakened One, out of inexhaustible compassion, would take pity on all beings, please turn the inconceivable wheel of Dharma.
On this day, I entreat the Most Honored One, that I may hear only the supreme wheel of the Dharma.
If the Great Sage would harbor compassion and kindness, just as the Buddha Konākamuni preached his teachings.
Just as Kāśyapa turned the wheel of Dharma, we pray only that the World-Honored One will proclaim the Way of the sutras.
Like rain from heaven, it provides abundant moisture, causing medicinal herbs to grow and the five grains to flourish.
With great clouds of compassion, pervading the entire world, the Tathāgata rains down the water of the True Dharma.
From the moment of his birth, he uttered sublime words; the Sage was spontaneously born with the resolve that he must deliver all sentient beings.
"The multitudes have all gathered together; parched with longing and empty with hunger, they seek only the flavor of the Dharma to dispel their thirst.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"In this way, son of good family!
The Brahma King entreated the Tathāgata with such earnestness.
Furthermore, the Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, not forsaking his great compassion, immediately turned the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma within the grove where the seers dwell at Vārāṇasī."

He cannot be restrained by śramaṇas, brahmins, great māras, the Brahmā kings, or worldly people; the sūtras and paths he expounds issue from extraordinary sounds, proclaiming to the trichiliocosm that the bhikṣu Kūṭa (translated in Chinese as *benji*, "original limit") is foremost in understanding the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One proclaimed these verses of praise:
"Profound and subtle, it cannot be grasped; Supreme, it is without action.
Kakuṇḍala has understood the original limit And harbors no more fetters or resentment."

“When the Tathāgata preached this sūtra of the Wheel of Dharma, incalculable and infinite numbers of people and various classes of sentient beings received the teaching and followed the discipline, witnessing the Tathāgata’s manifestation of great compassion;
and immeasurable, limitless, and unfathomable multitudes of living beings all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.”
"Yes, son of good family!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, regard sentient beings with compassion through sixteen matters and harbor great pity; they always maintain compassionate concern, never neglecting it for a moment.
Furthermore, those beings have no karma that does not inspire fear."

The immeasurable compassion cultivated by the Tathāgata is beyond all description; for the sake of each and every individual, he establishes his practice, enduring in the hells for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges without ever retreating. By these skillful means, he causes all sentient beings to follow the discipline and receive the teachings of the noble and holy Dharma.
