By this analogy, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, for the sake of all sentient beings—each and every one of those who have received a physical form and life—would endure the sufferings and afflictions of the hells for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges for each and every individual, desiring to cause all people to receive the teachings according to the discipline and enter the Dharma of the noble ones.
The Tathāgata does not grow weary or feel aversion, nor does he ever forsake his great compassion.
O son of noble family, know this!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess such sublime pity for sentient beings; they always harbor great compassion.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The various disciples and those of the class of śrāvakas harbor fear in their minds; their compassion is like that of one who fears for a fish, while their benevolence is like skin and flesh.
The benevolence of a bodhisattva, however, is like the marrow."

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, harbor boundless compassion; they should always encourage and assist those who seek the Buddha-wisdom—transforming the compassion of the śrāvakas so that they enter the mind of the Way, and upholding the compassion of the bodhisattvas—for it is because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have resolved upon the wisdom of the Way that they harbor this great compassion.
The compassion of the śrāvaka consists in observing with a mind of loving-kindness; the compassion of the bodhisattva consists in surveying and transforming others through instruction;

the great compassion of the Buddha consists in exhaustive guidance. The compassion of the śrāvaka consists in wearying of the performance of conditioned activities; the compassion of the bodhisattva consists in diligent progress toward higher stages; the great compassion of the Buddha consists in transcending all conditioned activities.
It is so, son of good family!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, always harbor great compassion for sentient beings; for the sake of even a single person, they remain in the world for one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, or ten trillion kalpas—throughout incalculable and unspeakable numbers of kalpas—and do not enter final extinction in nirvana, because they must surely deliver them.
"Noble son! You should understand this:
that Buddha, the Great Sage, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, dwells among sentient beings and harbors great compassion.
Chapter Nine: Proclaiming the Kalpas and Ages from the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*. The Buddha said:
“O son of good family!

In the past, in an age long ago—beyond all calculation, beyond all description, vast and remote for inconceivable eons—there appeared in the world a Buddha named Candanagandha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”

The world is called Fragrant Land, and the eon is named Supreme Fragrance. The lifespan of that Buddha is one hundred twenty-six million eight hundred sixty thousand years, and his assembly of śrāvakas numbers eight million six hundred eighty-six thousand; the assembly of bodhisattvas is beyond measure.

From a single pore of that Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, emanates a sublime fragrance that perfumes the entirety of the trichiliocosm; its pervasive power is so majestic and its exquisite quality so immeasurable.

In that Buddha-world, there has never been any foul odor; all the walls, trees, mountains, hills, valleys, and whatever forms and colors exist within that land are permeated by the fragrance of the Tathāgata, its scent so exquisite as to be beyond comparison.
For this reason, the world is named Fragrant Land (*Gandhavatī*).
All humans and sentient beings in that Buddha-land are permeated by the sublime fragrance of the Tathāgata, such that their body, speech, and mind are not subject to calamity or transgression.
If there are those who leave the household life to become śramaṇas under that Buddha, they shall all attain the four dhyānas upon smelling this wondrous fragrance.
That land had already been inhabited by a thousand Buddhas who all shared the same name, Candanagandha.
For this reason, that eon was named Uttarakuru-gandha.
After Candanagandha had completed his Buddha-work, he would then enter parinirvāṇa.
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, he surveyed the realms of sentient beings to see where there might be a person whom he should transform and lead according to the teachings of the Vinaya.

Then, with his Dharma-eye, he beheld a person to be transformed in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception—one who had planted many roots of merit in past lives and whose aspiration was set upon the subtle and wondrous. This person was one for whom the Buddha should provide transformation; having remained in that heaven for eighty-four thousand kalpas, when his term there ended, he would be born among humans. Free from the dust of desire, he would hear of the virtues of the Mahāyāna and would resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, never regressing.
At that time, the Tathāgata Candanagandha, the Arhat, through skillful means and out of his great compassion, manifested the causes and conditions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now is my time; I shall enter parinirvāṇa and desire to attain extinction."

At that time, that Buddha gave rise to great compassion; he entered the samādhi called "The Samādhi of Insatiable Concentration" and manifested a great parinirvāṇa. Thereafter, he widely distributed his relics, reaching everywhere without exception.
His True Dharma shall remain for one hundred and eighty-four million eight hundred and forty thousand years, during which this teaching will transform and deliver many beings.

In that age, there shall be no Semblance Dharma; by the power of samādhi and his supernormal faculties, that Buddha-Bhagavān shall establish himself in the divine state for eighty-four thousand kalpas, remaining there after having withdrawn his physical form so as not to manifest himself.
"In this way, son of good family,
you have brought many to spiritual maturity over eighty-four thousand kalpas.

Those devas, having completed their lifespan of eighty-four thousand kalpas in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception, will return to the human world and be born into the household of a noble elder, at the age of exactly eight."

Then the Tathāgata, the Arhat Samyaksaṃbuddha Candanagandha, arose from samādhi and manifested his buddha-body within the house of the venerable one, standing before his sons—yet no other person in the household saw him; only the eight-year-old boy beheld him alone.

That youth had previously resolved upon the Mahāyāna; accordingly, he preached the Dharma and expounded upon the afflictions and hardships of the household life, extolling the Great Way beyond all measure.

At that time, the youth’s mind was sincere, pure, and harmonious, and he gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), immediately attaining the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
When the Buddha perceived their minds, he bestowed upon them the prediction:

"After seventy-two thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed, you shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and become Most Perfectly Awakened Ones. You shall be named Ratnottama Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat."
The others did not hear the bestowal of the prediction; only this single youth alone knew it, for he was originally a fit vessel.

At that time, twelve thousand devaputras, having heard the prediction bestowed, became pure and sincere in their single-mindedness and resolved upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, each making this vow:

"When the Tathāgata Ratnottama attains perfect enlightenment, we shall be born in that Buddha-land. Whatever that Buddha proclaims shall surely be according to our wish, and we shall be born in that land in the presence of the Buddha Ratnottama."
"When the Buddha Candanagandha had bestowed the predictions upon the bodhisattvas, he then entered nirvana and attained parinirvāṇa; the devas and humans made offerings to his relics."
Therefore, son of good family!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are fully endowed with great compassion; their majesty is such that it cannot be reached by the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

When the holy teachings of the Buddhas are on the verge of being severed, they are immediately restored and established once more. The manifold merits generated by the Gods among Gods increase in their brilliance; the transformation of beings flourishes until their final nirvana, and those who contemplate repaying this debt of merit shall never fail or lose it."

When the Tathāgata preached this discourse on the meaning of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), among the great assembly, beings as numerous as the sands of three parts of the Ganges all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). A number of bodhisattvas equal to half the sands of the Ganges attained the patience that accords with the Dharma (*anulomikī-dharmakṣānti*); bodhisattvas equal to the sands of the Ganges established Great Compassion and attained *dhāraṇī*, just like the World-Honored Buddha, and furthermore, having attained this patience named *A-vyaya* (the Unshakeable), they perfected it.

At that time, when the assembly heard these words, they were filled with joy and exultation, and wholesome thoughts arose within them. Together they praised the virtues of the World-Honored One, raining down celestial flowers as an offering to him; musical instruments played spontaneously, and at that moment, there was none who was not filled with serene wonder.
Chapter Ten: On All Places. From the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Chapter Ten: On All Places. The Buddha addressed the sons of noble family:
“What is called the work performed by the Tathāgata?”
The Tathāgata’s activities are thirty-two in number.
What are these thirty-two?

They are that, by means of the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom, he understands as it truly is what is possible and what is impossible; he thoroughly penetrates all things—whether finite or infinite, conditioned or unconditioned.
What is meant by "impossible" (asthāna) and what is meant by "not impossible" (sthāna)?

That which is called "impossible" refers to having no refuge—namely, that one who commits evil with the body, speaks evil with the mouth, and harbors evil thoughts in the mind, yet desires to obtain what is pleasing, to surely attain their wishes, to receive a reward of joy, and to be reborn in a good realm: such a thing has never occurred.

That is to say, wherever one may be, if one acts with restraint—practicing virtue in body, speech, and mind—and desires to obtain what is agreeable, joy, peace, and the reward of merit by returning to a favorable destination, this shall certainly come to pass.

"One who is stingy and greedy yet desires wealth; one who violates the precepts and commits various evils yet hopes for rebirth among gods or humans; one who harbors poison and malice yet seeks physical beauty; one who is indolent yet seeks the Way; one whose will is confused, deluded, and dissolute yet wishes to enter quiescent extinction; one who harbors false wisdom and pursues what is improper yet desires to eliminate obstacles and attain the true state—such things cannot be realized."

Through giving one expects great wealth; through upholding the precepts, birth as a human being; through patience, physical beauty; through diligence, liberation; through meditative concentration, entry into tranquility; and through right wisdom, noble penetration. By eliminating all hindrances, wherever one dwells, these matters will certainly bear fruit.
"Furthermore, he foreknows that those who commit transgressions do not possess a settled mind, whereas those whose precepts are pure have a mind that is always tranquil;
that those who act perversely cannot attain the patient acceptance of accordance with the Dharma (*anulomikī kṣānti*), whereas those who have deep faith in emptiness attain such patient acceptance;
that those who harbor doubts find no rest in their minds, whereas those who have removed the web of fetters attain cessation."
"Knowing that a woman cannot become a Wheel-Turning King, a Lord of the Śakras, a Brahmā, or a Māra by means of this body;
yet before the World-Honored One, the Buddha knows that a woman, having transformed her female form, shall become a Wheel-Turning King, a Śakra, a Brahmā, a Māra, or a Buddha in the world."
"Just as a Wheel-Turning King governs the country with righteous rule, showing compassion to the myriad people and refraining from evil;
the people know that the Wheel-Turning King does not act with oppression or govern the state through perversity, nor does he harm or resent the myriad people."
"One knows that the people of Uttarakuru never commit evil to fall into the miserable hells, and that the people of that realm will surely be reborn in the blissful places of the heavens.

One knows that for those who kill yet desire long life, who steal yet wish not to lose their wealth, who are lustful yet seek miraculous birth, who speak falsehoods yet seek eloquence, who drink wine yet remain undisturbed, who use double-tongued speech yet seek harmony, who use harsh words yet seek praise, who use frivolous speech yet seek fame, who harbor anger yet seek a pleasant countenance, who engage in contentious recitations yet seek peace, and who hold wrong views yet hope for deliverance—none of these things will ever be realized."

The compassionate person who refrains from killing desires long life; the upright person who refrains from stealing desires that wealth shall not be lost; the chaste person who refrains from sexual misconduct desires a loyal and virtuous spouse; the faithful person who refrains from deception desires a fragrant breath; the wise person who refrains from intoxication desires sagacity in discourse; those who do not fight one another desire harmony; those whose speech is gentle rather than coarse and whose words are plain rather than ornate desire concord; those who practice patience rather than anger desire freedom from resentment; those who practice relinquishment rather than greed desire abundance; and those with right view rather than wrong view desire that their words be heard and accepted. They will surely attain these fruits: long life, security and non-loss of wealth, a loyal and virtuous wife and children, a fragrant breath, wisdom in explaining principles, harmonious relations with kinsmen, praise from the multitude, having their words heeded, abundant treasures, all looking up to their countenance, and recognizing the Way in every lifetime—all these matters shall bear fruit.
"One who foreknows the eightfold path will inevitably reach the realization of the fruit; knowing that the fruit has been attained, one enters the stage [of certainty].

One knows that by following the tracks of the Path, one will no longer undergo the cycle of birth and death eight times; furthermore, one knows that having returned, one will not wander back for three more cycles;
and one knows that after returning and wandering for two cycles, one will cast off the five aggregates and attain parinirvāṇa."
"Knowing that there is no returning, one does not return again to this world; knowing the place where one dwells, one attains parinirvāṇa.
Knowing there is nothing to which one is attached, one is no longer entangled in any location; knowing there is nothing to which one is attached, there is no further beginning or end."
"One knows that a noble sage does not abandon the Buddha-way to take refuge in heterodox teachings; one knows that a noble sage shall take refuge in the Buddha and place no faith in external paths.

Furthermore, one foresees and knows that when a bodhisattva attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they will never again regress to the Lesser Vehicle or the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas; the bodhisattva will surely accomplish the Way and never turn back."

"I have foreknowledge that once a Bodhisattva sits beneath the Bodhi tree, he will not rise until he has attained perfect enlightenment; seated beneath the tree, he will certainly and without doubt realize the unsurpassed, true, and correct path."

"I foresee that the Tathāgata’s wisdom and insight are vast and far-reaching, without obstruction; it has never been the case that one who seeks the Tathāgata’s wisdom would fail to penetrate it or encounter hindrances. It has never been the case that the Tathāgata’s noble wisdom could be diminished or rendered incomplete; the World-Honored One’s wisdom and insight are suspended high and wide, reaching everywhere, with nothing to which it does not penetrate."

He foresaw that if anyone were to wish to see the Buddha’s mind, it would be something unprecedented; for as for the Tathāgata’s mind, there is no one in heaven or on earth who can see it. He knew that among those in heaven or on earth who wished to see the Buddha’s crown, none would be capable of beholding it.
"He foreknows that the Tathāgata’s mind is always in a state of meditative concentration and has never been forgotten; he universally perceives the thoughts of all sentient beings.
He foreknows that the Buddha’s mind is never obstructed, and with his mind always fixed in one-pointedness, he perceives the primordial limit."

"I know in advance that from the very beginning the World-Honored One has been without fault; what he speaks is ultimate sincerity, his words fill the ten directions, and he is forever free from verbal transgression.

I know in advance that were one to seek faults in the World-Honored One, they would find none; for the Great Sages, the Buddhas, are pure in bodily conduct, surpassing the bright moon-gem, the sun, the moon, Śakra, and Brahmā; their purity is like space, such that nothing can equal it."
“The Buddha—the God among gods—possesses a path-wisdom that is transcendent and sublime, majestic and peerless, beyond all analogy.
It is so, noble son!”
"The Tathāgata’s powers are limitless in every respect; that which he speaks is boundless, and the true reality expressed through his words is never deceptive.
Thereupon the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The earth may yet be split asunder, And the unmoving void may be made to move, But the Dharma spoken by the Buddha Can never be altered."
One might wish to cause that which the Buddha has spoken to have a location;
even a great man could transform emptiness into five colors,
yet one cannot cause that which the World-Honored One has spoken to have a location.
That which the Buddha has proclaimed—above, below, and in between—is entirely sincere;
nothing can prevent it from reaching its mark.
Even if one were to speak of places where it does not apply, whether above, below, or in between, [it remains all-pervading].
These matters are entirely true and real, never subject to change.
Having clearly understood them in all their aspects, one preaches the Dharma;
therefore, it is truly without falsehood, for one perceives the nature of the mind and its intent.
The heterodox teachers and outsiders flee wherever they go;
because their methods do not reach everywhere, the Buddha’s perfect awakening is unlike theirs.
Knowing what is possible and what is impossible, he delivers sentient beings according to the time.
The renown of all Buddhas is vast; they immediately explain the place for them.
Sentient beings lack the capacity as vessels; the Buddha likewise observes them, examining them according to the time: by what means can he nurture them?
This is the foremost deed, the supreme path of all Buddhas;
by acting without fault or transgression, one thereby delivers immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings,
explaining what is possible and what is impossible.
"This is the power of the Great Sage, which no heterodox practitioners can attain.
*The Sutra of Great Compassion*, Scroll Three;
*The Sutra of Great Compassion*, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Eleven: Realizing the Three Times.
The Buddha again addressed the sons of good family:

“The Tathāgata discerns, individually and specifically, all karmic actions performed in the future, the past, and the present, as well as their underlying causes and conditions, their locations, and their retributive results.
How does he discern them? [The text continues:]”
Thereupon, the Tathāgata fully understood all that was done in the past— both virtuous retributions and unwholesome deeds—
as well as the manner of retribution for wholesome and unwholesome deeds to be performed in the future,
and likewise for those performed in the present.
In future ages, the karmic transgressions and meritorious virtues that each shall perform will all be clearly distinguished; the Tathāgata knows them all.

Whether what is done in the future will be extraordinary and superior to others, whether what is done in the future will lead to decline and loss, or whether what is done in the future will lead to increase and growth—the Tathāgata knows them all.
“If there is an increase in the karma being performed and established in the present, yet a decrease occurs in the future, the Tathāgata knows it all;
if there is a decrease in the present karma, yet a further reduction occurs in the future, the Tathāgata knows it all;
if there is an increase in the present, and likewise an increase in future matters, the Tathāgata knows it all.”
“If one has practiced flawed and base deeds in the past, yet practices the subtle deeds of a true being in future lives, the Tathāgata knows them all.”

"Regarding those who practice: whether they receive great merit for meager and slight efforts, or achieve extraordinary merit and transcendent achievements through the performance of great deeds and exceptional virtues beyond measure; or whether they give gifts for the sake of the Śrāvaka vehicle, or for the sake of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or for the sake of the Buddha-way—through all such acts of giving, the Tathāgata knows them all."

"If there be suffering encountered in the present, or excessive peace; if one performs good in the present yet obtains suffering, or performs evil in the present yet immediately encounters affliction; or if one performs evil in the present yet brings about happiness in the future, or performs good in the present and immediately receives the retribution of peace—the Tathāgata knows all such things."

"The causes and conditions of the offenses and merits of all sentient beings—past, future, and present—and the resulting retributions they bring about, are all exactly as they are and without variation; the responses of offense and merit are likewise without distinction, and the Tathāgata knows them all completely."
"Because he knows this, he teaches the Dharma according to the fundamental nature; this is the second activity of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgata understands causes and conditions, The clear-eyed one discerns retribution; He knows the various realms of existence, And the distinctions among all beings."
Unimpeded throughout the three periods of time, they know the conduct of sentient beings;
they understand how future retributions of peace and happiness lead to fortunate rebirths among devas and humans,
and likewise how conditions lead to suffering and affliction— they know all these states with perfect stability.
The karma created through good and evil deeds brings forth its corresponding fruits;
dwelling in peace, one understands this as clearly as a bright jewel held in the palm of the hand.
Even from a small undertaking, that which is obtained may be immeasurable.
Whether it be extensive or shallow, the Buddha knows its beginning and end.
Whether one practices the giving of a śrāvaka, or abides in the vehicle of a pratyekabuddha,
or establishes oneself in the most supreme activity— the Buddha knows them all as they truly abide.
That which causes the performance of asceticism may instead result in peace and happiness;
from happiness one may obtain suffering, yet through it one may abide in karma.
Or, that which is painful and evil conduct may conversely result in abiding in happiness.
Some may perform good or evil deeds, receiving retribution as suffering or grievous affliction;
some go from suffering to further suffering, while others proceed from happiness to happiness.
Sin and merit follow their own natural course, and the Buddha fully knows these karmic responses.

The successive transformations throughout the three periods of time, And the retributions arising from the causes and conditions of sentient beings— The Buddha understands these through his noble wisdom; They are not false, nor are they different.
Chapter Twelve: On Understanding the Categories of Sentient Beings, from the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*. The Buddha addressed the son of good family:

"The Tathāgata clearly understands that sentient beings and others have different inclinations, diverse aspirations for learning, and have not yet realized liberation; he knows all of these exactly as they are."
How is this known?

There may be some who dwell in lust yet whose intent is inclined toward liberation from hatred; or again, there may be some who dwell in hatred yet are liberated through lust; or again, there may be some who dwell in delusion yet believe they can be liberated from lust and hatred—the Tathāgata knows all such as these.

"Furthermore, there are some people who abide in virtuous conduct yet take pleasure in unwholesome liberation; or there are others who abide in unwholesome conduct yet resolve their faith upon the wholesome path—the Tathāgata knows them all."
“Furthermore, there are those who are single-mindedly devoted to what is inferior yet believe in subtle liberation;

the Tathāgata knows them all. Or there are those who are single-mindedly devoted to the subtle and whose aspirations delight in liberation; or those whose aspirations delight in being single-mindedly devoted to the inferior while abiding in a state that is extraordinary and transcendent; or those who abide in a state that is extraordinary and single-mindedly devoted, yet fall into the inferior and remain forever in the realm of perverse karma, lacking decisive understanding; or those who believe and delight in remaining in the indeterminate while accomplishing right karma; or those who delight in turning toward the gate of right concentration and thereby attain liberation—the Tathāgata knows them all.”

“The Tathāgata fully knows those who, through faith and delight, are destined to transcend the realm of desire; those who, through faith and delight, attain transcendence in the realm of form; those who possess a noble faith that transcends the three realms; those who, from the joy of faith, diminish their conditions to achieve distinction; or those who, through their fondness for distinction, lead to their own decline. All these the Tathāgata knows completely.”

"The various colors of their places of rebirth, the differences in their wealth and occupations, and the disparities in what they receive; whether they attain the *uṣṇīṣa* through their faith and aspirations or reach the limit of stability—the Tathāgata knows them all."
"According to what the mind knows, he immediately preaches the Dharma for them, causing them to attain understanding; this is the third activity of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The aspirations of those in the world are not the same; The inclinations of their minds differ from one another."
Their resolve and conduct cannot be limited, yet the Buddha knows them all without bound.
The Buddha knows where their wills are directed:
some are inclined toward faith and joy, while others dwell in desire, hatred, or greed; some dwell in anger, delusion, or stupidity.
Whether abiding in delusion or desire, or dwelling in the wholesome or unwholesome;
whether their conduct is extraordinary or ordinary—he knows them all as they truly abide.
Due to inferior or sublime [capacities], their dispositions and natures incline toward the profound and mysterious;
some, through extraordinary karma, apply themselves with single-minded devotion to faith and liberation;
others, starting from inferior faith, thereby attain the superior and sublime.
Some, through transcendent and extraordinary conduct, immediately attain inferior yet superior wisdom.
Yet others remain indecisive due to error; failing to comprehend through correct meditative absorption, they seek to cross the three realms through mere faith.
The Buddha knows the inclinations of their minds.
The various forms that arise, each distinct within them,
with differing characteristics emerging from the crown of the head— through faith, one attains liberation.
Regarding all sentient beings of the three realms, the Buddha knows them all and teaches the Dharma accordingly.
Receiving according to what they should receive—this is the activity of the Ten Powers.
Chapter Thirteen: On the Various Kinds of Beings. In the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Chapter Thirteen: On the Various Kinds of Beings, the Buddha addressed the son of good family:
“The Tathāgata fully knows the various kinds of forms among the beings in the world, their incalculable bodies.”
How is this known?
Whatever offenses have been accumulated by that body, the Tathāgata knows them all;
whatever merits have been accumulated by that body, the Tathāgata knows them all.
If one plants their own body in impurity and evil, resulting in a lack of protection and failure to attain liberation from the realms, the Tathāgata knows this all.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata fully knows the realm of the mind, the realm of the eye, the realm of forms, and the realm of eye-consciousness, understanding their origins, their ultimate ends, and the source from which they arise.
How is this known?
Its interior is empty, its exterior is also empty, and both its interior and exterior are empty;
the same is true for the ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind.
Regarding the realms of mind, phenomena, and consciousness, one thoroughly understands their origins and the source from which they emerge.
How does one know this?
Because the internal is empty, the external is empty, and both the internal and external are empty.
“The earth element, water element, fire element, and wind element are likewise entirely empty.
How is this known?
It is known because they are understood to be like space.”
He also knows the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
How does he know them?
He knows that they result from conceptualization and lead to this conditioned realm and unconditioned realm.

One knows that the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*) has the characteristic of non-activity; one knows that the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*) does not form perceptions through non-activity; one knows that the realm of afflictions (*kleśa-dhātu*) arises from adventitious dust and has the characteristic of desire; one knows that the realm of anger and resentment has the characteristic of being fundamentally pure and pristine; one knows that the realm of activity has the characteristic of ignorance arising from improper reflection; and one knows that the realm of nirvāṇa has the characteristic of luminosity arising from proper reflection.

“The Tathāgata fully knows the elements upon which the bodies of the people in the world depend; the elements in which they dwell, those by which they are oppressed, the manifestations of their conduct based on those elements, their devotion to those elements, their dispositions arising from those elements, their abiding because of those elements, and their birth from those elements. According to what he knows, he teaches the Dharma accordingly; this is the fourth activity.”
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“The Lion among Men understands all realms;
regarding the people of this world, he knows them according to their bodily conduct.”
That realm which arises is vast and universal, beyond all limit;
it is the source from which all emerges, abiding in omniscience.
It is that from which merit and demerit arise, and that by which all bodies are produced.
By virtue of that which is relied upon for refuge, and from whence the body is born;
by virtue of that wherein the realms are established, one attains liberation from all such elements.
Knowing this body as it truly is, the Most Excellent One is the Great Sage.
The element of the eye is likewise, as are the elements of form and mind;
the Most Excellent One knows them all to be empty, fundamentally pure and free from sorrow or distress.
The ear and nose are also thus, as are the elements of the tongue and the body.
One should know that the various elements of mind and phenomena are all empty.
Earth, water, fire, and wind—these elements are perfectly equal;
the Lion among Men understands them equally, like space.
The desire realm is likewise, as are the form and formless realms;
to know these various realms individually, one must understand they are established through conceptual thought.
The Buddha knows that because of adventitious marks, the arising of desire occurs as a natural process.
Abiding peacefully in the understanding of anger, one is likewise fundamentally pure.
To discern and awaken to this— whether regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) or the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
and even the reckoning of *nirvāṇa*— there are then no three perceptions.
The characteristics arising from the causal realms are likewise not understood through clarity;
all that emerges from causes is like a skilled artisan’s assembling and disassembling.
These worldly bodies are innumerable, their forms being manifold.
The Buddha fully understands and knows all things, yet he does not think, "I know.
Like space itself, the ten directions are without limit.
That Lion among Men universally knows all realms;
his most supreme and holy wisdom is utterly unsurpassed and bottomless,
beyond the reach of all people, such that they cannot know its limits.
This is the fourth meaning: the Sage, free from defilement, clearly understands all realms and thereby brings sentient beings to transformation and enlightenment.
By means of the Vinaya, he awakens the mind regarding the karmic actions of transgression and merit that one has performed.
No longer giving rise to anger, their resolve is entirely distinct. Chapter Fourteen:
Understanding the Roots of Sentient Beings From the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Chapter Fourteen: Understanding the Roots of Sentient Beings. The Buddha addressed the son of good family:
"The Tathāgata is fully able to understand the faculties and diligence of other sentient beings."

How does he understand this clearly? He knows those among sentient beings who possess dull and inferior faculties, as well as those with intermediate faculties; furthermore, he knows those whose faculties are sharp and penetrating, those with extraordinary faculties, and those with base and inferior faculties. He knows that because of these faculties, they rely upon thoughts and perceptions, and that from the very root of these conditions, emotional attachments arise; from the condition of hatred, the source of delusion emerges. The Tathāgata fully knows what kind of categories these faculties and mental conceptions belong to.

Even when the defilements of fragmentation give rise to lust, anger, and delusion, the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, likewise fully knows what kind of categories these faculties and mental conceptions belong to.

The Tathāgata fully knows how the various faculties function due to the conditions of lust, anger, and delusion; he knows how these faculties arise from unwholesome conditions, or from ignorance, or from various mental attentions.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows the faculty of the eye; he knows the faculties of the ear, nose, body, speech, and mind in the same way.

He fully knows these faculties: the male faculty, the female faculty, the life-faculty, the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of fear, the faculty of equanimity, the faculty of faith, the faculty of vigor, the faculty of intention, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of non-differentiation, and all the faculties that ought to be known.

The Tathāgata fully knows the origins from which these faculties arise: the causal conditions for the eye-faculty, the abiding of the ear-faculty, and the respective bases established for the nose, mouth, and body-faculties.

He fully knows how, conditioned by the ear, the basis for the nose-faculty is established; how, from the causal conditions of the nose, the tongue-faculty is established; how, from the causal conditions of the tongue, the body-faculty is established; and how, from the causal conditions of the body, the eye-faculty is established. The Tathāgata knows all this.
“The Tathāgata fully knows which sentient beings, by reason of their faculty of giving, should subsequently apply themselves to the precepts;
he discerns the increase, decrease, progress, and regression of these various faculties, and accordingly expounds for each the matter of giving.”
There may be sentient beings who, because they follow the root of ethical discipline (*śīla*), should practice giving; for them, the Tathāgata expounds the beginning and end of ethical discipline.
There may be sentient beings who, following the root of patience (*kṣānti*), should apply diligence (*vīrya*); for them, the Tathāgata immediately expounds the beginning and end of patience.
There may be sentient beings who, following the root of diligence, should practice patience; for them, the Tathāgata then expounds the beginning and end of that diligence.
There may be sentient beings who, through the faculty of single-mindedness, respond to wisdom; for them, the Tathāgata distinguishes and teaches meditative contemplation.

There may be sentient beings who, through the faculty of wisdom, respond to single-mindedness; for them, the Tathāgata distinguishes and explains the origins of the increase, decrease, progress, and regression of the various faculties, proclaiming the clarity of wisdom.

The faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, the Eightfold Noble Path, and the thirty-seven auxiliaries to enlightenment are likewise so; they are fully perfected and thoroughly examined. He expounds their origins and conclusions without exception, causing all beings to understand and discern them individually.
"There may be sentient beings who study the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas through the faculty of a śrāvaka; the Tathāgata, knowing their faculties, expounds the vehicle of the śrāvakas.

Or again, there may be people who study the vehicle of the śrāvakas through the faculty of a pratyekabuddha; the Buddha, knowing the direction toward which these various faculties tend, explains the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas for them.

Or there may be sentient beings who study the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas through the faculty of the Mahāyāna; the Tathāgata fully knows the destination of these various faculties and proclaims the practice of the Mahāyāna for them."

There may be sentient beings who each study the Mahāyāna by relying on different faculties; the Tathāgata, fully knowing that these various faculties are each distinct, provides explanations accordingly.

Regarding those classes of sentient beings who lack the faculties for practice and are unfit vessels for the Dharma, the Tathāgata perceives them as unsuitable recipients and causes them to train in contemplation.

Alternatively, when he observes individuals whose cultivation of the faculties accords with their suitability as vessels, the Tathāgata, mindful that they are fit vessels, expounds the Way of the Sūtras to them with earnest diligence.
"In this way, son of good family!

The Tathāgata fully knows the physical faculties of all sentient beings and others, as well as their various bodies, the destinies of their faculties, and the differences in their thoughts; he recognizes their origins and their endings."

If one does not dwell on them, one clearly understands that the various faculties (indriya) follow their respective categories; one knows the inclinations and conduct of people's faculties and what they are conditioned by.

For those who can be transformed, one employs skillful means according to the principles of their conduct—whether sitting, rising, walking, advancing, or retreating—and thereby fully penetrates their faculties.
“The Tathāgata fully elucidates all things; there is nothing he does not penetrate as he proclaims the sutras. This is the fifth activity of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon the Buddha spoke in verse:
“Knowing the faculties to be vast and infinite, He thoroughly understands the dispositions and natures of sentient beings.”
As for the nature of those faculties,
the Most Victorious One fully knows them all—
whether inferior, middling, or supreme; these various faculties are known by the Buddha.
Peerless in this way, according to the intent of what should be understood:
regarding the limits of desire, evil, and defilement, whether their roots are thin and sparse,
or if their nature is suddenly violent, or even if they harbor coarseness and brutality.
What is the cause for the Victor’s knowledge?
He understands their origins and endings; there is no distinction in what is unwholesome, and that upon which one relies should be liberated.
From the eye, the mind, the male, and the female, he likewise understands the faculty of the eye.
Suffering, pleasure, and joy—from what do they arise? From what cause does distress come?
It is through the path of contemplating the meaning, through diligence, intention, wisdom, and concentration, as well as knowing other matters; thus is the courage of the mind.
With the eye as a causal condition for the ear-base, one attains the nose, ear, and tongue;
through the body as a causal condition, the arising and establishment of the eye and ear are achieved.
To those whose root of virtue is generosity and who are intent on precepts and prohibitions, he speaks of the matter of giving;
to those whose root of virtue is morality and who study generosity, he speaks of the meaning of the dharma of precepts;
to those whose root of virtue is patience and who manifest diligence, he expounds upon the matter of forbearance.
Manifesting patience through diligence, he proclaims the matters of diligence;
reaching meditative concentration through the faculty of wisdom, he speaks of wisdom for the sake of others;
reaching patience through diligence, he speaks of industrious effort for the sake of others.
From the faculty of dhyāna they attain wisdom, and for others they preach meditative contemplation;
from the faculty of wisdom they attain dhyāna, and for others they preach noble gnosis.
From those with the faculties of the Śrāvaka vehicle, they proceed to the Pratyekabuddha.
The Most Victorious One preaches the path of the śrāvaka for those who seek the goal of the pratyekabuddha;
if one’s aspiration lies in the practice of a pratyekabuddha, yet one studies the practices of a śrāvaka,
the Buddha then sets aside the śrāvaka path and expounds the matters of the pratyekabuddha.
Its root lies in noble deeds; such a person studies what is inferior.
The Buddha taught the Perfection of Deliverance (Dānapāramitā), distinguishing it from the Pratyekabuddhas.
Seeing that there are practices everywhere, he discerns them through superior insight.
He descends with his fully matured faculties; the One of Ten Powers provides the explanation.
By what causes and conditions do people act through their various faculties?
Knowing the inclinations of their natures and dispositions, he understands the workings of their karmic retribution.

"From the exhaustion of all faculties, As if sitting upon the foundation of realized reality, One discerns through the light of one's own wisdom; This is the distinction made by the World-Honored One.
Chapter Fifteen: Universal Wandering The Mahākaruṇā-sūtra, Chapter Fifteen: Universal Wandering The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
“The Tathāgata knows all; he universally reaches everything without exception, knowing it as if it were manifest.
How does he know this? He knows that sentient beings must be saved within the realm of ultimate truth.”

Knowing that the realm of sentient beings may exist within wrong actions, he further discerns this realm of living beings, seeing how they are fixed or unfixed in the power of retribution for their engagement in wrong matters; it is likewise for them.

Those sentient beings must be established in certainty; having attained this merit through the retributive fruits of their past lives and karmic destinies, they possess clear discernment and diligent application, with faculties that are keen and sharp, and are thus fit to be instructed. The Tathāgata then extensively expounds the sūtras for them.

Such individuals as these are declared by the Worthy and Holy Ones to be worthy vessels; the Tathāgata then observes their past karmic conditions and traces, and accordingly expounds the path of the sūtras for them.

"The realm of sentient beings resides in indeterminacy; existing through the power of causes and conditions, it serves as the characteristic of instruction. One should appropriately seek training through the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
If, despite observing the prohibitions of the precepts, one does not attain liberation or reach salvation, the Tathāgata then leads them into the state of rootlessness (*amūla*)."
"Causes, conditions, retributions, and responses are like administering medicine according to the illness.

If one hears the sutras from the Tathāgata and follows and accords with the Way of the Teachings, one will thereby attain the fruits of virtue; it is for these reasons that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world."

Sentient beings are submerged and drowning; they remain forever in wrong actions and have not yet established the foundation of virtue. Their minds are inferior and weak, and their countenances are not fit vessels for the Dharma. Yet the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, preaches the Way of the Sūtras for them, enabling even those who are not fit vessels to attain liberation.
The Tathāgata beholds these who are unworthy vessels and observes them with protective care; for this reason, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dons the armor of the great vow to rescue and deliver them.
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows those who are attached to desire through three matters:

the World-Honored One appears in the world because of persons possessed by desire; he appears in the world because he wishes to cause those bound by desire to leave the household life; or he appears in the world due to the conditions of past-life greed and stinginess."
"Furthermore, one knows that there are three matters regarding anger:
because one is bound by the conceptualization of anger, one arises in the world;
or because one's aspirations are not fulfilled, one arises in the world."
Furthermore, because some are bound by the hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) from previous lives, they give rise to the thought of leaving the world.
The Tathāgata fully knows that there are three types of such deluded and ignorant persons:
those who act out of ignorance; those who are greedy for their own bodies; and those who are mired in hesitation. The Tathāgata knows them all.

"Furthermore, when the Tathāgata knows that one has attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) through ascetic practices, those with keen faculties attain supernormal powers by means of the intense pain resulting from asceticism; those with weak and inferior faculties quickly achieve supernormal powers through peaceful practices; those with sharp and penetrating faculties achieve supernormal powers and concentration through diligent and arduous practice; and even those with weak and inferior faculties attain supernormal powers by means of intense pain."

By means of the causal conditions of equanimity, they practice harmony and discern the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); though they do not place faith in the Path, they do not cease their efforts, and when they apply themselves fundamentally to bring those powers to fruition, the Buddha knows them all.

“Some have minds that are discordant and whose conduct is hurried and violent; knowing they can be transformed quickly to attain supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), I cause them to be free from darkness and filled with joy.
Some practitioners, through the power of accumulated merit, bring their practice to full completion; such is known by the Tathāgata, and they no longer need to study diligently.
Others bring their practice to full completion through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*), rather than through the power of accumulation.”
There are some practices that are accomplished through the power of accumulation but not through the power of the Path;
there are some practices that are accomplished both through the power of accumulation and through the power of the Path—
the Tathāgata knows them all.
Whether there are those whose conduct is characterized by a gentle and refined disposition yet whose actions do not accord with it, the Tathāgata knows them all;

or those whose actions accord with their capacity and achieve success yet whose disposition is not gentle and refined; or those whose disposition is not gentle and refined and whose actions do not succeed; or those whose disposition is gentle and refined and whose actions accord with what should be achieved—the Tathāgata knows them all.
"There may be some whose conduct is pure in body but impure in mind and speech;
there may be some whose conduct is pure in speech but impure in body and mind;
and there may be some whose conduct is pure in body, speech, and mind."
There are those whose conduct is impure in body, speech, and mind;
the Tathāgata knows them all.

Regarding such types, the Tathāgata fully knows their actions, the causes and conditions and retributions upon which they rely, and from whence they arise—all that is practiced by sentient beings, the Tathāgata knows it all.
“Wisdom that is without diminution, universally penetrating and seeing all—this is the sixth activity of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon the Buddha spoke in verse:
“For those who possess the causes and practices, He knows them all as they have gone by.”
Those of the determined class distinguish the realms of sentient beings.
Those who are undetermined act with hypocrisy;
being thus unfit vessels, they follow the karma of false views.
Those whose conduct is dominated by greed have three causes and conditions;
those of a hateful temperament likewise have three, and the same applies to those who are deluded and dull-witted.
Within this realm of worldly desires, there are immeasurable varieties of beings.
The World-Honored One knows them all: the causes and conditions corresponding to their conduct,
the diligent and arduous tasks they perform— those whose minds are keen and discerning,
as well as those of weak and inferior faculties, he likewise knows in this way.
Those whose faculties are keen and sharp, who come through the practice of peace and security—the Lion of the World knows and protects them all; such as these are no different [from him].
Those who act with harmony abide in tranquil purity.
Thus, by virtue of this, one swiftly attains purity;
one also quickly perfects one's practice, reaching the ultimate harmony of the Path.
Furthermore, by exerting oneself with even greater urgency, one becomes tranquil and immediately finds joy.
Gathering all that has been practiced, one accumulates its merit.
Some reach the wisdom of the Way without practicing the path;
others attain accomplishment by following the practice of the path.
One who knows both of these matters achieves them through extraordinary practice.
Among those who cultivate practice, some have dispositions that are harmonious and well-balanced;
others may act in accordance with what should be done, yet fail to conform to such proper conduct.
Possessing the conduct of a great person, with both matters purified,
the Buddha perceives all things universally, there being nothing he does not fully understand.
There may be someone who practices such conduct, whose body is cultivated in purity.
What they speak and what they think cannot be pure;
yet there may be those who cultivate themselves, whose physical and verbal actions are pure,
while that which their minds do has never been practiced with purity.
There may be those in the world whose body, speech, and mind are pure;
whatever beings do, the Buddha perceives and understands them all.
"Either they are able to achieve accomplishment, or they are unable to reach the ultimate;
this is the sixth karma understood by the Buddha who dwells in peace.
Chapter Sixteen: One-Pointed Concentration of Mind The Mahākaruṇā Sūtra, Chapter Sixteen: One-Pointed Concentration of Mind The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:

“The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, knows the karma of the samādhi of single-minded liberation and meditative absorption, as well as the origins from which worldly afflictions and anger arise; he knows them with precise accuracy.”
How is this known?
By what causes and conditions are sentient beings bound by the dust of desire, leading them to such circumstances as a result of retribution?
Furthermore, by what further conditions can they attain purity?
The Tathāgata knows them all.
"What is meant by causal retribution?
What is meant by karmic activity?"

From lack of heedful mindfulness, one brings about karmic retribution; from the activities of ignorance, sentient beings bring about the dust of desire; and from the activities of ignorance, one brings about volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

From volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arises consciousness (*vijñāna*); from consciousness arises name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); from name-and-form arise the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); from the six sense bases arises contact (*sparśa*); from contact arises feeling (*vedanā*); from feeling arises craving (*tṛṣṇā*); from craving arises grasping (*upādāna*); from grasping arises becoming (*bhava*); from becoming arises birth (*jāti*); from birth arise old age and death; from old age and death arise the dusts of desire. Thus, through the cause of karmic retribution, one brings about worldly activity.
From seeing arises attachment; from the point of attachment, there is karmic retribution and activity. Through these conditions, one incurs the bonds of craving, desire, and worldly toil.
What, then, is meant by "karmic retribution through conditions"?
How does one's activity cause sentient beings to attain purity?
There are two types of retribution and twelve matters; through these, sentient beings attain purity.
"What are the two? First, hearing the meaning of gentleness and compliance from others; second, reflecting upon the Dharma within one's own person as it truly is."
"Furthermore, there are two matters that lead to purity:

first, to unify the mind and devote oneself single-mindedly to study, so that the mind is not confused; second, to understand thoroughly the meaning of skillful means and tranquility, and to observe their source."
"Furthermore, there are two matters that lead to purification:
first, knowing that there is no place from which [phenomena] come, yet understanding the arousal of their manifestation; second, knowing that there is no coming, nor is there any destination."
“Furthermore, there are two matters that lead to purity:
first, contemplating that which is unarisen as having no fundamental location; second, attaining nirvana, which is pervasive and profoundly tranquil.”
"Furthermore, there are two matters that lead to purity:
first, the accomplishment of one's conduct such that nothing remains unfulfilled; second, the attainment of direct realization through the practice of clear wisdom."
“Furthermore, there are two matters that lead to purity:
first, to resolve to cultivate the Dharma and enter the gates of liberation; second, for its foundation to be pure, reaching the knowledge and vision of deliverance.”
"Furthermore, there are two matters that lead to purity:
first, reaching the wisdom of cessation without attachment; second, the wisdom of non-arising which is always without dependence."
“Furthermore, there are two matters that lead to purity:
first, to attain the Way and its virtue through ultimate sincerity; second, to achieve accomplishment by always examining reality.”
“The Tathāgata fully knows these two types of retribution and the purification of the karma of sentient beings.
Furthermore, the skillful means regarding the fetters of affliction (*kleśa*) are immeasurable, and the skillful means for purification are likewise infinite;
moreover, through the thorough contemplation [of these], one brings about the attainment of purification from those very afflictions and swiftly achieves accomplishment.”
Furthermore, through skillful means of purification, they gradually approach the Dharma by following the course of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) and thereby subdue those who are arrogant.
The Tathāgata’s noble wisdom fully understands this and eradicates its causal conditions.
"O son of good family!
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is tranquil regarding desire and detached from it.

When all evil and unwholesome states arise, he brings them to mind and they are suddenly stilled and become peaceful; practicing the first dhyāna, he is able to dwell with one-pointed mind in the realm of cessation, in a state of tranquil meditative absorption."

Emerging from the first dhyāna, he cultivates the eight gates of liberation, repeatedly practicing them in both forward and reverse order to perfect right reception; all that he perceives is known as the samādhi of right reception, manifesting equanimity and further revealing the concentrated mind.
The Tathāgata’s samādhi is fearless and invincible; none can destroy it.
The Tathāgata’s samādhi is without causes and conditions, nor does it arise from expedient means.
The Tathāgata is always in a state of meditative concentration, his single mind never forgetting; he is the most supreme among all samādhis, eternally abiding in one-pointed concentration.
He universally perceives all samādhis and meditative attainments; his mind never regresses and is never subject to increase or decrease, and that which he manifests is never indeterminate.
"The Tathāgata’s samādhi is from the beginning unarisen and cannot be observed; it is beyond the reach of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, surpassing all bodhisattvas and perfectly enlightened ones.
No one can transcend the Tathāgata’s samādhi; it stands preeminent and peerless, majestic and immeasurable, such that no sentient being can know it."

"The wisdom of the Tathāgata is pervasive and boundless; it is inexhaustible, infinite, and beyond all analogy. By means of skillful expedients, he transforms and enlightens the śrāvakas, causing them to attain a concentrated mind."

“The Tathāgata fully knows and understands the practices of all pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas, instructing them according to what is appropriate for the time; this is the seventh activity of the Tathāgata.”
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The causes and conditions of sentient beings, And their afflictions and desires— He knows them all with sovereign mastery; His wisdom is without limit or depth."
Whether their conduct is pure or otherwise impure,
the Buddha, possessing great wisdom and mastery, understands them all completely.
Through heedfulness regarding karmic retribution and the arising of clear wisdom from causes and conditions, he fully comprehends this.
Karmic formations arise from ignorance, and from those formations,
consciousness, name-and-form, and likewise the six sense bases— their fundamental conditions—
were all fully realized by the Blessed One as the workings of dependent origination.
Conditioned by the dust of toil and desire, whatever is craved and performed—
beholding these causes and conditions, one sees that such activities proceed from desire.
Bound by the fetters of conceptual thought, these serve as the causal conditions for dependent origination.
The dwelling place of all people arises from these causal conditions.
Regarding the vows made by all people, there are two causal conditions:
first, listening to others; second, carefully reflecting upon and receiving their words.
Having reflected within as is appropriate, one contemplates that all phenomena are entirely empty;
such a person attains liberation from the ocean and rivers of birth and death.
Observing with serene stillness, one diligently eliminates the two [extremes].
Contemplating and observing it, there is no coming and no going.
Weighing and examining its source, there is neither birth nor end.
When one enters the Way through that quiescent extinction, only then is one pure.
Abiding constantly in right practice, the wise cultivate the three [trainings];
those who are heedful revere the three gates of liberation.
Having perfected the wisdom of cessation, they reach the state of non-arising through sincerity.
This is the work of karmic retribution; with purity, he gives rise to the supreme vow.
With the most excellent single-mindedness, he knows [all things] and constantly dwells in right samādhi.
Having attained the state of nirvāṇa, his mind remains courageous and rises once more.
Observing and contemplating all things, whether adverse or favorable,
that Buddha, the Great Dharma King, abides in the meditative absorption of the eight gates of liberation.
With a single-pointed mind, he attains immeasurable billions of concentrations.
Peerless and all-seeing, his conduct is universally impartial.
His mind is settled in its practice, and the Dharma he follows is inexhaustible;
because of this practice, his supreme mind is nowhere fixed.
If the concentration of mind of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is likewise such,
then the various kinds of concentration of the bodhisattvas—
such as the concentration of the mind dwelling in peace— all transcend them.
"The deeds cultivated by the Tathāgata, He teaches and transforms through wisdom according to the occasion.
*Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Scroll Four;
*Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Seventeen: Knowing the Original Conduct of Sentient Beings.
The Buddha addressed the son of good family:

“The Tathāgata, having beheld himself and other sentient beings, knows their past deeds and practices—incalculable throughout one lifetime, ten lifetimes, a hundred lifetimes, a thousand lifetimes, a hundred thousand lifetimes, and countless incalculable ages; through hundreds of thousands of billions of lifetimes, and through the formation and destruction of worlds and the establishment and exhaustion of kalpas, all of which are likewise incalculable—and he knows them all completely, without anything remaining unpenetrated. There is no limit to his knowledge of the cycles of worlds and kalpas.”

He fully recounts their names, clans, dwellings, food and drink, complexions, physical forms, and the length of their lifespans; he describes the various experiences of suffering, pleasure, good, and evil they encountered in such-and-such places, as well as their deaths in one place and births in another, their deaths in one place and subsequent rebirths in that same place, including their speech, learning, dialects, and literary compositions.
Regarding the beginning and end of one's own self and all sentient beings, he expounds the Dharma for them with complete clarity.

"The Tathāgata fully knows the origins from which sentient beings come, their beginnings and ends, and the sufferings and joys they have experienced; according to the appropriate time and by examining their roots and branches, he preaches the Dharma for them."

One discerns the attachments held by the past mind and the conditions embraced by the mind that cause obstructions; or, regarding those causes that have not yet decayed or been discarded, from what origin did this mind originally arise?
The Tathāgata knows them all.

Such are the mental activities of each individual; according to those activities, obscurations arise. The Tathāgata is able to fully proclaim the origins and endings of their practices throughout countless *gaṅgā-vāluka* eons;
furthermore, he observes the origins and endings of the minds of all sentient beings in the ten directions as being equal and without distinction.

To speak of its primordial limit, the future is likewise so; that which the mind takes as its object is seen by the Tathāgata to be originally non-existent, and there is nothing beyond this that is not infinite. This is because the Tathāgata knows the minds of sentient beings of the distant past to be inconceivable and immeasurable, and the holy wisdom of the Buddha is beyond calculation.
“The Tathāgata observes the conduct of sentient beings:

their hearts harboring fear, being restless and uneasy, wandering through birth and death; he knows who is where, from whom each has come, those who have originally planted roots of virtue with their resolve set upon the Buddha-way, or those of the vehicles of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha; based on the virtues they have cultivated, he fully recognizes and remembers all as they receive the Tathāgata’s holy wisdom.”

"This is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the causal retribution of the roots of virtue planted by sentient beings; he preaches the Dharma according to their fundamental causes, causing those who hear it to establish themselves in non-retrogression, and enabling each to attain their proper place through the faith and inclinations of their own past conduct. This is the eighth activity of the Tathāgata."
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The number of kalpas is bottomless, numbering in the hundreds of billions; as for the lamps of the world, he fully knows all that occurred in antiquity."
Furthermore, one examines one’s own body and understands that of sentient beings; what is observed is as clear as a pearl in the palm of the hand.
Their physical features are likewise so; where they dwell until their final passing, the places they traverse, and the conditions upon which they depend to receive such bodies are all clearly seen.
That vehicle of equality expounds those teachings; it fully knows the minds of all beings throughout the past—
immeasurable and bottomless— as well as the dharmas they contemplate and the ways they proceed,
and the arising of their resolve through that most excellent great wisdom.
Regarding the minds within this interval, from the distant past, he dwells in knowledge that fully understands the conduct of beings.
Even if one were to weigh their origins and ends over kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, praising and expounding upon them, one could never reach their limit.
He proclaims for us the source of the primordial limit, which is bottomless in the future; he declares the practices performed in antiquity.
Peerless and matchless, his wisdom is inexhaustible; such is the World-Honored One, whose noble wisdom is like the ocean.
Even regarding the past, those who have honored and revered the Most Victorious One, abiding in the Buddha’s supernormal powers,
strengths, and fearlessnesses— recall all of these deeds performed in former lives.
The World-Honored One knows all that sentient beings think; according to their past origins and the various virtues they have planted, he fully recognizes this.
For those who abide in the Three Vehicles, he brings them to the stage of non-retrogression and the pure path of liberation.
Abiding in distinct consciousness, his virtuous deeds of past lives are beyond the capacity of all sentient beings to conceive.
This is the eighth activity of the Great Sage; through it he transforms sentient beings, and those delivered by him are bottomless.
Chapter 18: On Penetrating Vision. In the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Chapter Eighteen, "On Penetrating Vision," the Buddha addressed the son of good family:

"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, with the pure divine eye that surpasses that of ordinary beings, perceives all sentient beings—those who are born and those who die; the subtle and the defiled; the virtuous and the evil; the auspicious and the calamitous; the beautiful countenances and the ugly forms; those tending toward peace and those tending toward suffering. He knows, exactly as they are, the fruits of the retribution for the auspicious and calamitous deeds performed by these beings, according to their origins and their conclusions."

Such a person acts wickedly with the body, speaks wickedly with the mouth, and harbors thoughts of malice in the mind; they slander and revile the noble ones and fall into wrong views. By means of the deeds performed through these wrong views, when their life ends and the body perishes, they fall into the evil realms, suffering the torments of the hells.

Thereupon, those people whose bodily conduct was good, whose speech was good, and whose mental intentions were good—those who did not revile the noble ones, who followed right view, and who, by virtue of that right view, performed wholesome deeds—when their lives ended and their bodies dissolved, they proceeded to a state of peace and were reborn in a world of happiness.
"In that regard, the Tathāgata, by means of his divine eye, observes all Buddha-fields according to their respective directions as being equal to the realm of space—boundless and limitless.
Contemplating the dharma-realm, he finds it ungraspable and remains without attachment, transcending all traces of linguistic expression."

Among those sentient beings who have assumed physical forms, there are none who, having appeared in this world, are not seen to eventually pass away and be born again; likewise, all those Buddha-fields existing in the present are seen to undergo external disintegration and reformation.
Furthermore, all the bodhisattvas who appear likewise behold this [Buddha] passing away at the end of his life, coming to be born [elsewhere], and again leaving the household life;
or they behold those who appear sitting beneath trees, attaining supreme perfect enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, and relinquishing their lifespan to enter parinirvāṇa.
The liberation and parinirvāṇa of the śrāvakas all further perceive this dharma of the pratyekabuddhas, manifesting supernatural powers (ṛddhipāda) to bring benefit to sentient beings.

"There may be sentient beings whose forms do not appear—those whom non-Buddhists, heterodox scholars, or seers possessing the five supernormal powers cannot see through their clarity; those whom śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas cannot reach—the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, perceives all such classes with his divine eye (divyacakṣus)."

“The Tathāgata perceives the subtle spirits within sentient beings; their faculties are like chariot wheels and abound throughout the trichiliocosm, such that those who do not manifest cannot be fully enumerated.”
The realm of sentient beings is thus immeasurable, vast and boundless without limit or depth;
the Tathāgata’s divine eye is as sublime as this, perceiving all Buddha-lands and the various classes of sentient beings, including their origins, endings, and fundamental realms.

"Whichever sentient beings are to be transformed by the Buddha and follow the discipline, he causes them to practice the Buddha's precepts according to their original nature; he then establishes himself before them and transforms that person, while others nearby do not even perceive it. This is the ninth activity of the Tathāgata."
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgata’s divine eye Is pure and free from defilement;
Cultivated through immeasurable kalpas, It is the holy majesty of merit."
Beholding throughout the ten directions the various characteristics of all Buddha-fields—
whatever exists and whatever does not, and all that undergoes rise and fall—
as well as all those sentient beings therein, both those with form and those without form.
They return to the realms of good and evil, being born above, below, or in between;
passing away and coming again to receive a womb—those who commit evil fall into suffering, while those who accumulate merit find peace and joy;
the Most Victorious One knows all this completely.
All those assemblies of bodhisattvas, throughout all buddha-fields,
perform their practices with purposeful strides and manifest the act of leaving home.
Whether beneath the tree of enlightenment, they subdue the hosts of Māra.
All Buddhas know this, and with their divine eyes they behold it all.
When a Buddha acts as the Dharma King and attains supreme, perfect enlightenment,
he turns the wheel of Dharma to deliver and liberate all devas and humans.
Performing the sublime work of a Buddha,
whether by extending his lifespan or manifesting his parinirvāṇa, the Buddha perceives them all.
Those who listen to the Dharma of the Guide, contemplate it, and practice accordingly— [he perceives them all].
He has attained the most honored and pure karma, Establishing himself free from affliction and feverish distress.
Having personally heard the Way of the Sūtras, He reviles birth and death;
Having already crossed over to the other shore, The Most Victorious One beholds all of this.
The divine eye of those outsiders, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas,
and bodhisattvas perceives the realm of birth, yet does not fully comprehend it.
The divine eye of the Tathāgata is pure and free from defilement;
He perceives universally among sentient beings the subtle and wondrous abodes of their spirits.
Their manifestations are like chariot wheels;
the subtle and wondrous bodies of sentient beings exceed in number those of the gods and humans within the three thousandfold world system.
The various kinds of birth and death within the realms of sentient beings are thus;
knowing fully the perceptions of gods and humans, he universally manifests the Buddha-way for them.
Those whom the Tathāgata has enlightened and transformed possess faculties that are sharp and penetrating.
The Hero of the World stands before them, preaching the most sublime Dharma;
yet those standing at his side do not perceive the Tathāgata’s transformation.
This is the work of the Guide, the power of his divine eye.
Chapter Nineteen: The Exhaustion of All Outflows. In the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Chapter Nineteen, "The Exhaustion of All Outflows," the Buddha again addressed the son of good family:

"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*). With a mind free of outflows, he cultivates liberation; having crossed over by means of wisdom, he has realized the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and honors his conduct. Birth and death have been severed, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and he knows the source of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)."
The Tathāgata, by means of his untainted wisdom—which is pure, stainless, bright, and radiant—eliminates all obscurations and hindrances in every place where he dwells.
"The assembly of śrāvakas has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), yet they remain limited and obstructed, not having reached the place of ultimate rest.
As for the pratyekabuddhas, though they have exhausted all outflows, they are limited and obstructed regarding the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and lack eloquence (*pratibhāna*).

The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, has exhausted all outflows; his manifold practices are universally assembled and fully perfected. He has eliminated all places of abiding, maintains great compassion, possesses courageous eloquence and fearlessness, and his majestic spiritual power is so sublime that none can scrutinize it. It is beyond the reach of all worldly people, being equal toward all at once with a single mind."

"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, likewise has no place of obstruction for his karmic offenses; his majestic deportment and ritual propriety are without deficiency or omission. He is like empty space, fundamentally pure, and cannot be overcome by any māras or heterodox teachers."
Merit and renown constitute the Tathāgata’s wisdom that has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*); it does not coincide with or conform to any worldly dust, desires, or obstructions.

This untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) abides in firm stability; for the sake of sentient beings who are subject to the dust and outflows of existence, he preaches the Dharma free from outflows, expounding the sūtras to eliminate all attachments, which arise from insincere thoughts.

Sentient beings, by means of this, give rise to the various outflows and thus undergo the aggregates and sense bases; for this reason, you should observe and examine carefully. The Tathāgata provides analogies to reveal the fundamental nature and manifests himself before them, preaching the Dharma as appropriate, so that they may know that sensory desires are false and without reality, and so that they may understand through careful examination that in the True Truth there is no one who receives dharmas. This, noble son!
"This is the tenth deed of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One.
Thereupon the Buddha spoke in verse:
"That Guide possesses untainted wisdom; he illuminates and proclaims it widely and universally."
Pure and immeasurable, he possesses the ten powers;
by virtue of his preeminent majesty, he is capable of this, and with steadfast faith, he follows the Way.
Those whose wisdom has exhausted all outflows are called the assembly of śrāvakas; they have not yet eliminated the basis of cessation and remain bound by obstructions.
The one supreme among men, the teacher of the multitude, has already eliminated the basis of cessation and alone is free from all limits and obstructions.
Those who have attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha are likewise so; they lack great compassion and eloquence.
Yet there is the Buddha, the World-Honored One, whose outflows are exhausted, possessing inexhaustible compassion and immeasurable eloquence.
The Pure and Honored One, abiding in inexhaustible wisdom, knows the causes of the outflows for all these people.
Because they are attached to this, he provides [instruction] to sentient beings; yet they are unable to comprehend his true traces of the Arhat.
The Most Victorious One, out of compassion for these three, preached the Dharma of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
These various dharmas originally arise from the unarisen; by thoroughly understanding these manifold phenomena, one attains the supreme path of Buddhahood.
There is no person, nor even a life-span, yet we designate one as "a person," and the same applies to all that is done.
All sentient beings rely upon these various [conceptions]; out of compassion, the World-Honored One has therefore taught liberation.
Furthermore, they dwell therein without weariness, nor have they ever diminished the Buddha’s wisdom.
For this reason, being most excellent, they always maintain earnest diligence; with hearts constantly filled with compassion, they proclaim the Way of the Sūtras.
