The Buddha’s deeds are thus, his peerless match being such as this; these constitute the Ten Powers by which he subdues the heterodox.
Abiding in the Ten Powers, he establishes a mighty force and turns the supreme Wheel of Dharma, which is beyond measure.
Chapter 20: The Four Fearlessnesses. In the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Chapter Twenty, "The Four Fearlessnesses," the Buddha addressed the sons of good family:
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, possesses four fearlessnesses; he abides in truth and is courageous in his deeds."

I have attained the perfectly true and impartial awakening; having realized this for myself, no devas, worldlings, śramaṇas, brahmins, Māras, Śakras, or Brahmās can obstruct the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
It has never been the case that one who speaks without clear understanding could achieve supreme perfect enlightenment.
For what reason is the Tathāgata called "Equally and Perfectly Enlightened"?
Because he fully realizes that all dharmas are entirely equal and devoid of partiality.
The dharmas of ordinary beings and the dharmas of the Buddhas are entirely equal; therefore, one attains perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

The dharmas that are studied and those that are not studied, the dharmas of the *pratyekabuddhas* and the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, up to the dharmas of all Buddhas—all these are likewise equal; therefore, it is called perfect enlightenment.

Regarding the mundane and the supramundane, the culpable and the blameless, the tainted and the untainted, the conditioned and the unconditioned, the finite and the infinite—these two categories of dharmas are all equalized; therefore, one attains perfect enlightenment.
"Why are they equal? They are equal by virtue of emptiness; therefore, they are said to be equal.
All views are naturally equal through the absence of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), for conceptualization itself is natural."
Because of wishlessness and so forth, the three realms are naturally so;
because of signlessness and so forth, that which is conceptualized is naturally so;
because of absence of formation and so forth, formations are naturally so.
Because there is no arising and so forth, that which arises is spontaneous;
because there is no dependence and so forth, that upon which it depends is spontaneous;
because it is able to be as it is in thorough examination and so forth, the three periods of time are spontaneous.
Because wisdom and so forth are naturally [identical to] ignorance and craving;
because Nirvana and so forth are naturally [identical to] birth and death.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, is thus equal toward all dharmas; therefore, he has attained perfect enlightenment, and for this reason he is called the "Equally Enlightened One.

Just as the Tathāgata, having thoroughly understood all dharmas, attains supreme perfect enlightenment, so too does he establish himself in great compassion and, employing various skillful means and diverse causes and conditions, expounds the teaching to sentient beings according to their needs. Thus they take refuge in the Dharma, which arises from the Dharma, and immediately extinguish the source of suffering and affliction.

In this regard, there are those who claim to be teachers though they are not, who honor themselves as venerable though they are not, and who claim to have attained perfect enlightenment though they have not.
Therefore, the Tathāgata alone is free from fear among such classes of beings; he is transcendent, peerless, and without equal. This is the eleventh deed of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Because he has attained perfect enlightenment Regarding the equality of all phenomena,
Therefore, as the One of Equal Enlightenment, The Tathāgata manifests everywhere."
The dharmas of ordinary beings and the dharmas of the Buddha are likewise equal;
the dharmas of what is learned and what is not learned, as well as those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle,
all worldly dharmas, and the dharmas that transcend the world— [all are equal].
All wholesome and unwholesome deeds, and nirvana—all are of one and the same kind.
Understanding emptiness and signlessness, they abandon all aspirations;
seeing neither arising nor activity, they view these matters with equanimity.
"Equally clear regarding such karma, what has been taught is likewise thus;
by means of this one delivers sentient beings—this is the Dharma of the Great Sage.
The Buddha further addressed the son of good family:

"The Tathāgata himself knows that all his outflows are exhausted; among gods and humans, in this world of gods and men, none are able to revile the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, nor dare say that his outflows are not yet exhausted."

Regarding what is called the Tathāgata whose outflows are exhausted: the Tathāgata has already been liberated from the source of craving and desire; his mind understands all desires and is free from any obstruction.

Furthermore, as for the Buddha-mind, it has already transcended all outflows and eliminated all practices of worldly defilement without any obstruction; for this reason, he is named the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One.

Because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted, he manifests in the world. By means of the noble wisdom of the ultimate truth, no one dares to stand before him to obstruct the rain of Dharma; he causes the elimination of defiled practices so that they may realize the fruit of realization. For this reason, it is called "exhaustion."
There is no exhaustion that has not been exhausted, nor has there ever been an exhaustion that was produced; for this reason, it is called "exhaustion.

That which the Tathāgata calls the exhaustion of the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is something that can no longer be exhausted. Since there is nothing further to be exhausted, this is the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); that which is unconditioned is without grasping (anupādāna).

Neither abiding nor non-abiding—this absence of a fixed location is called "establishment. To accomplish the dwelling of all Tathāgatas in the unarisen, and for these dharmas to abide as the dharma-realm abides, is the wisdom of the worthy one.
One who responds in this way has no response; they neither enter parinirvāṇa nor achieve anything.
Such a semblance-dharma cannot be apprehended as having any outflows, forms, or colors, nor does it eliminate outflows.

“The Tathāgata, abiding in great compassion and skillful means, expounds the sūtras for the sake of all sentient beings to cause them to eliminate all outflows; this is the twelfth deed of the Tathāgata.”
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“The Most Victorious One has exhausted all outflows and desires; Never again shall there be greed or obstruction.
The Honored among Men is liberated from all birth and death; He has severed defilements without remainder.”
Abiding securely, they have cast off all ignorance; never again shall the darkness of delusion be found.
Among the various views of other beings, he is a lion among men; therefore, he is unimpeded and free from the dust of desire.
Abiding securely in what has been taught according to the occasion, they have exhausted all outflows and are free from birth and death;
having thoroughly investigated all phenomena as being non-existent, how could they ever cause what is ended to grow again?
That which is exhausted has no companion or faction; that which is already exhausted is conventionally termed "exhausted.
That which undergoes exhaustion consists of the two conditioned realms (saṃskṛta), yet even in those, the three characteristics are ultimately non-existent.
Abiding in this realm without grasping or fabrication, the Buddha has crossed to the further shore by means of noble wisdom;
understanding this, one should preach the Dharma—this is what is meant by abiding securely in the twelve dharmas.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:

“The Tathāgata has fully understood all obstructive dharmas of defilement and desire, yet he remains without hindrance; among the heavens and the world, among the devas and the people, none are able to disparage the Tathāgata by saying that his words do not accord with the Dharma.”
"In that regard, what is meant by 'falling away from the Dharma'?
Furthermore, there is one thing that causes one to fall away from the Dharma.
What do you say: is the disparagement of the Tathāgata not a single [act]?"
This refers to a mind that is agitated and unable to be single-mindedly diligent.
Furthermore, there are two other dharmas:
first, a lack of shame; second, a lack of remorse.
"Furthermore, there are three things:
first, committing evil deeds with the body; second, uttering coarse words with the mouth; third, harboring malicious intent in the mind."
“Furthermore, there are four things: two practices that lead from the attainable to the unattainable;
namely, first, stubbornness; second, anger; third, resentment; and fourth, delusion.”
"Furthermore, there are five things:
first, killing; second, stealing; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech; and fifth, intoxication from alcohol."
"Furthermore, there are six dharmas: first, a lack of reverent devotion;

second, stinginess regarding the sūtras; third, disparaging the prohibitions and precepts; fourth, failing to follow a concentrated mind; fifth, not maintaining mindfulness of the Dharma; and sixth, being arrogant toward the Dharma Master."
"Furthermore, there are seven dharmas: first, self-importance;
second, extreme pride; third, heavy pride; fourth, the conceit 'I am'; fifth, false pride; sixth, surpassing all haughtiness; and seventh, thinking 'none can equal me.'"
"Furthermore, there are eight things:
first, wrong view; second, wrong intention; third, wrong speech; fourth, wrong action; fifth, wrong livelihood; sixth, wrong effort; seventh, wrong mindfulness; and eighth, wrong concentration."
"Furthermore, there are nine things, namely the nine types of harm and affliction: first, those whom I respect are treated with contempt;

second, they are being treated with contempt now; third, they will encroach upon me in the future; fourth, those whom I detest are treated with respect and affection; fifth, they are being respected now; sixth, they will be respected in the future; seventh, they have previously harmed and insulted me; eighth, they are harming me now; ninth, they will harm me in the future. It is on account of these that the mind of affliction and harm arises."
"Furthermore, there are ten dharmas, namely the ten unwholesome karmic paths:

first, killing; second, stealing; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech; fifth, divisive speech; sixth, harsh speech; seventh, frivolous speech; eighth, ignorance; ninth, contention; and tenth, wrong view. These constitute conduct that follows from improper mindfulness."

"To see that one should accord with the Dharma yet not take delight in it; to fall into perversion and remain under the yoke of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); to rely upon the evils of false views and worldly attachment—thereby losing the True Dharma, becoming estranged from it, obstructed by it, and neglecting it."
The Tathāgata fully knows the conduct of body, speech, and mind; as he knows it, he knows all obscurations and hindrances, and his teaching is precise.
Such dharmas lead to obscurations and hindrances, and these dharmas must be eliminated.

Because he is able to eliminate them, he teaches the Dharma so that all sentient beings may remove their veils and coverings and transcend to liberation. This is the thirteenth activity of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Those supreme ones who have clearly realized the Dharma— if one practices under them yet fails to attain liberation,
clinging with a heart of attachment unable to let go, one is said to be devoid of shame and remorse."
The body, speech, and mind are likewise; at first, one was unable to guard them against greed, hatred, delusion, and fear.
One committed killing, theft, adultery, and intoxication through falsehood—the six ways of lost conduct and the seven forms of pride.
It is said that the eight wrong doors of liberation all obstruct and cause one to abandon the path to liberation.
If one cannot restrain the mind, it will fall into the ten unwholesome courses of action;
because of failing to relinquish them and failing to accord with right mindfulness, those of such a kind are not liberated.
Seeing that one follows after inverted attachments and relies upon the meaning of negligence, one should not practice such dharmas;
thus may one become a venerable among men.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
“The Tathāgata thoroughly understands the conduct of the noble ones; by immediately establishing equanimity, one exhausts suffering and affliction.
Sentient beings practice virtue and thereby attain birth; if one establishes equanimity, then harm and calamity are extinguished.”

Even if the devas and the people of the world were unable to obstruct the True Dharma of the Tathāgata—claiming that he is unworthy of being venerated by the assembly of sages or unfit for the Great Way—the Buddha would forever remain without fear.
"What is the fundamental tenet?
It is the path of the One Vehicle (ekayāna).
There are two dharmas for purifying sentient beings:"
The first is called tranquility; the second is called aspiration.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
the first is called emptiness, the second is called signlessness, and the third is called wishlessness.
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four foundations of mindfulness:
first, mindfulness of the body; second, mindfulness of feelings; third, mindfulness of mental formations; and fourth, mindfulness of phenomena."
"Furthermore, there are five dharmas:
first, the faculty of faith; second, the faculty of diligence; third, the faculty of intention; fourth, the faculty of concentration; and fifth, the faculty of wisdom."
“Furthermore, there are six dharmas:
first, mindfulness of the Buddha; second, mindfulness of the Dharma; third, mindfulness of the Saṃgha; fourth, mindfulness of giving; fifth, mindfulness of precepts; sixth, mindfulness of the devas.”
"Furthermore, there are seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhyaṅga*):

first, the factor of mindfulness; second, the factor of dharma-discernment; third, the factor of energy; fourth, the factor of rapture; fifth, the factor of tranquility; sixth, the factor of concentration; and seventh, the factor of equanimity."
Furthermore, there are eight factors conducive to the Dharma:
first, right view; second, right mindfulness; third, right speech; fourth, right action; fifth, right livelihood; sixth, right effort; seventh, right intention; and eighth, right concentration.

"Furthermore, there are nine dharmas that should be practiced: first, the first dhyāna; second, the second dhyāna; third, the third dhyāna; fourth, the fourth dhyāna; fifth, the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space; sixth, the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness; seventh, the meditative attainment of the sphere of nothingness; eighth, the meditative attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and ninth, the meditative attainment of the cessation of all sensation and perception."

"Furthermore, there are ten dharmas that should be practiced: first, abstaining from killing; second, abstaining from stealing; third, abstaining from sexual misconduct; fourth, abstaining from false speech; fifth, abstaining from divisive speech; sixth, abstaining from harsh speech; seventh, abstaining from abusive speech; eighth, abstaining from frivolous speech; ninth, abstaining from ill will; and tenth, being free from wrong views and abiding in right action."

This is called what should be practiced: being detached from that which arises. This constitutes the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—the aggregate of ethical discipline, the perfection of concentration, the integration of wisdom, the ultimate stage of liberation, and the penetration of the knowledge and vision of deliverance—whereby one fulfills the noble truths and remains detached from that which arises.
"Furthermore, what is called 'detachment from that which arises' refers to practicing the equanimous deeds of the noble ones (ārya).

As for those who correspond to the noble ones: they have no categories of dharmas, whether dual or non-dual; neither skillful means nor the absence thereof; neither progress nor retreat; neither arising nor non-arising; neither grasping nor abandoning. These are the paths by which one transcends all unequal practices of duality."
All phenomena are non-dual; thus, they arise as the basis for the cultivation of analytical wisdom.
The Tathāgata teaches this practice of non-arising to sentient beings;
if they can practice this, sentient beings will find their suffering and afflictions exhausted upon returning to it. This is the fourteenth activity of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Drawing near to this purity, one reaches the immeasurable; that upon which people rely, one attains through it to purity."
Most supreme and universally renowned, he knows all things completely; having mastered the scriptures, he delights in preaching the nectar of the Dharma.
Reaching the pinnacle of all virtues and the innumerable dharmas, his factors of enlightenment are pure; thus he becomes a Buddha, a World-Honored One.
The courageous practice this and thereby attain liberation; that which is expounded by the One of Ten Powers has no fixed location.
By recollecting accordingly as is appropriate, one extinguishes the afflictions; through the dharmas of skillful means, one flourishes in the abundance of sorrowlessness.
Not relying on the Dharma, not clinging to what is non-Dharma, one attains equanimous liberation; with diligence that is impartial,
taking virtue as its condition, one does not rely on the dharmas of the Path,
being as vast, empty, and thoughtless as space.
Like a magical illusion, like what is seen in a dream—thus one attains liberation from the destinies of birth and death.
This is the activity practiced by those of the Ten Powers; it is that which people attain throughout their wanderings.
"Therefore, through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he delivers and liberates them; he gives rise to and promotes loving-kindness and pity, and thus he is without peer.
Chapter 21: The Eighteen Unshared Dharmas, Part One. The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, is without flaw or omission; whether wise or foolish, they do not err regarding the True Dharma he has practiced. Why is this?

Because the bodily conduct of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, is without deficiency, he has attained the perfectly true and impartial awakening; his majestic power is sublime, and his physical form is exceptionally beautiful.”

His deportment, etiquette, gaze, and movements accorded with equanimity; he was clad in the Dharma robes and held the alms-bowl in his hand. Whether walking, stopping, coming or going, turning around, pacing up and down, sitting, standing, reclining, or lying down, as he entered and exited provinces, states, great kingdoms, districts, towns, and villages, his feet did not touch the ground. The thousand-spoked marks naturally manifested as wheels, and soft, exquisite, fragrant, and pure lotuses appeared upon the earth.

When the Tathāgata’s feet tread upon them, any insects, ants, or blood-bearing creatures that encounter the Tathāgata’s feet shall attain peace and security for seven days and nights; after their lives end, they will be reborn in the heavens.

His Dharma robes naturally remained four inches away from his body without clinging to it; even the winds of Sūramgama could not move the garments, and all sentient beings nearby attained peace and security.
Therefore it is said: "The body of the Tathāgata is without deficiency or flaw.

Furthermore, son of good family, whatever words the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, utters are never deficient; neither the wise nor the foolish can find an opportunity to seek out faults or shortcomings.

Why is this so? Because that which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, speaks is timely; his utterances are sincere, truthful, and without falsehood. His words accord with righteousness, conform to the Dharma, and follow the teachings of the Vinaya. His speech is impartial, his words and deeds correspond, and his discourse is free from contradiction or error regarding what is and is not the proper time.
All that is spoken from the mouth delights the hearts of all sentient beings; it is never redundant, for its meaning and principles are beautiful, essential, and achieve sublime adornment.
When the mouth utters a single sound, it accords with the inclinations and thoughts of all sentient beings, so that each hears and understands it with joy and attains clear realization.
For this reason, he is called the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, whose speech is without deficiency.

Furthermore, son of good family, the mental intentions of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, are likewise free from error; he does not allow the wise or the foolish who seek an advantage to cause him to lose his mindfulness of the Dharma.

Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata is always in a state of meditative concentration and never lacks tranquility; he embraces all classes of sentient beings to enable them to attain the fundamental nature of their own minds, and having eliminated all errors and delusions, he preaches the Dharma for them. These constitute the fifteenth of the Tathāgata’s activities.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"That venerable Great Being is without flaw; his bodily actions, his speech, and his superior thoughts are all in accord."
That Lion of the World, the Protector, is without deficiency and without fault; out of compassion he enters among them, manifesting with equal pity and sorrow.
Seeking the loss of Buddhahood, he finds none at all; by means of this Dharma of the sutra, he shows people the way to tranquility.
"To cause all to abandon these various flawed practices—
this is the most excellent fifteenth deed.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:

"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, has no coarse teaching; the sounds he proclaims ensure that none of the Māras and their retinues, nor those of external heterodox schools, such as the naked ascetics who practice extraordinary and divergent arts, shall find any opportunity."
The Tathāgata is without speech and without sound, being free from all attachments.
The Tathāgata is difficult to describe; all sentient beings receive his teachings through their opening of minds, yet not by means of the conditioned, nor do they abide in the unconditioned.
The bodily conduct of the Tathāgata is thoroughly perfected without exception, and his speech is free from deficiency.
Yet, in his current practice, he allows others to find their own convenience and does not contend with the world.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has no vocal sound; he always acts in accordance with emptiness.
The Tathāgata is without self and without anything perceived; furthermore, being free from the karma of craving, he is detached from all realms of existence.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has no disputes.
Even though he produces no sound himself, he expounds the Dharma by eliminating the sounds of sentient beings; this is the sixteenth activity of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"If one hears praise, one is not moved by joy;
if one hears disparagement, one likewise feels no sorrow."
Having removed all attachments, they harbor no expectations; having fundamentally cultivated wholesome conduct, their practice is free from clinging.
Cultivating the supreme truth, they always accord with the practice of emptiness; being without self and without grasping, they are free from both hatred and love.
"Abiding as they do, they expound the teachings of the sutras; this is their ultimate sincerity and their noble undertaking.
The Buddha further addressed the son of good family:
“The Tathāgata is ever mindful and never forgets; he is neither distracted nor confused, and his mind is not deluded or disoriented such that it would stray from the Dharma.

The Tathāgata is always in a state of meditative concentration; for the sake of the wisdom of all-knowledge and the various supernormal powers, he abides in liberation, meditative concentration, and right reception.”

Being incapable of forgetfulness, they universally perceive the dwelling places of the mental activities of all sentient beings; observing their roots, they preach the Dharma in accordance with the truth, never contravening the principles of the Dharma, their eloquence being clear and illuminating, compliant and without opposition.
That which is "unforgetting" means that his wisdom regarding the past, future, and present is free from all obstruction, such that he perceives the three periods of time.

Because of his own person, he never neglects or forgets his own mind; likewise, he extends compassion to all sentient beings of the ten directions, earnestly mindful of rescuing them by preaching the Dharma for them—this is the seventeenth activity of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"What the Guide contemplates, he never forgets; In accordance with the Dharma and dhyāna, he practices through the gates of liberation."
For all sentient beings, according to their inclinations, natures, and conduct, and in accordance with where they are headed, he preaches the Dharma for them.
What he discerns and understands he never forgets; he penetrates the three periods of time and acts without transgression.
"Being without forgetfulness and responding appropriately to their preaching of the Dharma—
this is the practice undertaken by all these Great Sages.
The Buddha further addressed the son of good family:
“The Tathāgata’s ultimate true mind is eternally tranquil; there is no state of non-concentration whether he is sitting or rising, walking, lying down or sleeping, or eating and drinking.
His speech is serene, and he is always with a single-minded focus.”

The Tathāgata’s samādhi is subtle and wondrous; his deliverance is infinite as he has transcended to the other shore. With single-minded contemplation, he is from the beginning free of any obscuration, universally observing all sentient beings of every form—those whose conduct is fixed in concentration and those who are not.

No one dares to perceive or examine the mind of the Tathāgata’s contemplative reflections, except for those whom the Tathāgata’s divine power establishes and through whom he manifests his majestic spiritual authority; only they are able to see it.

"Suppose that the Great Sage were always in a state of single-minded concentration and his samādhi were likewise such that he could not rise or descend to preach the Dharma to people, nor could he further observe them. Why is this so?
Because he constantly perceives the minds of all sentient beings.

"The sublime wisdom of the Buddha is thus lofty and majestic—unreachable, as profound as empty space, without interior or exterior, and penetratingly pervasive; this is the eighteenth activity of the Tathāgata."
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“The Buddha has no advancing or retreating; his mind is eternally fixed and stable.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, eating, or speaking, he remains serene, and none are able to disturb him.”
Supremely and eternally concentrated, none dare to confuse him;
throughout the eight directions, above, and below, none can ever find an opportunity, nor do they dare to know the state of his mind’s concentration.
"Because he establishes them according to their needs and preaches the Dharma for them, constantly expounding the principles of the Way—
this is the most supreme activity. —
*The Sutra of Great Compassion*, Scroll Five.
The Mahākaruṇā-sūtra, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
The Remainder of Chapter Twenty-one: The Eighteen Unshared Dharmas.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, possesses no manifold conceptions, nor does he have any discursive thoughts that would cause his mind to become deluded or forgetful."

Therefore, the Tathāgata has no notion of multiplicity: just as the soil of space cannot be exhausted, he does not perceive sentient beings as being distinct from one another, because they are fundamentally pure and lack multiplicity;
he perceives all Buddhas as having no variety of kinds, because the dharma-realm is indestructible and his wisdom is equal;
and he likewise has no thought of differentiation regarding all phenomena, because he is free from desire.

The Tathāgata does not show partiality or favoritism toward those who observe the precepts with mindfulness, nor does he revile those who violate them; he does not go to pay solemn respect to those who cultivate the Path, yet he does not disregard those who do not honor it; he does not consider the rules and teachings to be "mine," and he does not treat those who dwell forever in false views with contempt.
The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, acts with equanimity toward all phenomena; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One who has no manifold conceptions.

Since he has no manifold conceptions, he proclaims this absence of manifold conceptions, transforming and enlightening sentient beings so that they do not differ from one another. He eliminates all manifold conceptions and expounds the Dharma for them; this is the nineteenth activity of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Those who dwell securely on the Path, Free from manifold conceptualizations, In their final existence,
behold all buddha-fields."
When reckoned according to the scriptures, there is no difference between them;
those of great renown act with universal equanimity.
Whether they uphold the prohibitive precepts or have violated them;
Sentient beings are easy to transform, yet there are those who cannot be transformed.
The Honored Ones among two-legged beings maintain an impartial mind; they deliver sentient beings, even those who harbor various marks of greed.
The Buddha again addressed the son of noble family:
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, is free from hesitation; regarding all that he observes, he perceives their very roots and no longer needs to reflect."

Why is this so? The Tathāgata, the Great Sage, has already perfected his virtue and conduct; there is nothing he has not accomplished. His bodily actions are prudent and restrained, his mind is gentle and supple, and his observance of the precepts is pure and brilliant. His wisdom is peerless, yet it is not something to be gazed upon with awe, for the Tathāgata’s holy brilliance is not something that stands out as extraordinary.

The Buddha constantly observes and universally protects all with his wisdom and discernment; he does not follow the darkness of folly, but proceeds by means of transcending the world, nor does he fall into the deluded practices of worldly customs.
That which the Tathāgata protects arises from the noble and holy, and does not arise from what is unholy.

The Tathāgata turns the pure and unsurpassed Brahma-wheel; out of compassion for sentient beings, he attains mastery, walking alone throughout the ten directions without relying on others. Whatever he praises is free from partiality.
Furthermore, those whom the Tathāgata observes and protects are neither abrupt nor violent; they always proceed with orderly decorum and are free from error.

Wherever they go, they neither grasp nor reject, having already departed from the two extremes and all wandering currents, and having crossed the four great rivers. Even if one were to spend an entire eon weighing and measuring them, contemplating their origins and ends, one could never exhaustively fathom them. Each occupies a distinct place, beyond thought or non-thought; they know past thoughts without being disturbed by them, and do not manifest their own merit. Thus, they are thorough and real, without any discrepancy.

“The Buddha has thoroughly investigated and mastered all things, reaching everywhere without exception; such is the lofty and majestic great compassion (mahākaruṇā) of the Tathāgata in his observation. He protects all sentient beings by fully expounding the Dharma; this is the twentieth activity of the Tathāgata.”
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata’s observation and protection Have never known weariness;
He has well cultivated the meaning of the Path, His conduct being preeminent and extraordinary.”
With such a mind and body, with precepts and wisdom,
he is a supreme Great Being whose conduct is always sincere.
The Tathāgata has never harbored attachment to any harms.
Furthermore, they are without conceptualization or discursive thoughts, and they do not engage in deceptive acts.
That which they observe and protect is the truth, free from artificial embellishment;
thus, by means of this principle, they preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, is without greed or loss.
What is meant by ‘greed’?
One delights solely in wholesome dharmas.
What, then, are these wholesome dharmas?
They are such that the Tathāgata’s great compassion has never diminished, nor does it rely upon or cling to greed.
They are all without error regarding the sūtras spoken from great compassion, ensuring that sentient beings do not fall into delusion or exhaustion through greed for the precepts.
They transform and enlighten sentient beings without initial confusion or delusion, never abandoning tranquility, and there is nothing they initiate that is contradictory or abandoned;
they encourage all bodhisattvas so that they never forget, and they ensure that the Three Jewels are never interrupted.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, is free from all attachment; he takes delight in the holy wisdom and the true path of the Dharma. For this reason, he is called the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One.

Without succumbing to desire that would lead to depletion or loss, he proclaims the sūtras for the sake of all sentient beings, causing them to aspire to and delight in supreme, true realization and to be endowed with all supernormal powers and wisdom. This is the twenty-first activity of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The Most Victorious One is ever free from craving; He delights in the practice of virtuous deeds.
With compassion and kindness, he bestows the Dharma, To deliver and liberate all sentient beings."
Delighting in bringing relief to all living beings, he guides them according to the time;
most excellent, he does not impair the Path, and exhorts others not to sever the Three Jewels.
Free from greed, envy, anger, and malice, he does not follow the foolish prohibitions.
By means of various supernormal knowledges, he takes great delight in the teachings of the scriptures.
Seeing sentient beings indolent, the Most Victorious One transforms them to practice with diligence.
Having accumulated immeasurable karmic deeds of wisdom, he thereby delivers the multitudes.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, does not diminish or waste away in the matter of diligence; this is what is called the diligence of the Tathāgata.
What is meant by 'transforming and educating sentient beings'?"
Observing with diligence where they are to be found, one thereby delivers and liberates them without leaving a single person behind.
Ensuring that the hearing of the sutras is always clear and penetrating—this is called diligence.

“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having attained such a state, serves as a vessel for all who wish to hear the sutras; he does not grow weary even for an eon. Thus, for those who listen to and gather the profound Dharma, the Great Sage proclaims it without ceasing for an eon, teaching the scriptures to protect sentient beings by dispelling their need for food and sustenance.”

For the sake of a single person, the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, travels alone through Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; he transforms and guides them, causing them to resolve upon the Way. The Tathāgata’s body, mind, and speech never grow weary, and his body and mind remain serene and free from any idle attachment.

“The Tathāgata’s skillful means and diligent application of effort are such that there is none who does not praise them; by following equanimity, he employs this diligence to lead sentient beings to the sublime liberation of the Sage. This leads to the realization of the ultimate truth and even extends to the full manifestation of the Tathāgata’s meritorious achievements—this constitutes the twenty-second activity of the Tathāgata.”
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"That Lion among Men, by the power of his diligence,
constantly extols this power of diligence."
The power of his diligent exertion has never suffered any decline;
the sūtras and dharmas he expounds do so because they accord with those who are fit vessels for the Dharma.
Abiding securely in his vigor, none are able to fathom or exhaust its full extent.
In body, speech, and mind, he has never known weariness or fatigue.
Having attained equanimity through diligence, he is entirely free from fault or transgression.
With a heart imbued with compassion, he constantly teaches for the sake of sentient beings.
The Buddha again addressed the son of noble family:
"The thoughts and intentions of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, have never been forgotten midway, nor have they ever diminished; that which the Tathāgata intends is never abandoned midway."
Why is this so? Son of good family!

From the initial attainment of enlightenment until reaching the path of supreme perfect awakening, one universally perceives all that sentient beings have harbored in their minds throughout the past, future, and present; one remembers and recognizes it all without ever forgetting, eternally preserving and universally comprehending the conduct of sentient beings.
The Tathāgata never again deliberates or dispatches wisdom to investigate further; what the Tathāgata contemplates is truly without loss or diminution.

He enters the three realms and various natures of sentient beings, and he enters the faculties of all people to observe their conduct. What the Tathāgata brings forth involves neither observation nor deliberation, yet he expounds the sūtras for the sake of sentient beings;
he foreknows the timing of advancement and retreat, as well as slowness and speed, and thus distinguishes and bestows upon them their predictions of enlightenment.
Why is this so? Because his intention remains forever and is never forgotten.
Since his mind is thus settled, he forgets nothing; he perceives sentient beings and immediately preaches the Dharma for them. This is the twenty-third activity of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"What the Hero of the World contemplates, his mind never forgets;
furthermore, the Most Supreme Honored One does not need to recall or deliberate again."
In his every step and movement, he is as if already a perfectly awakened one; he knows the minds of sentient beings without omission.
Furthermore, he never relies upon conscious cognition, yet he perceives the long-standing dispositions and conduct of all beings.
"Causing them to establish themselves in that which is without activity; the Honored One among Men becomes the Dharma King for the multitudes.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, possesses the samādhi of unerring concentration and correct reception; all dharmas are without partiality, and all dharmas are as they truly are.
For what reason does the Tathāgata not lose his concentration?”
Because one practices with equanimity that is without end, the samādhi is likewise equal.
The Tathāgata is equal regarding the limit of desire, and the limit of non-desire is likewise equal;
as the limit of birth and death is equal, so too is the limit of nirvāṇa.
Because of this equanimity, one is able to enter right samādhi; this is what is meant by that.
One praises the Tathāgata’s samādhi as being non-forgetful. Why is this so?
Thus, in this state of equanimity, there is neither negligence nor forgetfulness, nor is there any regression.
The meditative concentration of the Tathāgata does not involve the eye, nor does it involve the ear, nose, body, speech, or mind as they engage with their respective objects.

The faculties are not fixed; this samādhi is not dependent on the element of earth, nor does it depend on water, fire, wind, or space. Furthermore, it does not rely upon the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; it does not long for the present life, nor does it depend upon future lives.

Because he is without attachment, he suffers no depletion; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, whose concentrated mind is never forgotten. Furthermore, he expounds the sūtras for the sake of sentient beings, causing those who are fit vessels to attain a concentrated mind. This is the twenty-fourth activity of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“The Most Victorious One is eternally settled; his concentrated mind is never diminished.
He accords with all phenomena, having correctly emerged from the Buddha’s state of concentration.”
Not relying on earth, water, fire, or wind, nor on the realms of desire, form, or formlessness—
the Great Sage does not cling to these, and thus his samādhi is not impaired.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"The wisdom of the Tathāgata has never been diminished.
What is meant by 'knowing'?"
Reverently penetrating all dharmas, there is nothing he does not understand; his wisdom does not depend on others.

For the sake of other sentient beings, he proclaims the holy knowledge, employing skillful means according to the times so that his resolutions are inexhaustible. He clearly understands all chapters and phrases, manifesting their traces, and causes them to enter the single stage of abiding as taught in the sutras for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
Should anyone come to inquire about going and coming, advancing and retreating, he resolves their web of doubts so that all become serene.

His wisdom penetrates everywhere to proclaim and expound the Three Vehicles, discerning their respective destinations. According to the eighty-four thousand types of conduct of sentient beings, he preaches eighty-four thousand treasuries of Dharma scriptures; this is the Tathāgata’s wisdom—boundless, immeasurable, and inexhaustible.

The infinite wisdom he expounds is never exhausted; furthermore, he reveals such inexhaustible wisdom to sentient beings and preaches the Dharma for them—this is the twenty-fifth activity of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“The Buddha’s wisdom of perfect enlightenment, Presently aspiring to the vehicle,
Skillfully proclaiming analytical understanding— This is the perfection of mastery.”
He preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings according to what their fundamental natures delight in;
thus, by means of a single word or letter, he enters into bottomless chapters and verses.
Knowing the conduct of sentient beings, his discernment reaches the infinite.
Thus, for these classes of beings, eighty-four thousand treasuries were proclaimed by the One Who Abides in Peace; his wisdom never diminishes.
This is the work of the Ten Powers, and therefore he is called the Honored One Among Men.
The Buddha again addressed the son of noble family:
"The liberation of the Tathāgata is without diminution.
Why is it said that the Tathāgata teaches that the śrāvakas attain liberation through sound, while those who are pratyekabuddhas attain liberation by understanding causes and conditions?"
All Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have attained liberation by being free from all obstructions and dualities.
Why is it called "liberation"?
Because there is no past realm, no conjunction with future realms, and no abiding in the present realm.
When the eye is free from the two types of feeling regarding forms, it is called liberation;

likewise, when the ear regarding sounds, the nose regarding odors, the tongue regarding tastes, the body regarding tangibles, and the mind regarding mental phenomena are free from the two types of feeling, they attain liberation, which is that upon which the mind relies.

The mind is fundamentally pure, and he fully understands this; therefore, it is said that at the very moment of generating the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta), one accomplishes the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

The Tathāgata preaches the sūtras to all sentient beings according to the occasion, causing them to leave behind attachment to sensations and to be without clinging. This is the twenty-sixth activity of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The assembly of śrāvakas attains liberation by relying on sound;
those training as pratyekabuddhas take dependent origination as their wisdom."
Transcending all hindrances, stainless as space—this is the state of the Buddhas, who have no dependence or attachment.
If the mind remains bound to past events, though it be pure and liberated, this is still called "clinging of the mind."
"According to their needs for liberation, you shall examine the faculties of sentient beings and deliver them,
ensuring that none are harmed or diminished.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, truly knows all past bodily actions and the karma that was created; he clearly perceives their origin and does not lose or retreat from it.

Regarding the various superior practices observed by the Tathāgata, he transforms sentient beings according to the appropriate time; whether through preaching to deliver the multitudes, remaining silent to deliver them, or even through eating and drinking, he brings them salvation.”

He displays dignified deportment and ritual propriety to lead sentient beings to follow the teachings of the Vinaya; or he manifests the thirty-two marks of a Great Man so that they may be saved; or he reveals the eighty minor marks so that they may attain liberation; or when sentient beings wish to behold the Tathāgata’s cranial protuberance—its majestic power so sublime that it cannot be gazed upon directly, its radiance surpassing the sun and moon, transcending all comparison—they are led to liberation through the increase of their joy; or there are sentient beings who, upon approaching to see the Buddha, immediately follow the teachings of the Vinaya; or by emitting light, they are delivered upon beholding its brilliance; or by seeing him walking, whether lifting or lowering his feet, they are delivered through their joy; or as he enters a city or emerges from it, he causes them to receive transformation and edification.

The movements, gestures, deportment, and ritual etiquette of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, all benefit sentient beings through these actions; there are none who do not undergo transformation, and never is an action performed in vain. Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata’s true and perfect physical karma, rooted in primordial wisdom, is entirely beneficial and never wasteful. This is the twenty-seventh karma of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"His eyes behold him, his majestic deportment and ritual decorum; whether he enters or departs, his every step;
his various marks and secondary characteristics, as well as the radiant splendor of his crown."
By means of this, he transforms and enlightens, delivering all sentient beings.
Should the Guide manifest his radiant light, countless multitudes of living beings shall enjoy peace and security for billions of years.
"Beholding their majestic radiance, they follow them to receive instruction; all those Honored Ones Among Two-Legged Beings constantly cultivate this practice.
The Buddha further addressed the son of good family:
"Whatever actions are uttered from the mouth of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, all constitute the faction of wisdom and are characterized by clear and sovereign understanding. Why is this?
Because all the sūtras and teachings spoken by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are entirely timely, and what they speak is never false."
Excellent! You act according to what is appropriate; that which you proclaim is with utmost sincerity and without deception, free from any fault or transgression.

Your movements are composed and serene, never abrupt or violent; you are free from coarseness and have never been deluded or confused. You always maintain integrity and straightforwardness, without flattery or deceit.

From the outset, they do not engage in harsh speech nor utter coarse words; being free from attachment and clinging, their speech is gentle and supple. Their conduct and movements accord with the Dharma and are never weak; by nature, they are neither flighty nor narrow-minded.
He does not engage in trivial or fragmented conduct; his gait is steady and composed. His speech is harmonious and elegant, his voice soft and gentle, and his resonance fragrant and beautiful.

He chooses his words carefully, speaking slowly and at ease, uttering them only when the time is right. His compositions are brilliant and exquisite, replete with profound flavor, and entirely free from any harshness or coarseness.
He speaks of being free from illness; he speaks only after reflection, thus protecting his own person.

His actions accord with the proper seasons, his thoughts are timely, and he extinguishes greed, eliminates hatred, burns away ignorance, subdues all demons, and wards off various evils. He heals all ailments, distinguishes the principles of meaning, and delights the minds of the wise.
The tone is like that of the sorrowful phoenix, and the voice is like that of the Lord of Devas; its resonance is mournful yet harmonious, like the currents of rivers and seas;
the sound is as tranquil as the earth, like the king of vultures summoning his retinue.

His voice is as stable and secure as Mount Sumeru; the words he utters far surpass those of the scarlet-beaked bird. His tone is compassionate like that of mandarin ducks calling to one another, like a king of geese leading his flock, or like a king of deer summoning his herd. Furthermore, it is like the sound of the *konghou*, lute, zither, flute, *se*, and drums; when these instruments are played in harmony with the rhythm, their melodies blend together in both sorrowful and joyful ways.
Yet the Buddha’s resonance is soft, supple, pure, and harmonious, exceeding those musical scales by hundreds of thousands of billions of times.
The voice is profound, subtle, and free from defilement; those who hear it find joy in their hearts as it enters their ears, thereby accumulating the roots of virtue.

The verses and phrases he proclaims are inexhaustible; they are appropriate to the occasion and harmonious from beginning to end, never losing the meaning of the words and perfectly accordant with the Dharma. Each is delivered through skillful means, never failing to accord with the proper timing.

He observes the increase and decrease of the faculties of all people and teaches the Dharma accordingly: he adorns them with generosity; he nurtures their precepts so they are always pure and refined; he gathers and accumulates patience; he excels in diligence to fully master the holy work; and he contemplates wisdom while gathering clouds of compassion. He never tires of his pity and mercy, and his joy shines forth brilliantly.
Without abandoning what he protects, he establishes the Three Vehicles;
he ensures the Three Jewels are not severed, distinguishes the three lofty assemblies, and purifies the three gates of liberation.

Having cultivated utmost sincerity and extensively proclaimed wisdom, he is not reviled by the enlightened; he is praised by all the worthy sages, his resolve is profound and vast like space, and all meritorious achievements are fully perfected.
"O son of good family!

The Tathāgata’s speech and teachings are so sublime and majestic that they accord with the proper measure; moreover, they transcend all this such that no analogy can be found. Therefore, it is said: 'all that is spoken.'"

“The Tathāgata’s speech possesses a resonance of wisdom that is transcendent and extraordinary; it surpasses all other sounds and voices, and within the three realms, there is none that can equal it, for it is the supreme among wisdoms. There is no one who does not respond to his summons and comply with him—this is the twenty-eighth activity of the Tathāgata.”
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"His speech is peerless and harmonious; With stainless purity, he transcends all virtues.
He utters a single sound that enters into all voices, And its resonance pervades the entire trichiliocosm."
Causing the śrāvakas to hear this teaching, and likewise those of the pratyekabuddha vehicle;
some, upon hearing it, broaden their resolve and give rise to the aspiration to seek the Buddha-way.
Hearing the teachings of loving-kindness in their proper sequence, each articulates their words without confusion;
when expounding the sublime Dharma, their minds remain free from any thought of retreat.
Just as the mountain echoes back when its sound is called upon, so too does the Supreme among Men respond to what is said;
whatever he proclaims delights the hearts of the multitude.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
“The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, accords with all that is intended in the minds of sentient beings; he takes them as his assembly of wisdom, reaching everywhere without exception.”

Why is this? Because one observes that the Tathāgata is without mind, thought, or consciousness; from the beginning, he is free from conceptualization yet possesses both advancement and retreat, illuminating with wisdom to dissolve all darkness.

The wisdom of that Tathāgata reaches universally into the mental activities of all sentient beings and likewise enters everywhere into their existing intentions, transcending the objects of consciousness and thought of all living beings, and fully digesting all dharmas.

That samādhi-concentration has nothing upon which to rely; it transcends the aggregates and hindrances, departs from the practice of the twelve links of dependent origination, forever abandons the three perceptions, removes foul impurities, subdues the works of Māra, and eliminates the defilements of falsehood, flattery, and sycophancy.
Abandoning the notion of self, they uproot the seeds of ignorance and delusion;
purifying their spiritual practice with a mind like space, they remain free from conceptualization and do not disrupt the dharma-realm.
"O son of good family!
Such is the wisdom associated with the mental karma of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Truly Enlightened One; this constitutes the twenty-ninth activity of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"One should not call it 'supreme,' for the noble mind of the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings has accumulated the wisdom of all the sages; the karma of this Guide is pure.
This wisdom in which he dwells abides within the nature of sentient beings."
Pervasively entering all things without exception, they abide within the natural dharma-realm.
Their meditative concentration is thus, fully equipped with every excellence;
in their observation of mind, intellect, and consciousness, there is no conceptualization whatsoever.
"Having transcended all realms of Māra, Surpassing all harmful karma,
Naturally like empty space, Free from defilement and without location.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, possesses unimpeded wisdom regarding the past; the vision he beholds is a knowledge that suffers no diminution or loss.
To what extent does this reach?
He knows the number of all those Buddha-lands of the past—whether they were merged or formed—as well as their increase and decrease.”
He discerns all the grasses, trees, mountains, valleys, medicinal herbs, and groves within that land;
he fully recognizes all the sentient beings, crawling creatures, breathing beings, and various species of physical forms in that Buddha-land;
and he thoroughly understands the languages, voices, and types of the people, as well as all the flying and wriggling insects.
He also fully expounds the number of Buddhas who have appeared, both past and future, in that land;
he also thoroughly elucidates the number of scriptural fascicles proclaimed by those Buddhas and all that they have illuminated;
and he likewise knows the limit of the śrāvakas they have transformed, as well as how they have opened the way for pratyekabuddhas to enter the vehicle of discipline.
I venture to exhort and guide them so that they may study as Bodhisattvas, causing them to give rise to the unsurpassed, true, and correct Mahāyāna and to become fully endowed with it;
I shall also thoroughly care for all that pertains to the excellence or deficiency of their Buddha-land, their verbal teachings, and their conduct, ensuring they attend to one another;

and I shall also clearly discern the speech, actions, and movements of the assembly of bhikṣus, how those above and below accord with one another, and what is appropriate in their advancing and retreating.
There are those who observe the length of lifespans—whether they endure for long, or meet with untimely death—and the Tathāgata likewise understands them;

he further knows how years are established according to the Dharma, and he fully knows the length of breaths, beauty and ugliness, food and drink, clothing, dwellings, and occupations. The Tathāgata knows all these things.

Regarding the past lives of sentient beings—their cycles of birth and death, their future rebirths, the diversity of their faculties, the differences in their conduct, the distinctness of their dispositions, and the unique nature of the mental states and objects they harbor—the Tathāgata knows them all completely; he knows the full extent of their thoughts, whether they be few or many, and whether they be beautiful or ugly, good or evil, without ever being distracted.
As for the limit of their number, it is seen directly before one's eyes; one does not employ dual wisdom to reflect upon them again.

The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, likewise does not dispatch the mind to pursue or infer past events in order to know them; rather, through his wisdom-mind, he perceives and foresees everything in its entirety, without needing to contemplate them repeatedly.
Such is his wisdom—so lofty and immeasurable—that he perceives the nature of sentient beings and teaches the Dharma for them without ever ceasing; this is the thirtieth deed of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“The Buddha’s noble, sagely wisdom Is infinite and unimpeded;
Throughout the lands of all Buddhas, He proclaims and disseminates the scriptures.”
Exhorting the realms of all sentient beings, he causes them to have deep faith in the Buddha-way.
Within the lands of all Buddhas, he knows their conduct and its progress or regression,
the fundamental capacities of the various people, and the inclinations toward which their natures tend.
All medicinal herbs and trees, the beauty or ugliness of sounds,
the names of past thoughts, and all deeds that have been performed—
the Perfectly Awakened One has fully realized them all, seeing them exactly as they are.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, truly knows the future without any diminution or loss; his wisdom is unimpeded, perceiving all things with complete success."
How is this known?
Regarding what shall arise and be established, or what shall be destroyed, in future ages—whether their convergence or their dispersal—the Tathāgata knows them all.

Regarding the fires that burn at the arising of a kalpa, the color and appearance of its waters, the restoration of that Buddha-land, the dimensions of its ground—its breadth, length, width, and extent—and the number of its atoms; furthermore, in each and every Buddha-land, the various Buddhas who arise to teach and transform the multitudes, the number of their śrāvakas, the assembly of pratyekabuddhas, and the bodhisattvas; their food and drink, clothing, dwellings, and groves; their inhalation and exhalation, walking, moving, and gesturing; the places where they travel and reside; and their majestic deportment and ritual etiquette—the Tathāgata fully knows all these, as well as the sentient beings transformed by each Tathāgata, whether they are established in the vehicle of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, or if they study the Mahāyāna.

Regarding all classes of sentient beings in each and every buddha-field who are destined for rebirth there—the various thoughts that arise in their minds and the various thoughts that are extinguished—the Tathāgata knows them all;
having fully realized this, the Tathāgata no longer needs to reflect upon them again.

Examining the inner thoughts of the mind, he observes the future and perceives everything clearly; thus, he extensively expounds the path of the sutras for the sake of sentient beings—this is the thirty-first activity of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"In future ages, whatever exists in the world, whether it be formed or again destroyed—
the buddha-fields, sentient beings, and the number of all Buddhas."
Those Buddhas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, all achieve these numbers.
Their minds have never been subject to forgetfulness;
their intentions observe and universally penetrate the future.
"For the sake of sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma according to the occasion; this is the practice performed by the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, perceives the present without impairment; his wisdom beholds all things without obstruction. What does he perceive?

He knows the exact number of all lands within the worlds of the ten directions in the present; he knows the number of all Buddhas currently residing there, as well as the numbers of all Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas currently existing; he knows the number of constellations, their forms, and their movements and revolutions; he clearly discerns the limits of all trees, medicinal herbs, mountains, forests, streams, and valleys in the present, as well as the distances and boundaries of the lands in the ten directions, down to the number of dust motes within those realms.”
Regarding the waters of the ten directions, he knows by dipping a single hair into them how many drops there are;
regarding the realms of fire in the ten directions, whether flames arise or subside, he fully understands their presence, absence, and location;

regarding the winds of the ten directions, he also fully knows their forms and colors, the causes from which they emerge, their coming and going, their circulation, and their formation, destruction, and increase.

The empty spaces of the ten directions are vast, remote, and boundless; their distances number in the billions, being limitless and shoreless. The Buddha knows them all completely, without failing to perceive even as much as a hair or a speck of dust.

He knows the three types of conduct in the present, the realms of sentient beings, their progress and regression, ease and difficulty, the depth of their roots, and the speed with which they receive instruction.

The Buddha knows the transgressions committed by sentient beings in the hells in the present, the specific causes by which their offenses lead them there, the places where they shall be reborn upon emerging from those states, and he further knows the skillful means to be employed to eliminate their calamities.

Furthermore, he knows the types of present sentient beings—those that crawl, breathe, and wriggle—and the karmic actions by which they fall into these hardships; having understood what is appropriate for them, he can eliminate their calamities and sins, as well as the places where they are destined to be reborn.

Furthermore, he knows that those currently in the realm of hungry ghosts have fallen into this affliction due to stinginess and greed; he understands the means by which they should eliminate their offenses and resolve the conditions for their future rebirths.

He knows the thoughts harbored in the minds of all present sentient beings and the diseases of their afflictions and sensual desires; furthermore, he knows those who have abandoned desire and are free from defilement.

Furthermore, he knows by what discipline all sentient beings of the present shall be transformed and guided; or again, there may be those who do not follow past teachings, and he knows through his insight the intentions of beings born in the heavens as they decline and pass away, and where they will go—the Buddha knows all this.

"Thus, from beginning to end, he has never entertained such thoughts; through the two wisdoms, he reflects deeply and enters into non-duality, yet for the sake of sentient beings, he extensively expounds the Dharma of the sutras—this is the thirty-second activity of the Tathāgata."
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The supreme wisdom of all the Victors is universally pervasive; it is limitless, immeasurable, and inconceivable."
Equal to empty space, void and beyond all analogy, it is that which no world can ever attain.
All sentient beings—those currently existing and those yet to be formed—the Tathāgata knows them all;
beholding their very roots and origins, this is the work of the Buddhas.
"See them all thoroughly and completely. 22.
In the *Tathāgata-mārga-varga* of the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, the twenty-second chapter on the Tathāgata’s Path, the Buddha again addressed the sons of good family:
"This is the path and practice traversed by the Tathāgata."
The Tathāgata uses these practiced deeds to transform and enlighten sentient beings; he expounds written words through wordlessness, which is difficult to encounter and difficult to accomplish.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Tathāgata’s utmost sincerity cannot be restrained by any training or discipline;
his karma is immeasurable and inconceivable, such that no devas, nāgas, spirits, or people of the world can calculate, weigh, or comprehend what he knows.
Originally there was nothing spoken, yet characters appeared; this is difficult to fathom and impossible to suppress, pervading all Buddha-lands with a universal concentration of mind.

It manifests all Perfectly Enlightened Ones who have already transcended; it is free from all erroneous karma and devoid of conceptual thought, equal to the samādhi of empty space, observing all dharma-realms without any differentiation.
Why is this so? What the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, proclaim has no variation; the causes from which they arise have no partiality.

It is the same for all sentient beings and their lands: what is taught is entirely identical. The spiritual power of the Way is not distinct, liberation is without difference, and the nirvana reached is likewise without variation.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has attained supreme perfect awakening as a single flavor within all dharma-realms; he is without obstruction or hindrance regarding the realm of sentient beings, and through skillful means, he fully understands them by means of unobstructed dharmas, thereby turning the wheel of Dharma for sentient beings so that they may attain the stage of non-retrogression and non-regression."
For example, son of good family!

Just as a master jeweler refines a pure and stainless gem, polishing it until it shines; when he holds this jewel in his hand and places it into turbid water, the water becomes still, clearing away the murkiness and becoming transparent.
No longer requiring diligent effort or laborious toil, one then takes out and places [the water] into food flavors, or pours it into jars and pots;
or if into a bowl, one causes the water within it to become entirely clear and transparent—the labor expended is not even worth mentioning.

Subsequently, it is placed within the essence of a great medicinal drug and washed repeatedly with subtle and heavy agents; once thoroughly cleansed and all thorns and brambles removed, it is then called a "night-luminous jewel."

"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, is likewise; observing the defiled realms of all sentient beings, he expounds for them impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, as well as the calamities of sorrow, bitterness, pain, and poison."
Sentient beings are deluded, delighting in birth and death while suffering from the afflictions of weariness; only then does the Tathāgata cause them to enter the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones.
The Tathāgata exerts diligence toward them without difficulty, and only thereafter do they reach emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

The Tathāgata guides them with compassion; through diligent effort that is free from attachment, they subsequently attain the stage of non-retrogression and proclaim the path of the Sūtras, purifying the three spheres of action.
"What is meant by the Buddha-realm that causes sentient beings to enter its sphere?
Having attained transcendence and entered the Dharma of the Tathāgata, it is therefore called the essential core of the Unsurpassed Benefactor."
It is so, son of good family!
For this reason, you should form this contemplation:

the samādhi entered by the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, is inconceivable; he cultivates equanimity and penetrates the three periods of time, ensuring that the Three Jewels are never interrupted.
The Tathāgata abides in that inconceivable state of the path’s practice, which is likewise empty; his body is spontaneous and none can attain it.

He manifests forms in all buddha-fields, yet regarding all dharmas he never acquires anything; without discrimination, he acts with mastery, teaching and transforming beings according to their voices and sounds.

When proclaiming the sūtras for the sake of sentient beings, they remain detached from all mental objects of perception, yet they fully know and see the mental activities, dispositions, and inclinations of sentient beings, as well as the pure resolve of the assembly of bodhisattvas.
It is for these reasons that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
appear in the world. Such, noble son,
is the meaning of the Tathāgata’s ultimate accomplishment.

Because there is no fundamental karma, one is said to have no place of abiding and does not distance oneself from reality; furthermore, there is no slackening or cessation, and one bestows the prediction of bodhisattvahood without interrupting the teaching. This is what is called the path and practice of the Tathāgata.

When the Buddha preached this discourse on the deeds of the Tathāgata, immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite buddha-fields in the ten directions shook in six ways. A great radiance shone universally throughout all realms, and celestial flowers and fragrances rained down upon the pure, precious lion-thrones of the Buddhas.

The great assembly of śrāvakas gathered there, along with devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, male novices, and female novices, all together listened to the Tathāgata proclaiming this Dharma-scripture on the path of practice; they were filled with such joy and exultation that they could not contain themselves.

A virtuous mind arose within them, and each brought various kinds of flowers, renowned incense, blended perfumes, flower garlands, ointments, robes, banners, canopies, and great pennants; they played various musical instruments, such as zithers, lutes, and harps, to make offerings to the Tathāgata.
They took the jewels from their heads and scattered them;

some brought sesame oil, some held the "Thunder-Sound" [incense], some took their hair, or removed jeweled necklaces—adorned with pearls, such as moon-bright pearls (*candrakānta*) or moon-bearing pearls (*candraprabha*), as well as *vimukti* flowers; some offered flawless and pure offerings, some obtained seals of authority and the grace of amnesty, some had precious fruits, some used hawks or birds, some used threads and fibers, some offered things that were tranquil and not dependent on emptiness, some head-jewels and necklaces, some neck-beads, or whatever ornaments they possessed on their hands or feet—they all offered these to the Buddha, scattering them everywhere.

Furthermore, some took luminous jewels, or purple-gold ornaments, and scattered them upon it; others offered the horse-treasure, the celestial king’s exquisite deep-blue great sapphire, fire-colored jewels, moonlight jewels, and various other kinds of rare and wondrous precious gems as offerings and scatterings.

Purple-polished gold, scattered pieces of white silver, *mūlaka* blended incense, *dantaka* blended incense, *candana* blended incense, *kṛṣṇa-manojña* blended incense, vermilion-red pearls, and various human-like blended incenses spontaneously fell and scattered like rain.

There were also various celestial flowers, including rain-of-intent flowers, infinite-intent flowers, moon-crossing-moon flowers, and soft-sound-great-soft-resonance flowers; these flowers dazzled the eyes.

The various flowers upon the great earth and the lands have wheels free from defilement, with a hundred petals, or a thousand petals, or even a hundred thousand petals; their light shines afar and their fragrance pervades everywhere. Their scent is exquisite and overflowing, such that all who behold it find joy; their radiance blazes forth, holding fast to its flames, and their colors are infinite, adorned with interlacing patterns.

Blue lotuses, water lilies, and various other flowers fell spontaneously; furthermore, the earth was rained upon with *sumanā* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *aśoka* flowers, and *kumbha* flowers, as well as *tenghuang* (paulownia) blossoms, which fell slowly, steadily, and harmoniously.
The *konghou* lute, musical instruments, flutes, drums, and wind instruments, along with various performers of dance and song, resounded spontaneously.
Furthermore, there fell a rain of celestial flowers and incense, various perfumes, manifold jewels, necklaces, precious gems, garments, and bedding.

The bodhisattvas who had gathered from the ten directions leaped up and stayed suspended in mid-air, casting their own bodies down as an offering to the Buddha; as each threw themselves down, they did not begrudge their own lives or bodies.

At that moment, the air was spontaneously covered everywhere by a high jeweled throne, adorned with jeweled lattices and draped with countless strings of pearls and necklaces; it was embellished all around with interlaced purple gold, its exquisite decorations being truly beyond anything found in the world.

Various kinds of precious lotus flowers emerged—every kind of rare jewel and necklace, and every single pearl—each numbering in the countless and inexpressible; these manifested bodhisattvas all saw together.
As soon as the bodhisattvas had emerged and come forth, they circumambulated the Buddha seven times and then returned to sit upon their precious lotus flowers.
In the immeasurable and innumerable various lands of the ten directions, each and every one of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, together praised them all.

They made offerings through the essentials of the sūtras; by means of these offerings, they attained purity. Each together praised his virtues for the duration of an entire kalpa without reaching the end, because they were making offerings to the Dharma.

By means of his majestic spiritual power, the Buddha dispatched his disciples to this Sahā world; the offerings they brought into this Sahā realm possessed a precious adornment that surpassed this world, and the magnificence of their jeweled seats was so extraordinary as to be beyond compare.

At that time, countless sentient beings in the great assembly, seeing these transformations, all resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; the multitude of bodhisattvas was beyond measure, and they attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the assembly of bodhisattvas all around him and said:
"O you true gentlemen, who among you is capable of bearing such a pure adornment—the dwelling place of a bodhisattva and that which they ought to establish?"

"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has sent his messenger to dwell throughout this place, protecting and watching over it; it is free from all conceptual thought and devoid of sound.

The carpets, rugs, and cushions spread upon it shall serve as the seat for Maitreya Tathāgata after he has attained Buddhahood, during the sixteenth year following his enlightenment. This is the essential core of the sūtra titled 'The Chapter on the Great Assembly of the Unobstructed Gate,' which is the destination of the bodhisattvas' practices and vows; you shall also extensively propagate and analyze its meaning."

At that time, all the bodhisattvas gathered there shall likewise give rise to the aspiration to make offerings to this Dharma, to Maitreya Tathāgata, and to the assembly of bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named King Who Shifts All Dharmas. He rose from his seat, knelt with his right knee on the lotus flower, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!

I am able to sustain and protect this pure adornment, bringing its extremes to rest through the absence of conceptual thought, applying myself with single-minded diligence without slackening or abandoning it.
He shall attend upon Maitreya until he becomes a Tathāgata, constantly making offerings to him, as well as to all the Tathāgatas, the Worthy Ones, the Truly Self-Enlightened Ones of the Bhadrakalpa.

At that time, there was a Māra-deva named Karoti-sthita-dṛḍha-sthāna, who brought four realms and arrived at that assembly, addressing the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, King of the Transformation of All Dharmas:
"O son of noble family!"
"What is that vessel?
For what kind of beings is it used, so that they may receive this sublime purity and prevent it from being destroyed or dispersed?
The Bodhisattva King Who Shifts All Dharmas replied to the Mara Who Acts:
“Son of good family, you should know that all vessels inevitably come to ruin and decay; none endure eternally, and none are capable of receiving anything.
Only emptiness remains indestructible, free from obstruction or hindrance, and is the most supreme and honored among all vessels.”
"O Benevolent One, you should examine my body with close attention; do not blink your eyes, and you will surely be able to behold the vessel of the Infinite.

Then, the Bodhisattva King of the Transformation of All Dharmas observed the movements [of the other], and gazing at his body without blinking, he immediately saw within the navel of the Bodhisattva King of the Transformation of All Dharmas the world-system of the Radiance of the Water-King.
Why is it called "Radiance of the Water King"?
