Because that Buddha-world is entirely filled with water pervading the entire land; if one looks from afar, it appears like a single great ocean.
There is a Tathāgata there named Rucirapadmaśrī, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently exists and dwells, preaching the Mahāyāna exclusively for the sake of bodhisattvas.
Within that water-element there was also a lotus named Jewel Adornment (*ratnavyūha*), upon which that Tathāgata and the various bodhisattvas were seated.
At that time, Māra, with palms joined in reverence, stood before them and prostrated himself, taking refuge in the Bodhisattva King of the Transformation of All Dharmas (*sarvadharmavikurvaṇarāja*).
The Bodhisattva Moving All Dharmas King addressed the Mara Who Acts:
"O Noble Lord!
Do you not see the vessels of the bodhisattvas?"
He replied, "I have seen it; its vessel is infinite.
He reported this, saying:
“Your Majesty, you are capable of receiving this water.

Such celestial vessels as these, though they may be destroyed by the retribution of hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of kalpas, will never be exhausted in their adornment and decoration; no one can consume them.”
Then the Māra Kṛtaka prostrated to the Buddha and said:
“I pray only this, World-Honored One!

Formerly, my thoughts were set upon trivial matters; it was because I had not yet seen these true sons of the noble ones and had not yet heard the essentials of this sutra that I desired to become a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha and attain parinirvāṇa.”

Today, having witnessed the majestic and sublime spiritual power of the Bodhisattva King of All Moving Dharmas and having heard this sutra, my mind is moved and transformed; I have established a resolute intention and shall now give rise to the unsurpassed mind of true and correct enlightenment.

What I have now undertaken I dare not violate or abandon; for the sake of the Most Perfectly Awakened One’s compassion for sentient beings, for their great peace and security, and for their extensive protection, even if my own body were to be boiled in the hells for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, only then would I achieve unsurpassed, true, and correct awakening. Though I should encounter such calamities, I shall not regard them as a grievance, nor shall I forsake the Buddha-way.
At that time, the Buddha praised the Māra for his deeds, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
For the sake of the Great Way, you have single-mindedly donned the great armor of the vast vow."
"Now that you, O Benevolent One, have thus established your vows, what you have sworn shall surely bear fruit.
*Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Scroll Six;
*Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 23: The Eight Dharanis. Chapter Twenty-Three: The Eight Dharanis.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Siṃhaketu, who was seated in the assembly and asked the bodhisattva Jñānarāja:
"O son of noble family!

By abiding in which dhāraṇī does a bodhisattva receive and uphold all the sūtras spoken and expounded by the Buddhas without end, thereby delighting sentient beings with excellent teachings so that none fail to suddenly perceive light as if seeing through the darkness?"
The Bodhisattva Sarvavidrāja replied to Siṃhavikrama:
“When a bodhisattva abides in these eight dhāraṇīs, they gladden sentient beings and cause them to attain clarity and understanding; their wisdom is inexhaustible.”
What are these eight? There are dhāraṇīs:

first, Pure Radiant Sound; second, Inexhaustible Dharma Treasury; third, Immeasurable Advancement and Retreat; fourth, Ocean Seal Mind; fifth, Lotus Adornment; sixth, Entry into the Unobstructed Seal; seventh, Entry into Discriminative Eloquence; eighth, Establishment of Buddha Adornments. These are the eight.
"When a Bodhisattva dwells here, whatever they eloquently proclaim brings joy to sentient beings.
At that time, Siṃhavikrānta again asked the Bodhisattva Sarvaguṇarāja:
"O noble son!..."

It would be better to humble oneself and show compassion for all beings by once again explaining the meaning of these eight dhāraṇīs in detail and expounding their essential purpose; if the bodhisattvas hear of the eloquence obtained through these dhāraṇīs, they will surely apply themselves diligently to their study.
The King of Universal Wisdom said:
"Listen, son of good family; I shall now explain for you the meaning of the eight dhāraṇīs and the vast dispersal of their respective refuges.
What is meant by 'Pure Radiant Sound'?"
If a bodhisattva abides in this dhāraṇī, the gateway they enter will be without obstruction; it is exceedingly pure and returns to the firm essentials.

With their mind established in rectitude, they preach the sūtras, and their voice penetrates and is heard throughout one buddha-field, or two, or three, or four, or five, or ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or even a hundred or a thousand buddha-fields.

The sound of their teaching proclaims throughout all Buddha-lands; whether ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, or a billion Buddha-lands hear that sound of their teaching, or even if it penetrates immeasurable and boundless Buddha-lands, it proceeds according to what is desired by their minds.
He desires that his vocal teachings may pervade how many Buddha-lands; he is fully capable of accomplishing this to an infinite extent.

Acting according to his own will, from a single lion throne, he expounds the Dharma for all sentient beings of the ten directions. He desires that those within twenty li hear it, or thirty li, or across a single Mount Sumeru, or even up to the Brahma Heaven, teaching in accordance with the original intentions of each sentient being.
Seated upon the lion throne, he established his resolve and preached the Dharma for all sentient beings, delighting their hearts so that none failed to attain understanding.
As soon as his body was settled upon the lion throne, the Buddhas of the ten directions all manifested their forms, and he heard the Dharma they preached;
having heard it, he attained the power of *dhāraṇī*, recognizing and recollecting it all without ever forgetting again.
By means of this Dharma-scripture, one understands its meaning; whatever teachings they proclaim can be heard and received without anyone being able to obstruct or interrupt them.
Entering into the matter of a single phoneme and sound, they are able to expound all written characters, universally entering into all sounds and causal phrases.
By entering into words, one enters immeasurable gateways and speaks of all phenomena as having no characteristic of coming—because all phenomena have no location and nowhere to abide;
because all phenomena are spontaneous and do not recur;
and because all phenomena are embraced and arrive without reaching anywhere, for they are pure in their functioning.
All phenomena are rootless, because they lack a place of origin;
all phenomena are boundless, because they are not established;
all phenomena are inexhaustible, because they have no abiding place.
All phenomena are unarisen, because they have no course of action;
all phenomena do not arise, because they have no agency;
all phenomena do not exist, because they lack causes and conditions.
All phenomena are not disordered, because they have no equal controller;
all phenomena are not extinguished, because they have no arising;
all phenomena have no activity, because they have no aspiration.
All phenomena are without conceptual proliferation, because they are devoid of ideation and the notions of what is appropriate or inappropriate;
all phenomena are ineffable, because they have forever entered the state of non-action;
all phenomena are without instruction, because there would be error in that which is spoken.
All dharmas are without anger, because they are free from resentment;
all dharmas are without conceptualization, because they are free from attachment;
all dharmas are without discursive thought, because they are free from falsehood.
All dharmas are without attachment, for they have nothing to rely upon;
all dharmas are without instruction, for they are equal to emptiness;
all dharmas are without speech, for they are devoid of thought.
All dharmas are without end, for they have no master;
all dharmas are without birth, for there is no teaching;
all dharmas are entirely pure, for they have no coming.
All phenomena are without self, for the self is naturally non-existent;
all phenomena are without person, for they are utterly pure;
all phenomena are without a life-principle, for nothing endures eternally.
All dharmas are without life, for they enter into the ultimate meaning;
all dharmas are truly empty, for they are quiescent within;
all dharmas are without conceptualization, for their fundamental limit has no limit.
All dharmas are wishless, because they have nothing to be grasped;
all dharmas are without activity, because they are unconditioned;
all dharmas are unconditioned, because they transcend the activity of arising chapters and phrases.
All dharmas are not solid, because they have nothing upon which to rely;
all dharmas are without attachment, because there is nothing to be cultivated;
all dharmas are spontaneous, because they are without self.
All phenomena are without action, for their activity is pure;
all phenomena are without karma, for there is nothing into which they enter;
all phenomena are without retribution, for there is nothing with which they conjoin.
All phenomena are without conjunction, for they cannot be destroyed;
all phenomena are without relinquishment, for there is nothing to be grasped;
all phenomena are without blinking, for they cannot be seized.
All phenomena are without acquisition, for they have no point of reference;
all phenomena are without contact, for they have no agency;
all phenomena are without outflows, for they have no locus for leakage.
All dharmas do not exist, because there is no accomplishment of intent;
all dharmas are pure, because they are without factionalism;
all dharmas have no ownership, because they are without multiplicity.
All dharmas are formless, because the four great elements are impermanent;
all dharmas are without sensation, because there is nothing encountered;
all dharmas are without perception, because they transcend all mental conceptions.
All phenomena are without activity, for they are free from all desires;
all phenomena are without consciousness, for there is nothing to be craved;
all phenomena are without boundaries, for they are equal to space.
All phenomena have no relinquishing, for they transcend all realms;
all phenomena have no objective domain, for they have no point of origin;
all phenomena have no craving, for they are devoid of conceptualization.
All phenomena are formless, for they have no location;
all phenomena are shapeless, for they have no descent;
all phenomena are unturbid, for they eliminate all agitation.
All phenomena are without recollection, for they are without grasping;
all phenomena are without conceptualization, for they are without duality;
all phenomena are without a shore, for they have transcended the traces of the realms.
All phenomena are without refuge, for they are detached from any location;
all phenomena are impermanent, for their conditions are impure;
all phenomena are nameless, for they are beyond all wonderment.
All phenomena are without confusion, for each follows its own course;
all phenomena have no abiding, for nothing remains;
all phenomena have no decay, for nothing is consumed by fire.
All dharmas are without evil, for they are free from all evils;
all dharmas are like water, for they wash away all defilements;
all dharmas are without calamity, for they are utterly pure.
All dharmas are profoundly pure, because they are incalculable;
all dharmas are beyond reckoning, because they are without attachment;
all dharmas are without seeking, because they are without movement.
All phenomena are without agitation, for they cannot be shaken;
all phenomena are unconditioned, for they are equal to emptiness;
all phenomena are void and non-existent, for there is nothing to be done.
All phenomena have no root, for they have no course of action;
all phenomena have no manifestation, for they have nothing to illuminate;
all phenomena have no radiance, for they have relinquished all light.
All dharmas are incomparable, for they are without deviation;
all dharmas are without partiality, for they are equal to the void;
all dharmas are without darkness, for there is nothing to be seen.
All dharmas are without radiance, for they have no factions;
all dharmas are without fault, for they are free from transgression;
all dharmas are hymns of praise, for they perform wholesome karma.
All dharmas enter into emptiness because they are deceptive;
all dharmas have no progress because there is nothing established;
all dharmas have no vision because they have no categories.
All phenomena have no tasting, because they lack flavor;
all phenomena have no softness, because they lack smoothness;
all phenomena have no consciousness, because they lack all phenomena.
All dharmas are without conditions, for they are free from mind, thought, and consciousness;
all dharmas are without deliberation, for the Way is impartial;
all dharmas are fundamentally pure, for the sense bases have been extinguished and will not arise again.
"In this way, son of good family!
Having attained the pure light of sound, the bodhisattva extols the meaning of all causes and conditions, words, and phrases."

If one were to proclaim the scriptures for an eon, or even beyond an eon, without abandoning any conditions, characters, or phrases, and without finding it difficult to adapt to what is appropriate for the time—summarizing the essentials—one would use every text and each individual character to preach the Dharma to the multitude; yet those words and letters would never be exhausted. One would dwell well in the eye of the Dharma, expounding the meaning of the words with precision, such that the speech is brilliant and magnificent.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva abides in *dhāraṇī*, thoroughly mastering purity; his deportment accords with the occasion, his eloquence is brilliant, and his mind is radiant.

He cultivates a heart of loving-kindness, and his giving is likewise pure—being without stinginess regarding either the gift of Dharma or the provision of food and clothing. His precepts are pure and his conduct is without flaw; his patience is pure and his mind harbors no malice; his diligence is pure as he performs deeds of peace and stability; his single-mindedness is pure, tranquil and free from darkness; his wisdom is pure, casting off obscurity and illuminating extensively; and his actions are pure, free from any transgression or failure.
Their eyes are pure, and their three eyes are stainless;
their ears are pure, and they attain the divine ear to hear the karmic teachings expounded by all Tathāgatas;
their noses are pure, and they smell the fragrance of the Tathāgata’s Dharma of precepts.
Their tongues are pure, having no attachment to worldly flavors but being intent upon the flavor of the Dharma;
their bodies are pure, such that all births are never defiled by the impurities of the womb;
their minds are pure, skillfully employing expedient means to universally enter all dharmas according to the occasion.
Their appearance is pure, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence;
what they hear is pure,
consisting of pleasing sounds free from discordant noise.
Its fragrance is pure; wherever it is perceived, one is perfumed by the scents of precepts, learning, and giving.
Its flavor is pure; with every taste, and further with every subsequent taste, he achieves the marks of a Great Man.
Its texture is pure; his hands and feet are as soft and supple as those of an infant.
Their Dharma is pure, attaining the radiance of the Dharma;
their intention is pure, so that the sūtras and teachings they hear they cherish and remember without forgetting;
their resolve is pure, transcending the paths of Māra.
Their gait is pure, and they universally enter the profound, wondrous, and infinite sūtras.

Once a bodhisattva dwells in this dhāraṇī, the number of buddha-fields they freely traverse according to their will, instruct, and teach is equal to the number of those fields illuminated by their light.

Furthermore, its radiance proclaims all the Dharma teachings expounded by the Buddhas of the ten directions; by means of this, one attains this dhāraṇī, because it is thereby obtained as something extraordinary and beyond words.
"Yes, son of good family!
This is the dhāraṇī of Pure Radiant Sound; that which it produces, that into which it enters, and that which it can proclaim are immeasurable."

This dhāraṇī of Pure Sound distinguishes the inconceivable destinations; its expressions are infinite, its resolutions are limitless, and its range of influence is vast and boundless, entering into all things without obstruction.
The Buddha said:
"Noble son! What is called the dhāraṇī of the inexhaustible treasury of Dharma?"
It is said that form is inexhaustible; because form is impermanent, it is called inexhaustible.
To speak of the impermanence of form is, because form is suffering, also to speak of its affliction;
because form is without self, it is also spoken of as being without self.
Because form is tranquil, it is also said to be tranquil;
because form is elusive, it is also said to be elusive;
because form is like foam, it is also said to be a mass of foam.
Because form is like an illusion, it is also described as an illusion;
because form is like a mirage, it is also described as a mirage;
because form is like the moon reflected in water, it is also described as the moon in water.
Because form is like a dream, it is also described as a dream;
because form is like an echo, it is also described as an echo;
because form is like a reflection, it is also described as a reflection.
Because form is like a reflection of the face, it is also called a "face-reflection";
because form does not exist, it is also said to be "non-existent";
because form is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is also called "beyond training."
Because form has no ultimate limit, it is also said to be without ultimate limit;
because form is empty, it is also said to be emptiness;
because form is without conceptualization, it is also said to be without conceptualization.
Because form is wishless, it is also said to be wishless;
because form is without activity, it is also said to be without activity;
because form is without arising, it is also said to be without arising.
Because form has no arising, it is also said to be unarisen;
because form is fundamentally spontaneous, it is also said to be fundamentally spontaneous;
because the function of form is fundamentally non-existent, it is also said to be fundamentally non-existent.
Because form is naturally so in the past, it is said that the past is naturally so;
because form is naturally so in the future, it is said that the future is naturally so;
because form is naturally so in the present, it is said that the present is naturally so.
Because form is tranquil, it is also called serenity;
because form is still and silent, it is also called stillness and silence;
because form is without wandering, it is also called non-wandering.
Because form is without frivolous conceptualization, it is also said to be without frivolous conceptualization;
because form is inconceivable, it is also said to be inconceivable;
because form is without appearance, it is also said to be without appearance.
Because form has no substance, it is said to be without substance;
because form has no person, it is said to be without a person;
because form has no life-span, it is said to be without a life-span.
Because form has no life-force, it is also said to be without life-force;
because form has no nourishment, it is also said to be without nourishment;
because form is deluded and ignorant, it is also said to be deluded and ignorant.
Because form is devoid of benevolence, it is also said to be without benevolence;
because form is devoid of a self-soul, it is also said to be without a self-soul;
because form is like a bundle of firewood, it is also said to be a bundle of firewood.
Because form is like grass, trees, walls, fences, tiles, stones, and the like, it is also described as being like grass, trees, walls, fences, tiles, stones, and the like;
because form is like the characteristic of deception, it is also described as the characteristic of deception;
because form consists of the four great elements, it is also described as the four great elements.
Because form is without sound, it is also said to be without sound;
because form is without informative intimation (*vijñapti*), it is also said to be without informative intimation;
because form is unapprehendable, it is also said to be unapprehendable.
Because form is pure in mindfulness, it is also called "purity of mindfulness";
because form arises through conditions, it is also called "arising through conditions";
because form is uninterrupted, it is also called "the uninterrupted."
Because form is impermanent, it is also said to be impermanent;
because form is like a house, it is also said to be like a house;
because form is without sensation, it is also said to be without sensation.
Because form arises from demerit and merit, it is also called demerit and merit;
because the dharma-realm of form is suffering, it is also called the dharma-realm;
because form abides within the dharma-realm, it is also called abiding in the dharma-realm.
Because form is unmoving within the fundamental limit of the dharma-realm, it is also called the "fundamental limit";
because form is without self, it is also called "selfless";
because form is without sensation, it is also called "without sensation."
Because form has no burden, it is also said to be without burden;
because form has no thought, it is also said to be without thought;
because form has no timidity, it is also said to be without timidity.
Because form is immeasurable, it is also said to be immeasurable;
because form is boundless, it is also said to be boundless;
because that form is fundamentally pure in the Way, it is also said that the Way is pure.
Because form is empty and so forth, it is also said to be empty and so forth;
because form is fundamentally pure in *nirvāṇa*, it is also said that *nirvāṇa* is pure.

To state the essentials: the five aggregates, the six sense-fields, all phenomena, all names, physical forms, phrases and tracks, paths, specialized chapters, and all bodies of consciousness—all enter into what is revealed by this single sound.

"It is said that the treasury chest of the four great jewel-treasures is the inexhaustible wisdom; the wisdom consulted and revealed therein is likewise inexhaustible, and this treasury chest of the holy Dharma scriptures also enters into that inexhaustible wisdom."

The wisdom thus proclaimed is the dhāraṇī of the inexhaustible treasury of Dharma; all that is expounded and propagated—even if one were to praise this virtue of the inexhaustible treasury of Dharma for an eon, or even beyond an eon—it would still not be exhausted.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"What is called the immeasurable *dhāraṇī* of retrogression and advancement?
It revolves within that state, severing the calculation of permanence and returning to its source."

The twelve links of dependent origination proceed from ignorance as a condition to volitional formations; from volitional formations to consciousness; from consciousness to name-and-form; from name-and-form to the six sense bases; from the six sense bases to contact; from contact to craving; from craving to feeling; from feeling to clinging; from clinging to existence; from existence to birth; from birth to old age, sickness, and death; from death to lamentation, sorrow, and mental distress; and from these they lead to the affliction of the great suffering of the five aggregates.

Having eliminated ignorance, the great affliction of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, craving, feeling, sensation, existence, birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, sorrow, and despair has been forever removed.
Because he enters the bottomless from the immeasurable by means of infinite gateways, it is therefore called the *dhāraṇī* of the immeasurable withdrawal and advancement.
"To both receive and to relinquish is called revolving; that which neither receives nor relinquishes is what is meant by this.
To both arise and to cease is why it is called revolving; that which neither arises nor ceases is what is meant by this."

To be joined with worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) and thereby give rise to contention and litigation is what is meant by "revolving"; to return to fundamental purity, being without attachment or negligence—this is what is meant.

To have practices regarding all phenomena, accepting what is appropriate and inappropriate, or mindfulness and lack of mindfulness, is what is meant by "reversing"; to be without ideation (*asaṃjñā*), without mindfulness (*asmṛti*), and without acceptance or rejection—this is what is meant.
That various views arise due to causes and conditions is what is meant by "revolving"; to sever these views of causes and conditions—this is what is meant.
The reason why name and form revolve and turn back is that there is neither name nor form; this is what is meant.
The reason why the conditioned and the unconditioned revolve and turn back is that one is purified within the three spheres; this is what is meant.
The reason why the internal and the external revolve and turn back is that one does not dwell in consciousness; this is what is meant.
The reason why the retributions of sin and merit are overturned is that there is no such thing as the retribution of sin or merit;
the reason why the good and the unwholesome are overturned is that there is ultimately nothing practiced, abiding neither in the good nor in evil;
the reason why the out-flowing and the non-out-flowing are overturned is that there are no two distinct things.

This refers to the fact that what is obscured by calamities and transgressions, and the darkness of worldly toil (*kleśa*), are fundamentally pure and spontaneous; this is what is meant by "reversion.
This refers to the fact that calculating a self and not-self are fundamentally pure at their limit; this is what is meant by "reversion.
This refers to the fact that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and *nirvāṇa* are fundamentally pure at their source, for all phenomena are *nirvāṇa*; this is what is meant by "reversion."
"Yes, son of good family!
This is the exposition of the immeasurable *dhāraṇī* of advancing and retreating without limit.

If there is a bodhisattva who dwells in this immeasurable *dhāraṇī* of advancing and retreating, whose will is non-arising and who penetrates that phenomena are without origination, they could not reach the end of expounding the sūtras throughout incalculable hundreds of thousands of kalpas; for the wisdom of this *dhāraṇī* is subtle and profound in its meaning."

If one enters this Dharani of Immeasurable Retreat and Advancement with wisdom and proclaims its meaning, one will be able to awaken to and understand the gateway to the pure path, illuminating the darkness so that nothing remains obscure.
The Buddha addressed the son of good family:
"What is called the *dhāraṇī* of the ocean-seal mind?
It is like this, son of good family!"

Within all the world-systems of the four quarters, whatever forms and appearances there may be—such as mountains, valleys, trees, and all varieties of growing grasses and medicinal herbs; the radiance of the sun and moon, luminous gems, water-splendors, and the appearance of blazing lightning; the appearance of provinces, great kingdoms, districts, counties, towns, dwellings, and houses; gardens, groves, bathing pools, rivers, springs, and flowing streams; the activities of worldly existence, the observation of one’s own physical form—whether beautiful or ugly, good or evil, or of middling or superior quality—all such forms and their returns depend upon the great ocean without distinction. This is what is called the great ocean.
If a bodhisattva abides in this *dhāraṇī* of the ocean-seal mind, they equally seal the bodies of all sentient beings and likewise equally expound the teachings of written words.

Using the seal of an impartial mind, they seal both sentient beings and the Buddhas endowed with the ten powers; the infinite Great Dharma proclaimed from their mouths—all these scriptures emerge from the mouths of these bodhisattvas, being sealed by the seal of the Buddhas.
The Dharma taught brings boundless joy.
When expounding the seals of all dharmas, there is no wisdom that is to be sealed; whatever is preached is entirely the Seal of the Tathāgata.
One discerns the various truths, yet that which is without a seal has forever nothing upon which to act, and the mind is naturally tranquil.
As for the Seal of Detachment, one attains the dharma of detachment and the practice of purity;
as for the Seal of Crossing Over, that which is expounded reaches the ultimate, penetrating all things without exception;
as for the Seal of Designation, it proclaims all names and phenomena, each being clearly understood.
The seal of joy eliminates desire, greed, negligence, and attachment;
the ten seals are the fulfillment of the ten powers;
the seal of being armored against fear thoroughly purifies all mental states.
The Seal of Burning Away causes one to abandon burning heat;
the Seal of the Six Causes one to accomplish the six supernormal powers;
the Seal of the Left-Shoulder-Throwing causes one to cast aside heterodox paths.
The seal of "A" (its) signifies the teaching of ultimate truth;
the seal of "Ri" signifies that one's practice accords with reality;
the seal of "Tsa" signifies the eradication of all fundamental roots of existence.
The *kā* seal signifies being free from all conditioned activities;
the *sa* seal proclaims the manifestation of ultimate sincerity because it reveals power;
the *jā* seal signifies the deliverance from birth, old age, and death.
The seal of its resolve refers to the purity of the mind;
the seal of its realm refers to the indestructibility of the dharma-realm;
the seal of its tranquility refers to the perfection of serene detachment.
The seal of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mudrā*) is so called because it is quiescent, void, and non-existent, such that there is nothing that cannot be exhausted;
the seal of exhaustion (*kṣaya-mudrā*) is so called because it dissolves and exhausts all conceptualization, such that wisdom does not arise;
the seal of establishment (*sthiti-mudrā*) is so called because the mind of awakening dwells in the truth.
The Seal of Knowledge distinguishes all categories of sentient beings;
the Universal Seal proclaims all that arises and declines;
the Seal of Existence awakens to and discerns both existence and non-existence.
The "seal of greed" eliminates the obstacles of greed, lust, anger, hatred, and delusion;
the "seal of self" means that one's own person has already attained penetration and realized perfect enlightenment;
the "seal of spontaneity" means that the body itself is liberated.
The seal of "morning" means that in the morning one spontaneously relinquishes all signs of attachment;
the seal of "number" means the eradication and expulsion of their root source;
the seal of "place" means knowing all things as they truly are in every place.
The seal of non-existence signifies that there are no manifold distinctions;
the seal of fruition signifies the attainment of the realization of the fruit;
the seal of the aggregates signifies the removal of all hindrances of the aggregates.
The seal of swiftness is because it is free from the sickness of deviance;
the seal of giving is because one attains the fragrance of the incense of generosity and precepts;
the seal of firmness is because one has already reached the severance of stubborn and rigid natures.
As for the ultimate seal (*akṣara-mudrā*), it thoroughly elucidates written characters and unfolds their fundamental source.
"In this way, son of good family!
When a bodhisattva preaches the Dharma and expounds various texts, they fully know all seals of textual expression; this is called the ocean-seal entrance to the *dhāraṇī* gate."
The Buddha addressed the son of good family:
"What is called the Lotus Array Dhāraṇī?

If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters an assembly and, wherever he dwells, proceeds to preach the sūtras, whenever he makes such a proclamation, lotuses of exquisite and wondrous color will immediately spring up there."

As soon as the Bodhisattva sat upon the lotus flower in mid-air, a rain of lotus flowers fell. Furthermore, each of those lotus flowers produced various kinds of sounds, preaching the Dharma—speaking only of profound meanings, without any mixed phrases or ornate teachings—citing authoritative scriptures and metaphors, drawing from the essentials of the true canon, and analyzing the ultimate significance of the teachings.

The twelve divisions of the scriptures are: first, the *sūtra* of what has been heard; second, the *sūtra* of attainment; third, the *sūtra* of listening; fourth, the *sūtra* of analysis; fifth, the *sūtra* of manifestation; sixth, the *sūtra* of timely response; seventh, the *sūtra* of birth; eighth, the *vaipulya* (extensive) *sūtra*; ninth, the *sūtra* of marvelous events; tenth, the *sūtra* of parables; eleventh, the *sūtra* of abiding understanding; twelfth, the *sūtra* of practice.
The Dharma he expounds causes all who hear it to immediately exhaust all suffering.
Thus, the Bodhisattva naturally exerts diligence without relinquishing his constant meditative concentration.
At that time, the sūtras expounded by Padma appropriately sever all suffering and perform the work of a Buddha.

Furthermore, from every single pore of that Bodhisattva, light rays issued forth and were transformed into lotus flowers; upon each of these lotus flowers, a Bodhisattva was manifested, who proceeded to the countless, boundless Buddha-fields of the ten directions to pay homage to and appear before the various Buddhas.
"It is so, son of good family!
This is called the Lotus Adornment Entrance to the Dhāraṇī Gate.
The Buddha further addressed the son of good family:
"What is meant by 'entering the gate of the unimpeded dhāraṇī'?

It means that even if one does not forget a single word after it has been spoken, nor two, three, four, or even up to a thousand words, one shall never forget them in whatever place one is born; furthermore, one will be able to recognize and remember hundreds, thousands, and even billions of various teachings."

He proclaims [the Dharma] for the sake of the multitude, never neglecting it from lifetime to lifetime; his faculties are harmonious and joyful, his complexion is peerless, and he stands preeminent among the masses, delighting all people without any resentment or agitation.

They may hear what is taught by the speakers from as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in immeasurable Ganges Rivers; or they may penetrate and traverse as many Buddha-lands as there are motes of dust in a Buddha-field. Regarding these various Dharma-gates thus expounded, they employ skillful means according to the occasion.

Furthermore, that Dharma-gate simultaneously pervades all Buddha-lands, as numerous as the atoms within those worlds; whether it be two, three, four, or five up to ten, a hundred, a thousand, or immeasurable [worlds], the sound of what is taught accords with the voice [of beings] yet remains without attachment and without abiding.

Their voices were gentle and harmonized with the hearts of the multitude; their words were beautiful and timely, their principles elegant and subtle, never failing in propriety, so that all rejoiced and entered the gate of non-obstruction.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"What is called the dhāraṇī of entering into discernment?
It is to thoroughly understand its meaning, such that the wisdom of the proclaimed intent is inexhaustible."
Regarding the analysis of phenomena, the correct wisdom proclaimed therein cannot be conceptualized;
regarding analysis according to the occasion, the clear wisdom explained therein cannot be exhausted;
regarding analytical eloquence, the correct knowledge proclaimed therein has no limit or bottom.

When a Bodhisattva has attained such wisdom, all sentient beings in the eastern direction can be gathered together in one place; though each expresses themselves according to their own will—with diverse languages and various sounds—and challenges the Bodhisattva with questions according to their own capacities and the extent of their knowledge, he is able to respond to them all and fully elucidate their meanings.

It is the same for the south, the west, the north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir; when they come to challenge the Bodhisattva and each ask about the meaning, he simultaneously and exhaustively responds to them all.

According to the clarity or turbidity of their voices, they fully comprehend various kinds of speech; each, following their own original mind, attains entry into the Way. Each hears their respective words and sounds without confusion; thus, through a single sound they enter countless sounds, and through countless sounds they enter a single sound. This is called the *dhāraṇī* of "Distinguished Adornment."
The Buddha addressed the son of good family:
"What is called the dhāraṇī for establishing the perception of the Buddha?

If there is a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī, when he occupies the great Dharma-seat amidst the assembly, a jeweled canopy will constantly appear above his head in mid-air, and a transformation Buddha will dwell upon it—his body adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics of purple-gold color. By virtue of his own merit, he will stand close to the Tathāgata’s right hand."

As soon as the emanation Buddha raised his hand and placed it upon the head, at that very moment the Bodhisattva’s body was transformed into the form of a Buddha, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence; his speech was established to be like that of a Buddha, and his mind became imbued with the mind of a Buddha.

Being thus able to accomplish and establish such a Dharma, one enters the mental perceptions of all assemblies and proclaims the Dharma according to their fundamental practices. Whether for one day, two days, up to five days, half a month, one month, half a year, one year, five hundred years, or a thousand years—from following one’s own will at leisure for an infinite and incalculable number of years—one preaches the sutras for the sake of all sentient beings while remaining free from the need for food and drink. The scriptures proclaimed are inexhaustible; the body does not grow weary and the mind does not slacken, for all this is established by the Tathāgata.
When one is reached by the response of the Sage, one then attains the four great wisdoms.
What are these four?

First is the wisdom that understands the aspirations and conduct of all sentient beings; second is the analytical wisdom of phrases and sentences, which is thoroughly fluent and unobstructed; third is the wisdom of the infinite proclamations of sacred knowledge; and fourth is the wisdom that, according to the original nature of each person and the vehicle they study, comprehends their ultimate intent and explains the Dharma accordingly.
It is so, son of good family!
The Tathāgata has established this dhāraṇī; for those who enter its gateway, there is that which is proclaimed.
Furthermore, the meaning of this dhāraṇī can be expounded upon; it cannot be fully recorded, it is without limit, and it penetrates the realm of the Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvaguṇaviśuddharāja, beholding the Tathāgata speak such a meaning, praised him with these verses:
"Having abided [in meditation], he has proclaimed The practice of the eight dhāraṇīs;
What is declared by this vehicle Is attained through discernment and brings forth clear understanding."
Though he preaches billions of sutras, his words reach no limit;
yet in the distinctions of their meaning, the speaker suffers no loss.
The Buddha’s voice is exceedingly gentle, its resonance subtle and delightful.
Proclaiming throughout rivers of sands, across immeasurable thousands of Buddha-lands,
may sentient beings hear it and thereby attain nirvana;
this dhāraṇī is pure, its resonant voice reaching without limit.
Expounding for countless eons, their Dharma is inexhaustible;
a single phrase or word is proclaimed beyond what can be spoken.
All manner of elegant compositions, the wise master according to the occasion.
This is the treasury of the Dharma, the awakening mind without limit or bottom.
Having abandoned all that is non-receptive, their conduct is exceedingly pure;
they do not cling to the middle way, nor do they follow the realm of regression.
This courageous one universally contemplates the Dharma, practicing it with single-minded diligence;
having attained dhāraṇī, he eradicates the roots of all [afflictions].
Regarding all forms and species throughout the four quarters of the world, [he acts thus].
All are equal in their seal; like the ocean and rivers, they are free from discursive thought.
Whoever attains this dhāraṇī of the Ocean Seal, for that practitioner, the gateway of seals and all that is taught therein is inconceivable.
If he is in the midst of the great assembly, and the Great Being expounds the Dharma,
then from the midst of the void there falls a vast rain of various lotus flowers.
Furthermore, these lotus flowers proclaim billions of teachings of the Dharma.
The dhāraṇī of the Lotus Adornment possesses such pure virtues as these:
from a single utterance, verses of two, three, five,
or six lines are heard by each according to their own kind, yet the sounds are never confused.
Even with a thousand billion hundred nayutas of words, one could never exhaust them;
having attained dhāraṇī, what they realize is without obstruction.
Their eloquence in proclamation explains the meaning of the Dharma according to the occasion.
Sentient beings from the ten directions come, each raising difficult questions;
he dispels them all and resolves their doubts regarding the Vinaya.
Having attained this dhāraṇī, such is what his mind realizes.
When such great beings and true sages sit upon high thrones,
the Buddhas stroke the crowns of their heads with their right hands;
these people attain eloquence that is no different from that of the Buddhas themselves.
Because he has attained this Buddha-transformation through the sublime and supreme dhāraṇī,
even if this bodhisattva were to attain such a dhāraṇī,
the virtues harbored within his mind would be boundless and beyond conception.
Even if one were to preach for billions of kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
extolling his merits, their scope could never be exhausted.
Like a lotus that arises spontaneously, he emerges throughout the three periods of time.
Firmly abiding like Mount Sumeru, his followers cannot move him.
Should he attain the supreme dhāraṇī,
his wisdom will flow everywhere, pervading the three periods of time.
If one is amidst a great assembly, Brave and fierce like a lion,
Taming all those of external paths, Subduing them so they may attain accomplishment.
Should one ever obtain This supreme dhāraṇī,
Wherever he travels, he completely casts off all fears.
His radiance surpasses the great light, illuminating according to the season.
His conduct is like water, washing away all impurities and defilements.
His conduct is like fire: signless and without thought;
His conduct is like wind: unattached to any sensory realm;
His conduct is like a physician: healing all ailments and misfortunes.
Bestowing the medicine of Dharma according to the time, providing relief through water and fire;
those who attain it possess the most supreme and wondrous dhāraṇī,
their wisdom free from anger or resentment as they explain the teachings in accordance with the faculties [of beings].
Their conduct is like the brightness of the moon, capable of dispelling the darkness of the multitude in the night;
their minds are equal, luminous, and upright, as they radiate great brilliance.
Those who attain this hold the supreme, peerless dhāraṇī.
Sentient beings come to gaze upon him, Beholding him without ever reaching satiety.
His conduct is like the light of the sun, Illuminating the darkness;
He opens the way for sentient beings of the three realms, Enabling them to attain awakening and understanding.
If one attains this supreme dhāraṇī,
the source of the afflictions of craving for the masses will be dried up;
their conduct will be like that of a king who governs his realm.
As taught by King Śāntamati, one should give the Dharma as it has been heard.
Whoever attains this supreme dhāraṇī will have nothing to receive and will not be attached to any states of existence.
Their conduct is like that of a dragon; their will is firm and possesses divine transformations.
They raise clouds and rain for all living beings, and likewise emit flashes of lightning.
Those who have attained this supreme dhāraṇī,
He pours forth the rain of all dharmas, extinguishing the heat of all afflictions;
his conduct is like that of Śakra, yet he is not deluded by appearances,
for his mind is vast and he contemplates the Dharma.
Those who have attained this supreme dhāraṇī,
all those gathered in the assembly gaze upon his countenance;
in the practice of his compassion, he wanders equally like Brahmā.
Peerless among all, they come to be born in this world.
Those who have attained this supreme dhāraṇī will be born in the Brahma-heaven, remaining ever pure wherever they dwell.
Thus one achieves the five great supernormal powers, always transcending and excelling the multitudes;
one wanders through hundreds of thousands of Buddha-lands, beyond calculation and inconceivable.
Whoever attains this supreme dhāraṇī, [shall possess these qualities].
He makes offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, countless in number;
praised by all those Buddhas, wherever he may dwell,
they all take pity on him and regard him as their only son.
Whoever attains this supreme dhāraṇī,
before long shall achieve the merit of a Buddha;
their eloquence will be vast and far-reaching, and what they expound will be inexhaustible.
They expound various subtle and wondrous, innumerable sūtras.
Those who have attained this supreme dhāraṇī possess conduct as adorned as a floral garland and eloquence like a flowing spring.
With a firm resolve among the assembly, awakened and thoroughly proficient,
their wisdom is boundless and their conduct is like space.
Those who have attained this supreme dhāraṇī—
He shall be free from pride, abandoning flattery and self-importance;
with wisdom and skillful means, he shall roam at ease,
able to practice with diligence, and should cultivate loving-kindness and compassion.
Whoever attains this supreme dhāraṇī shall completely eliminate all the defilements of conditioned existence;
they will understand the speech of sentient beings and discern the goodness or evil of what is said.
Having understood the inclinations of all people and the activities of all their faculties,
those who have attained this supreme dhāraṇī shall find that the meaning of what they proclaim can never be exhausted.
Diligence, divine concentration, and mental focus, The faculties and the five powers,
The factors of enlightenment and the path—
such as these, Are supreme in their tranquility. Whoever attains this Supreme dhāraṇī,
He then contemplates all phenomena, attaining a state of profound purity;
regarding the various perfections (pāramitās), he has already reached the further shore.
His mind is steadfast and clearly penetrating, and through wisdom he thoroughly understands the four foundations of mindfulness.
Having attained this supreme dhāraṇī,
that person naturally understands it; dwelling securely in all practices,
they become serenely tranquil, harmonious and benevolent, free from negligence.
In their conduct of dignified deportment and ritual propriety, they dwell with discernment and composure.
Those who have attained this supreme dhāraṇī have never been subject to the afflictions of the mundane world.
Having accomplished such a dharma-illusion, with a mind-nature free from defilement,
wherever one is born from a womb, one cannot be stained by impurities.
Whoever attains this supreme dhāraṇī, [is thus purified].
Then they dwell upon lotuses, standing before all Buddhas;
their body, speech, and mind possess no deficiency in majestic power,
universally giving rise to all wisdom, which flows everywhere to reach all sentient beings.
Whoever attains this supreme dhāraṇī,
established through the transformations of all Buddhas, shall preach the Dharma and stand firm;
having already perfected great wisdom, they shall practice the Way for the sake of sentient beings.
Throughout incalculable eons, one could never exhaust the praise of its virtues.
For whoever attains this supreme dhāraṇī,
even if they wished to offer praise, they would be unable to reach its ultimate source.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra:
"Excellent, excellent!
You have skillfully explained this entry into the practice of the dhāraṇī of praise."
Why is this so? Because this Dharma is spontaneous;

it has nothing upon which to rely and does not depend on others, for once one has entered it, one need no longer inquire further about the profound and wondrous gateways of dhāraṇī from the Buddhas of the past.
"For this reason, son of good family, you should form this contemplation: they are equal and without distinction.

Chapter Twenty-Four: On the Past.
The Buddha addressed the son of good family:

"In the distant past, in an age long ago—immeasurable and incalculable eons, vast and remote beyond conception—there was a Buddha named Vimalaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, World-Honored One."
The world was named "Excellently Free from Defilement," and the eon was called "Illumination.
That realm was pure; its ground was made of lapis lazuli, as clear as a bright mirror, and as level as the palm of a hand.
The soil of that realm is of lapis lazuli; there grow trees made of the seven treasures, whose branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are likewise composed of jewels.

Furthermore, various precious lotus flowers arise spontaneously, as large as chariot wheels, in many colors; those who see them feel joy in their hearts, for their forms are exquisite and their fragrance is pure and most beautiful.

The jeweled lattices, dwellings, and monasteries, as well as the clothing, food, and drink of the devas and humans, were just like those in the sixth heaven, the Heaven of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods.
The people are pure and refined, walking with serene composure; their lust, anger, and delusion are meager and slight.
Their conduct and teachings are such that in that Buddha-world there are no sun or moon.

That Buddha, Stainless Radiance, emits a great brilliance from his body that pervades all buddha-fields; it is perpetually bright day and night, such that dawn and dusk cannot be distinguished—when the lotuses close, it is known as darkness, and when the lotuses open, it is known as light.

“The assembly of bodhisattvas of that Tathāgata Vimalaprabha consists of eight hundred billion; there are immeasurable and incalculable numbers of both ordained bodhisattvas and lay bodhisattvas who have established themselves in the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.”

In that Buddha-land, the heterodox teachings are unheard of and there are no other vehicles; there is only the cultivation of the Mahāyāna. All practices are pure and refined, and beings are established in non-retrogression.
World-Honored One, how do you preach the Dharma for them?
He expounded only the wisdom of emptiness and the teachings of emptiness and signlessness.
"The Buddha's lifespan shall be half an eon.
The dwellings of the people shall consist of various kinds of jewels, and the Buddha’s every step shall accord with the seasons."
The same is true for the various devas.

Those who dwell in houses and pavilions erected upon the earth are called humans; those who reside in houses, mansions, and towers established in the void of space are called devas. There is no difference between them in matters such as rising and sitting, or eating and drinking.
Furthermore, in that Buddha-field there were no longer any secular rulers; only the World-Honored One, Vimalaprabha, was the supreme sovereign of the Great Dharma.

Devas and humans came to serve him as their teacher without any distinction; they had no different names, their activities were not separate, and they harbored no divergent thoughts. They did nothing but revere the Tathāgata, inquiring about and receiving the sūtras, and contemplating their meaning.
There are no women there, nor any names for sinful states, nor any transgressions of sensual desire.
The sentient beings in that land study only three practices:
first, the precepts; second, guarding the mind; and third, training in wisdom.
What is meant by precept?
It is to practice all forms of supernormal wisdom, maintaining mindfulness without abandonment, and relinquishing all conditioned activities.
What is meant by guarding the mind?
Abiding in meditative concentration, one attains the supernormal powers.
What is meant by "wisdom"?
Abiding in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one attains analytical discernment.
Thus it is, son of good family!
To train in this manner is called "training in transcendence.

These bodhisattvas do not receive formal prohibitory precepts; their land is pure and magnificent in such a way that the World-Honored One’s preaching of the Dharma is solemn, wondrous, and peerless, standing out as beyond all comparison.

At that time, among the bodhisattvas in that buddha-field, there was a bodhisattva named Prabhāketu. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
What is meant by the term "dhāraṇī"?
In what state does a bodhisattva abide so that they can uphold everything spoken by all Buddhas and expound it for sentient beings to bring their minds to joy?
The Buddha told Prabhāketu:
"Furthermore, son of good family!
There is a dhāraṇī named Ratnāvabhāsa; when a bodhisattva abides in this, they receive all that is preached by the Buddhas and gladden the hearts of sentient beings."
Prabhāketu asked again:
“We only pray that the Tathāgata will proclaim the Ratnaprabhāsa-dhāraṇī; having heard its principles and meanings, we shall uphold them according to the teaching and attain this dhāraṇī.”
Then, the Buddha Vimalaprabha immediately spoke these verses in praise of the Bodhisattva Prabhaketu:
"If you wish to attain the Jewel Radiance, Forever eliminate all defilements and impurities,
Be unstained by stains within the midst of stains, And relinquish every single form of attachment."
The mind is ever pure and free from attachment; this is the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī.
One who attains this dhāraṇī possesses a brilliance that illuminates all;
their body and speech are pure, and the nature of their radiance is free from defilement.
Cultivating a mind of loving-kindness with equanimity is the *dhāraṇī* of Ratnaprabhāsa;
Having already transcended the thirty-two [marks], and being liberated from all conceptualizations,
one is then free from all expectations— this is the *dhāraṇī* of Ratnaprabhāsa.
Wherever one enters through practice, one embraces valor;
Great virtue is like space, and clear understanding is like empty stillness— This is the *dhāraṇī* of the Jewel Radiance.
It does not sever the Three Jewels, And it cuts off the three defilements and the three periods of time.
Exhausting the source of all suffering—this is the Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī;
It harms greed, lust, hatred, and delusion, removing all dust and defilements.
The jewel-tree of the mind of desire— The Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī is supreme.
All sounds that exist—superior, middling, and inferior in the world—enter into every resonance;
the Jewel Radiance sustains this freedom from defilement.
Through diligent application to the profound Dharma, one masters the meanings of countless sublime phrases.
Not clinging to self or person, the dhāraṇī is free from these two;
having attained analytical eloquence, one firmly abides in the four paths.
The four dhyānas shake the Brahma realm—this is the Ratnaprabhāsa-dhāraṇī.
The meaning of the foremost Dharma-treasury, He opens up and receives the practice of the four immeasurables;
Venerably cultivating the five supernormal powers, He is the Honored One of the Jewel-Radiance Dhāraṇī;
Truly abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness, He constantly accords with the four right efforts.
Reverently relying upon the four bases of psychic power is the dhāraṇī of the Jewel Radiance;
Having already received and upheld the five faculties and established oneself in the five powers,
Possessing the seven factors of enlightenment is the dhāraṇī of the Jewel Radiance.
Reverently following the eightfold path, one transforms through the contemplation of tranquility;
reaching luminous liberation, this is the dhāraṇī of Jewel Radiance.
Sporting in the stages where one dwells, one draws near to and accords with the path of liberation.
Severing all afflictions—this is the *ratnolkā-dhāraṇī*;
Illuminating all worlds, the site of enlightenment of tranquil light;
With pure eyes shining far and wide—this is the *ratnolkā-dhāraṇī*.
The divine eye is purified in this way; the wisdom-eye illuminates the darkness.
The pure eye is the eye of Dharma; this is the purity of the Buddha-eye.
This dust is purified of Māra; herein the five aggregates are eliminated and destroyed.
They are also purified of the Māra of death; by the power of taking refuge, they subdue Māra.
Abiding in this dhāraṇī, they reach lands numbering in the hundreds of millions of nayutas, where they behold buddhas in the tens of billions and hear these supreme sūtras.
By listening to the vast and wondrous Dharma, one’s mental power embraces the dhāraṇīs;
discerning their meanings and purports, one proclaims them for the sake of gods and worldlings.
With a clear mind and awakened intent, one understands and realizes the retributions that correspond to actions.
That Dharma enters into wisdom; abiding in dhāraṇī, one attains this.
Eloquence is without obstruction; the three types of penetration and the three eyes are purified.
One attains the meaning of the three liberations and, through diligence, reaches dhāraṇī.
Countless *dhāraṇīs*, infinitely and immeasurably expounded—
Upon attaining this supreme *dhāraṇī*, one obtains everything.
Their meditations and doors of liberation, Their meditative absorptions and ultimate *samādhis*—
Delighting in supernormal powers, one should enter this dhāraṇī.
Just as all the waters of the ocean, the king of rivers, flow back to the myriad streams and rivers, so it is with this supreme dhāraṇī:
the gateways to the Dharma are immeasurable.
Entering into the inexhaustible intention, one fully understands infinite wisdom;
its merit is boundless, having attained this through the practice of *dhāraṇī*.
With physical forms and manifold marks of excellence, and with a lineage and wisdom that are pure, one attains this state.
With palms as stainless as precious jewels, they have attained such dhāraṇīs;
entering the profound and essential treasury, they embrace the patience of non-arising,
abide on the stage of non-retrogression, and preach these dhāraṇīs.
Countless bodhisattvas, seeking the unsurpassed path,
Having attained this dhāraṇī, find it no difficulty to become Buddhas.
The Most Victorious Ones of the ten directions, out of compassion for sentient beings, preach the Dharma.
One who has attained this dhāraṇī possesses uninterrupted eloquence;
they delight billions of sentient beings by knowing their faculties and the inclinations of their minds.
Even before a word has been spoken, one who has attained this dhāraṇī [achieves this].
Then they turn the wheel of Dharma, delivering hundreds of thousands of sentient beings;
establishing them in the Noble Vehicle, they dwell courageously in this dhāraṇī.
Even if one were to praise their meritorious achievements for countless nayutas of kalpas, it would not exhaust them.
"Even one who has attained this dhāraṇī cannot fully exhaust its exposition.
"In this way, son of good family!

When the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vimalaprabha had finished preaching this dhāraṇī, thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas within the great assembly attained this dhāraṇī, and the Bodhisattva Prabhāketu likewise attained this Ratnaprabhāsa-dhāraṇī."
"O son of noble family!
What do you think?
Was the Bodhisattva Prabhāketu at that time anyone other than this person?"
Do not hold such a view.
Why is this? It is because you yourself are that very person.

For this reason, Sarvaśūra, you are now capable of delivering all those who are defiled and evil; furthermore, regarding these questions to the Tathāgata, you have mastered the verses and phrases, being free from hesitation and having resolved the net of your doubts.

For this reason, the valiant one of the present age has fully set forth his previous questions; he does not find it difficult to resolve these dhāraṇīs from the Tathāgata, proclaiming them to illuminate the world so that the minds of beings may become expansive and clear.

“O Benevolent One, because you have attained mastery through the practice of the Dharma-eye contemplation, you have now once again obtained this dhāraṇī. With courageous resolve, you shall proclaim it yourself.

Chapter 25: The Chapter on the Foundation of Wisdom and the Deeds of Insight from the Mahākaruṇā-sūtra. At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa was present in that assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How does a bodhisattva attain the *Ratnaprabhāsa* dhāraṇī, such that having already acquired it, they no longer forget it, thereby benefiting sentient beings and establishing their own karmic deeds through the power of the dhāraṇī?”
The Buddha told Zhiji: "Noble son!

If there is a bodhisattva who abides in the root of wisdom and performs the work of wisdom, they shall then attain the *dhāraṇī* of Jewel Radiance; no longer being subject to forgetfulness, they will benefit all sentient beings."
The Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
Pray explain for us: what is meant by the ‘root of wisdom’?”
"What is meant by the karma of wisdom?
The Buddha said, "Listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it for you."
The Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa received the instruction and listened attentively.
The Buddha addressed the son of good family:

"Listen closely to the essential meaning and keep it in mind; this is the root of wisdom (*jñāna*). To then fully explain the Dharma as you have heard it for others is the work of insight (*prajñā*)."
To observe and discern is the root of wisdom; to inspire the assembly so that they attain understanding is the activity of insight.
To observe in accordance with reality and know its source is the root of wisdom; to transform and establish sentient beings according to the times is the activity of insight.
To cultivate impartial conduct without partiality is the root of wisdom; to uphold upright practice without harboring heterodox doubts is the activity of insight.
The mind being without arising and entirely without attachment is the root of wisdom; though the mind does not arise, being able to proclaim the sūtras is the work of insight.
Contemplating in quietude with a tranquil mind is the root of wisdom; the body and mind being at ease and free from agitation is the work of insight.

The mind always delighting in oneness so that myriad affairs do not arise is the root of wisdom; recognizing the path of the One Vehicle and not deviating from or abandoning it is the work of insight.
To cultivate serene detachment and universally observe all phenomena is the root of wisdom; to attain clear liberation and eliminate all darkness is the karma of insight.

To adhere to single-mindedness and the three gates of liberation is the root of wisdom; to realize and testify to the events of the past, future, and present through the three types of supernormal knowledge is the karma of insight.
To faithfully follow the discourse of the Way without doubt is the root of wisdom; to cross over all obstacles and hindrances is the karma of insight.
A mind that is not timid, but harbors courage and wisdom, is the root of knowledge; the rest of body and mind, free from frantic striving, is the practice of wisdom.
A mind that is serene and not impulsive is the root of knowledge; contemplation that is vast and expansive, accompanied by full mindfulness and recollection, is the practice of wisdom.

To immediately awaken to and restrain oneself whenever there is transgression is the root of knowledge; for the mind to be constantly in right concentration and attain its proper state is the practice of wisdom.

To practice the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and to fully expound the teachings on the mind is the root of knowledge; for the mind to have no abiding place and no conceptualization is the work of wisdom.

To uphold the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) so as to abandon the roots [of affliction] is the root of knowledge; having already purified the source and eliminated all blemishes, to clearly comprehend all phenomena is the work of wisdom.

To cultivate and train in the bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*) so as to rise up suddenly and weightlessly is the root of knowledge; having no further activity yet possessing far-reaching spiritual power is the work of wisdom.
Cultivating the five faculties so that their source is eternally tranquil is the root of wisdom; discerning the ultimate destination of all faculties is the work of insight.
Abiding in the five powers so as to be immovable is the root of wisdom; subduing the dust of demonic afflictions so that desires do not arise is the work of insight.

Thoroughly understanding the seven factors of enlightenment and attaining the patience of compliance is the root of wisdom; discerning that all karmic actions are naturally spontaneous is the work of insight.

To gather [teachings] from various paths with courage and fluency, without obstruction, is the root of wisdom (*jñāna*); to distinguish between what is not the Dharma and establish it within the Dharma, using the metaphor of a floating raft, is the activity of insight (*prajñā*).

To clearly recognize suffering and its origin while cultivating the path is the root of wisdom; to clearly realize the truth of cessation where the root of wisdom is inexhaustible is the activity of insight.
To recite the scriptures and understand their phrases and meanings is the root of wisdom; having mastered the scriptures and being able to practice them accordingly is the activity of insight.
To be able to retain and uphold all that one hears is the root of wisdom; to guide the multitude toward the various meanings of the Path without contradicting their principles is the work of insight.
To experience sounds and echoes without attachment is the root of wisdom; to accord with the scriptures and discern their correct purport is the work of insight.
To contemplate all phenomena as being entirely impermanent is the root of wisdom; to fully understand that there is nothing to be practiced among all dharmas is the work of insight.
To contemplate that all myriad things are entirely suffering is the root of wisdom; to reckon that all dharmas are fundamentally empty and non-existent is the practice of insight.
To examine all dharmas and find no self is the root of wisdom; to observe that all sentient beings are fundamentally and entirely pure is the practice of insight.
To hear the Dharma of the True Truth without harboring fear is the root of wisdom; to discern the ultimate destination of all dharmas is the practice of insight.
To contemplate the profound stillness of *nirvāṇa* with serene detachment is the root of wisdom; that all phenomena are fundamentally pure and quiescent is the work of insight.

To hear the meaning of the scriptures without harboring hesitation or the difficulty of fear is the root of wisdom; to clearly understand their principles and know their true destination is the work of insight.

To listen to the Dharma with careful scrutiny, without doubting its depth and thoroughness, is the root of wisdom; to possess the eloquence to distinguish the teachings and analyze their fundamental nature is the work of insight.
Listening to all sounds without fear is the root of wisdom; expounding them at the appropriate times so that each may find their proper place is the work of insight.
Hearing the Buddha’s eloquence without harboring weakness or timidity is the root of wisdom; recognizing that eloquence and proclaiming it everywhere is the work of insight.

For the sake of sentient beings, compassionately upholding the practice of the Dharma is the root of wisdom; not abandoning compassionate pity and bestowing kindness upon the multitude is the work of insight.
To give rise to compassion for oneself as well as for others is the root of wisdom; to be unattached to both these matters while giving rise to unobstructed compassion is the work of insight.
To love and rejoice in the Dharma with a heart of gladness is the root of wisdom; to be neither elated nor dejected, free from transgression or loss, is the work of insight.
To be free from the bonds of affliction and harmful things through contemplation is the root of wisdom; to clearly understand the movements and postures of one’s own body is the work of insight.
Constantly keeping the Buddha in mind with no other thoughts is the root of wisdom; clearly realizing the Dharma-body without any dependence is the work of insight.
Constantly keeping the scriptures in mind and understanding their principles is the root of wisdom; being able to discern and remain free from the phenomena of desire is the work of insight.
Constantly keeping the Noble Assembly in mind and making offerings to all paths is the root of wisdom; attaining the unconditioned and observing the dustless state is the work of insight.

Constantly recollecting generous giving to relieve all who are in poverty and distress is the root of wisdom; relinquishing all defilements and conforming to the intent of the Way is the karma of insight.

Constantly recollecting the precepts and being self-restrained is the root of wisdom; having already practiced the conduct of non-apprehension and distinguishing the various prohibitions and precepts is the karma of insight.

Constantly recollecting the divine messengers so that the mind may be opened and liberated is the root of wisdom; when one’s Dharma is pure and detached from defiled dust, this is the karma of insight.
If one hears something and elucidates its meaning, this is the root of wisdom (*jñāna*); if one does not compare oneself with worldly people, this is the activity of insight (*prajñā*).
That one’s undertakings are settled and without error is the root of wisdom; that one fully understands the absence of action and the absence of retribution is the activity of insight.
Not harboring arrogance and not being self-important is the root of wisdom; attaining ultimate insight and thereby accomplishing great wisdom is the activity of insight.
To reflect upon one’s own conduct is the root of wisdom; to cause both oneself and others to arise in these two matters together is the work of insight.
To be able to uphold the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma-sūtras is the root of wisdom; to discern the eighty-four thousand modes of practice is the work of insight.
To understand the times and proclaim the sūtras accordingly is the root of wisdom; to preach the sūtras as appropriate without error or omission is the work of insight.

To transform sentient beings and establish them in the Way is the root of wisdom; to use the perfection of wisdom and skillful means to instruct sentient beings so that they are established in non-retrogression is the karma of insight.
To never fear birth within the five destinies is the root of wisdom; to provide much protection and guardianship wherever one is born is the karma of insight.
To diligently cultivate oneself until attaining the patience of the echo is the root of wisdom; to constantly practice cultivation without harboring any sense of self-birth is the karma of insight.

To personally attain the stage of compliant patience (*anulomikī-kṣānti*) is the root of wisdom; to achieve the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is the work of insight.

To resolve the mind to diligently cultivate the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*) is the root of wisdom; to transcendantly advance to the stage of the invincible (*abhiṣeka* or *anābhibhūta*) is the work of insight.

Having completed one's practice and sitting beneath the Bodhi tree is the root of wisdom; that which is to be fully understood—the severing of doubts and obstacles and the realization of equality—wherein, at the very moment of first generating the resolve, one accords with the truth according to the occasion and achieves the unsurpassed, right, and true path as the most perfect awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), is the work of insight.
The Buddha, wishing to further explain and clarify this meaning, then spoke in verse:
"If one listens to and receives his Dharma, And inquires with diligence and without negligence,
Such pure people Consult and revere the root of wisdom."
Having heard it, one is able to expound it; with a compassionate heart, one spreads it among all people.
Such a Bodhisattva is preeminent, performing the work of wisdom.
To contemplate with a virtuous mind is the very foundation of clear intelligence.
To analytically explain the sphere of practice is the work of wisdom;
to act in accordance with right mindfulness is the root of knowledge.
To speak of this practice to others is the work of wisdom.
When the mind reaches the state of non-arising, this is the very root of wisdom;
when mental activities have no destination, this is the function of insight.
Cultivating pure and upright conduct is the foundation of wisdom.
To proclaim, turn, and practice what is to be done is the work of wisdom;
To be single-mindedly devoted to the practice of the path of tranquility is the root of knowledge.
When body and mind do not conceive of a self, this is the work of wisdom.
To fear the habitual cycle of birth and death is the root of wisdom;
To delight in the path of the One Vehicle is the work of insight;
To take pleasure in tranquil contemplation is the root of wisdom.
Contemplating the matters of clarity and liberation is the activity of wisdom;
Diligently applying oneself to the three gates of liberation is the root of knowledge;
Clearly realizing the three types of penetrating knowledge is the activity of wisdom.
Thoroughly cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness is the root of wisdom;
being mindful of neither intention nor self is the work of insight.
Abandoning evil and practicing wholesome conduct is the root of wisdom.
To be fundamentally pure and free from these phenomena is the work of wisdom;
to diligently attain the four bases of psychic power is the root of knowledge.

Deep faith and pure liberation are the root of wisdom;

when one's resolve is clear and serene, this is the root of knowledge.
Not dwelling in any place whatsoever—this is the work of wisdom.
To personally realize the concentration of consciousness is the root of wisdom;
to practice pure and correct meditative attainment is the work of insight.
To skillfully establish the five faculties is the root of wisdom.

to practice the five powers is the root of knowledge;

understanding all phenomena is the activity of insight.

skillful means regarding the nature of suffering is the root of knowledge.

guiding and governing oneself according to the principles of meaning is the activity of insight.

to seek its principles as they correspond is the root of knowledge.

its nature being pure is the activity of insight.

to be thoroughly proficient in the teachings of the sūtras is the activity of insight.

Not departing from the Buddha’s eloquence is the root of knowledge.

that the mind attains neither duality nor liberation is the work of insight.

constantly contemplating the scriptures is the very root of knowledge.

to awaken to and realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the work of insight (*prajñā*).

to contemplate precepts with complete purity is the root of knowledge;
to abide in the untainted prohibitions is the activity of wisdom.

if one is mindful of the pure and further purified, this is the work of insight.
